The supper, served on new silverware, on Sèvres porcelain, and on damask linen, breathed substantial magnificence. Chevet had prepared the supper; the wines had been chosen by the most famous merchant on the Quai Saint-Bernard, a friend of Camusot, Matifat, and Cardot. Lucien, who for the first time saw Parisian luxury in operation, thus went from surprise to surprise, and concealed his astonishment like the man of wit, heart, and style that he was, in Blondet’s words.

As they crossed the drawing room, Coralie had whispered in Florine’s ear:—Get Camusot so thoroughly drunk for me that he will be obliged to remain asleep at your place.

—So you have _made_ your journalist? Florine replied.

—No, my dear, I love him! Coralie retorted, with an admirable little movement of her shoulders.

These words had resounded in Lucien’s ear, carried there by the fifth deadly sin. Coralie was admirably well dressed, and her attire skillfully brought her particular beauties into relief; for every woman has perfections of her own. Her dress, like Florine’s, had the merit of being made of a delightful new fabric called _silk muslin_, whose first offering belonged for a few days to Camusot, one of the Parisian providences of the Lyon factories, in his capacity as head of the Golden Cocoon. Thus love and attire, that cosmetic and that perfume of woman, heightened the attractions of the happy Coralie. An anticipated pleasure, one that will not escape us, exerts immense seductions upon young men. Perhaps certainty is, in their eyes, the whole attraction of houses of ill repute; perhaps it is the secret of long fidelities? Pure, sincere love, first love in short, joined to one of those fanciful fits of passion that excite these poor creatures, and also the admiration caused by Lucien’s great beauty, gave Coralie the wit of the heart.

—I would love you ugly and sick! she said in Lucien’s ear as she sat down at table.

What words for a poet! Camusot disappeared, and Lucien no longer saw him when he looked at Coralie. Could a man who was all enjoyment and all sensation, bored by the monotony of the provinces, drawn by the abysses of Paris, weary of poverty, tormented by his forced continence, tired of his monastic life in the Rue de Cluny and of his fruitless labors, withdraw from this brilliant feast? Lucien had one foot in Coralie’s bed and the other in the birdlime of the Newspaper, toward which he had run so hard without being able to catch it. After so many watches mounted in vain in the Rue du Sentier, he found the Newspaper seated at table, drinking chilled wine, merry and good-natured. He had just been avenged for all his sufferings by an article that, the very next day, was to pierce two hearts into which he had wished, but in vain, to pour the rage and pain with which he himself had been drenched. Looking at Lousteau, he said to himself:—There is a friend! never suspecting that Lousteau already feared him as a dangerous rival. Lucien had made the mistake of displaying all his wit: a dull article would have served him admirably. Blondet counterbalanced the envy devouring Lousteau by telling Finot that one had to capitulate to talent when it was of such strength. This judgment dictated Lousteau’s conduct: he resolved to remain Lucien’s friend and to come to an understanding with Finot in order to exploit so dangerous a newcomer by keeping him in need. It was a course quickly decided upon and understood in its full extent between the two men through two phrases spoken from ear to ear.

—He has talent.

—He will be demanding.

—Oh!

—Good!

—I never sup without fear with French journalists, said the German diplomat with calm and dignified good nature, looking at Blondet, whom he had seen at the Comtesse de Montcornet’s. There is a saying of Blücher’s that you have been charged with making come true.

—What saying? said Nathan.

—When Blücher arrived on the heights of Montmartre with Sacken in 1814—forgive me, gentlemen, for taking you back to that fatal day for you—Sacken, who was a brute, said: So we are going to burn Paris!—Take great care not to; France will die only of _that_! Blücher replied, pointing to the great canker they saw spread out at their feet, ardent and smoky, in the valley of the Seine. I bless God that there are no newspapers in my country, the minister resumed after a pause. I have not yet recovered from the terror caused me by that little fellow with the paper hat who, at ten years of age, possesses the reason of an old diplomat. And so, this evening, it seems to me that I am supping with lions and panthers who do me the honor of sheathing their claws in velvet.

—It is clear, said Blondet, that we can tell Europe, and prove to it, that Your Excellency vomited up a serpent this evening, that you nearly inoculated Mademoiselle Tullia, the prettiest of our dancers, with it, and, on that basis, make comments about Eve, the Bible, and the first and last sin. But do not be alarmed: you are our guest.

“I saw that perfectly well,” resumed the canon. “But at this moment you are saying to yourself: This Spanish canon is inventing anecdotes and squeezing history to prove to me that I have been too virtuous...”

Lucien began to smile when he saw his thoughts so accurately divined.

“Well then, young man, let us take facts that have passed into the realm of commonplace,” said the priest. “One day France is almost entirely conquered by the English; the king has only one province left. From the midst of the people two beings arise: a poor young girl, that same Joan of Arc of whom we were speaking; then a burgher named Jacques Cœur. The one gives her arm and the prestige of her virginity, the other gives his gold: the kingdom is saved. But the girl is captured!... The king, who can ransom the girl, lets her be burned alive. As for the heroic burgher, the king allows his courtiers, who make a quarry of him, to accuse him of capital crimes. The spoils of the innocent man, hunted down, surrounded, struck down by justice, enrich five noble houses... And the father of the Archbishop of Bourges leaves the kingdom, never to return, without a penny of his property in France, having no money of his own other than what he had entrusted to the Arabs, to the Saracens in Egypt. You may still say: These examples are very old; all this ingratitude has had three hundred years of Public Education, and the skeletons of that age are fabulous. Well then, young man, do you believe in France’s latest demigod, Napoleon? He kept one of his generals in disgrace; he made him a marshal only reluctantly and never willingly made use of him. That marshal’s name was Kellermann. Do you know why?..... Kellermann saved France and the First Consul at Marengo by a daring charge that was applauded amid blood and fire. That heroic charge was not even mentioned in the bulletin. The cause of Napoleon’s coldness toward Kellermann is also the cause of the disgrace of Fouché, of the Prince de Talleyrand: it is the ingratitude of King Charles VII, of Richelieu, ingratitude...”

“But, Father, supposing you were to save my life and make my fortune,” said Lucien, “you are thus making gratitude easy enough for me.”

“You little rascal,” said the abbé, smiling and taking Lucien by the ear to twist it with an almost royal familiarity, “if you were ungrateful to me, you would then be a strong man, and I would not hold it against you; but you have not reached that point yet, for, a mere schoolboy, you tried to become a master too soon. That is the failing of the French in your time. They have all been spoiled by Napoleon’s example. You resign your commission because you cannot obtain the epaulette you desire... But have you subordinated all your desires, all your actions, to a single idea?...”

“Alas! no,” said Lucien.

“You have been what the English call inconsistent,” resumed the canon with a smile.

“What does it matter what I have been, if I can no longer be anything!” Lucien replied.

“Let there be, behind all your fine qualities, a force semper virens,” said the priest, intent on showing that he knew a little Latin, “and nothing in the world will withstand you. I already love you well enough...”

Lucien smiled incredulously.

“Yes,” resumed the stranger, responding to Lucien’s smile, “you interest me as though you were my son, and I am powerful enough to speak to you with an open heart, as you have just spoken to me. Do you know what pleases me about you?... You have wiped the slate clean within yourself, and you can therefore listen to a course in morality that is taught nowhere; for men, when gathered in a crowd, are even more hypocritical than they are when their interests compel them to play a part. Thus one spends a good part of one’s life weeding out what one allowed to grow in one’s heart during adolescence. That operation is called acquiring experience.”

As he listened to the priest, Lucien was saying to himself: “Here is some old politician delighted to amuse himself on the road. He enjoys making a poor boy whom he finds on the brink of suicide change his mind, and he will drop me at the end of his jest... But he has a fine grasp of paradox, and he seems to me every bit as able as Blondet or Lousteau.”

Despite this judicious reflection, the corruption that this diplomat was attempting upon Lucien was sinking deeply into a soul quite disposed to receive it, and wrought all the greater havoc there because it was supported by famous examples. Captivated by the charm of this cynical conversation, Lucien clung all the more willingly to life because he felt himself being drawn back from the depths of his suicide to the surface by a powerful arm.

In this, the priest was plainly triumphant. And so, from time to time, he had accompanied his historical sarcasms with a mischievous smile.

“If your way of treating morality resembles your way of viewing history,” said Lucien, “I should very much like to know what, at this moment, is the motive behind your apparent charity?”

“That, young man, is the final point of my sermon, and you will allow me to reserve it, for then we shall not part today,” he replied, with the subtlety of a priest who sees his stratagem succeeding.

“Well then, talk to me about morality?” said Lucien, saying to himself: “I am going to make him show himself off.”

“Morality, young man, begins with the law,” said the priest. “If religion alone were at issue, laws would be useless: religious peoples have few laws. Above civil law stands political law. Well then, do you want to know what, for a statesman, is written across the brow of your nineteenth century? In 1793 the French invented popular sovereignty, which ended in an absolute emperor. So much for your national history. As for morals: Madame Tallien and Madame de Beauharnais behaved in the same way; Napoleon married the one, made her your empress, and never consented to receive the other, although she was a princess. A sans-culotte in 1793, Napoleon put on the Iron Crown in 1804. The ferocious devotees of Equality or Death in 1792 became, by 1806, accomplices of an aristocracy legitimized by Louis XVIII. Abroad, the aristocracy that reigns today in its Faubourg Saint-Germain did worse: it practiced usury, kept shop, made little pies, worked as cooks, farmers, and shepherdesses. In France, therefore, in political law as in moral law, one and all have belied their beginnings by their endings, their opinions by their conduct, or their conduct by their opinions. There has been no consistency, either in government or among private individuals. And so you no longer have any morality. Today, among you, success is the supreme justification for every action, whatever it may be. The deed is therefore no longer anything in itself; it lies wholly in the idea others form of it. From this, young man, comes a second precept: keep up a fine appearance! Conceal the reverse side of your life, and display a very brilliant face. Discretion, that motto of the ambitious, is the motto of our Order: make it yours. The great commit almost as many acts of cowardice as the wretched; but they commit them in the shadows and parade their virtues: they remain great. The lowly display their virtues in the shadows and expose their wretchedness in broad daylight: they are despised. You concealed your greatness and allowed your wounds to be seen. You openly had an actress as your mistress; you lived at her home, with her: you were in no way blameworthy, everyone considered both of you perfectly free; but you flew in the face of society’s ideas, and you did not receive the consideration society grants to those who obey it. If you had left Coralie to that Monsieur Camusot, if you had concealed your relations with her, you would have married Madame de Bargeton, you would now be prefect of Angoulême and Marquis de Rubempré. Change your conduct: put your beauty, your graces, your wit, your poetry on display. If you permit yourself petty acts of infamy, let them take place within four walls: then you will no longer be guilty of leaving a stain upon the scenery of that great theater called the world. Napoleon calls that washing one’s dirty linen in the family. From the second precept follows this corollary: everything lies in form. Grasp clearly what I call Form. There are uneducated people who, driven by need, violently take some sum or other from another person: they are called criminals, and they are forced to answer to justice. A poor man of genius discovers a secret whose exploitation is equivalent to a treasure; you lend him three thousand francs—following the example of those Cointets who found your three thousand francs in their hands and are going to strip your brother-in-law—you torment him in such a way as to make him surrender all or part of the secret; you answer only to your conscience, and your conscience does not bring you before the Court of Assizes. The enemies of the social order take advantage of this contrast to yelp at justice and wax indignant in the name of the people because a man who steals chickens by night within an inhabited enclosure is sent to the galleys, while a man who ruins families is imprisoned for scarcely a few months; but those hypocrites know perfectly well that, in condemning the thief, the judges maintain the barrier between rich and poor, the overthrow of which would bring about the end of the social order; whereas the bankrupt, the skillful captor of inheritances, the banker who kills a business for his own profit, merely bring about transfers of fortune. Thus society, my son, is forced to distinguish, on its own account, what I am teaching you to distinguish on yours. The great point is to make oneself equal to the whole of Society. Napoleon, Richelieu, the Medici made themselves equal to their age. You—you value yourself at twelve thousand francs!... Your Society no longer worships the true God, but the Golden Calf! Such is the religion of your Charter, which in politics no longer takes anything but property into account. Is that not saying to all its subjects: Try to become rich!... When, after having known how to obtain a fortune legally, you are rich and Marquis de Rubempré, you will allow yourself the luxury of honor. You will then profess such great delicacy that no one will dare accuse you of ever having lacked it, if indeed you did lack it while making your fortune—which I would never advise you to do,” said the priest, taking Lucien’s hand and patting it. “What, then, must you put into that handsome head?... Only the following theme: Set yourself a dazzling goal and conceal the means by which you attain it, while concealing your progress. You have behaved like a child; be a man, be a hunter, lie in wait, conceal yourself in ambush within Parisian society, wait for prey and for chance, spare neither your person nor what is called dignity; for we all obey something—a vice, a necessity—but observe the supreme law! secrecy.”

“Yes,” said Bai, “a stirring day—a day well spent.” He went on chattering animatedly: about the dancing—what a sight, those village children—and the “ladies”—“Miss Julie,” a fine girl in boots, a spirited girl—and Marie—well—we shall see what she has been up to ... I know her....

The other two did not speak. Neither of them was listening, either. It was so quiet that they could hear their own footsteps on the ground. At the end of the avenue, the cemetery’s iron gate rose up with its great cross.

“But Bai,” said Katinka.

“Do you think there are ghosts here?” said Bai. He opened the side gate.

They went in. At the gate, Katinka took Huus’s arm. The cemetery lay in the twilight like a large garden. Roses and box hedges and jasmines and lindens gave off a heavy fragrance, and gray and white stones rose between the hedges.

Katinka held Huus’s arm very tightly as they walked.

Bai went ahead. He trotted along the shrubbery, flinging out his arms as if he meant to flush out chickens.

Katinka stopped: “Just look.”

A clearing had been cut through the trees, so that one could look down across the fields to the fjord. The twilight hovered like a veil over the darkly gleaming surface of the water, still and dreamlike.

It was silent, as though life had died away beneath the fragrant air ... Motionless, they stood close against one another.

Slowly they walked on. Katinka stopped from time to time and read the inscriptions on the stones that shone out in the twilight. She read them, names and years, in a soft and trembling voice.

“Loved and missed.”

“Loved beyond the grave.”

“Love is the fulfillment of the law.”

She stepped closer and lifted the branches of the weeping willow: she wanted to read the name on the stone.

Then there was a rustling behind the willow.

“Huus,” she said, clutching his arm convulsively.

Something fled away over the wall.

“It was a couple of people,” said Huus.

“How frightened I was,” said Katinka, holding her hands to her breast.

She continued to walk close against him while her heart pounded.

They spoke no more. Now and then there was a rustling in the shrubbery, and Katinka started.

“My little friend, my little friend,” Huus whispered as if to a child. Katinka’s hand trembled beneath his.

Bai stood at the end of the path.

“Are you there?” he said.

He opened the gate. It clapped shut in its iron hinge behind them.

Out in the avenue, Bai took Huus aside:

“It is a damned scandal,” he said ... “that such a thing should #exist#—a desecration of the holy place ... Kiær had told me ... what it was like—with those scoundrels....

“But damn it, I didn’t think it was possible....

“Not even to have any feeling for death—the Garden of Death—ugh, damn it....

“Devil take me, one can’t even be left in peace on the benches....”

Huus could have struck him.

       *       *       *       *       *

They came down through the streets. The booths stood closed and deserted. Here and there, by a solitary streetlamp, a tradesman was gathering up his wares.

The din from taverns spilled into the street. Sleepy and with heads bowed, people drifted home in pairs.

Marie appeared in the hotel gateway. She was heavy with sleep and weary.

Katinka waited by the carriage. All around them horses were being harnessed and carriages driven away. The “Nightingales” sang loudly out into the courtyard,

They took their seats. Bai wanted to drive and sat with Marie.

    Oh you—my Valdemar!
    I love you....

“They keep at it,” said Bai.

They drove through the night; past the woods; out across the flat fields.

Marie, asleep, hung bent over the basket in her lap. Huus and Katinka sat in silence, staring out at the countryside. Now and then Bai spoke.

“Ho, ho—my beasts—

“Come now—so slowly—”

And it grew quiet as before.

Bai wanted “a little pick-me-up” and managed to rouse Marie until she found a bottle of port.

“Will you have some?” he said.

“No—thank you,” said Huus.

“That’s damned wrong.” Bai took the bottle from his mouth. “A stomach has to have something against the cold of the night.”

Bai took another swig. “That is something one learns in the field,” he said.

He began to talk about the Prussians and the war.

“Good-natured people,” he said, “taken one by one—great eaters—terrible gluttons—but good hearts—really good hearts—one by one—but in the #corps#—the devil take them....”

No one answered. Marie nodded off again.

Katinka only wished that he would be quiet.

“But terrible eaters,” Bai said again.

He began to grow patriotic and spoke of old Denmark and a bloody banner. Then he lapsed into silent reflections when no one answered.

Only the clatter of the horses in their harness could be heard. Now and then a cock crowed across the fields.

“Put the shawl on,” said Huus. “It is cold.”

Gently he laid the blue shawl around Katinka’s shoulders.

Little by little, day dawned over the fields.

       *       *       *       *       *

“I suppose there’ll be breakfast,” said Bai. They were home and stood at an ungodly hour on the steps in the gray morning.

“Yes, if you like,” said Katinka.

But Huus had to go home. It was high time.

“Well,” said Bai, “as you wish.” He yawned and went inside. Marie had been dragged away with the baskets.

Huus and Katinka were left alone. She leaned against the doorpost. They were silent for a moment.

“Then thank you for today,” she said. It came softly and uncertainly.

“As though it were not I who should be thanking you.” It came as an outburst, and in an instant Huus had seized her hand and kissed it twice, three times, with hot lips.

And then he was in the carriage and gone.

“What the devil came over him?” said Bai, coming outside. “Is he gone?”

Katinka stood in the same spot. “Yes,” she said, “he drove away.”

She steadied herself against the door and quietly went inside.

       *       *       *       *       *

Katinka sat by the open window. Day had broken. Larks and all the birds exulted above the broad meadow. The summer fields were filled with song and sunshine and twittering.




IV


The chained dog slept in the hot courtyard and would not be roused. A pair of scoured tubs had been set out to dry in the sun.

Katinka opened the hall door; only the humming of the flies could be heard through the bright, cool rooms.

She went through the garden room and out into the garden. There was not a soul there, and it was utterly silent. On the croquet lawn, balls and mallets lay abandoned. The rosebushes drooped in the heat.

“Is that you, dear Mrs. Bai?” It came in a half-whisper from the summerhouse, and Mrs. Linde nodded: “Yes, Linde is reading his sermon, you know.

“They are all out in the back garden—the Kiærs came, you see, a whole wagonload of them with their guests ... And it is inconvenient, of course, when Linde is reading his sermon....”

“Are the Kiærs here?” said Katinka.

“Yes ... they came here for coffee—they are in the back garden—and the new doctor too ... And you, who have been to the fair ... Huus told us about it.”

August was drawing to a close, and they were already dining by lamplight, the doors open onto the green sunset where a spindle of rosy copper still floated. The deserted sea, a swallow’s blue-black, slept, and when the diners fell silent, one could hear the small, weary, regular wash of the neap tides. Among the shadows, Philippe sought Vinca’s gaze, to test the strength of that invisible thread which had bound them to one another for so many years and preserved them, exalted and pure, from the melancholy that weighs upon the ends of meals, the ends of seasons, the ends of days. But she lowered her eyes to her plate, and the light from the hanging lamp polished her rounded eyelids, her round brown cheeks, her little chin. Then he felt abandoned and sought—beyond the lion-shaped peninsula that jutted out over the sea, crowned by three trembling stars—the road, white in the night, that led to Ker-Anna. A few hours more, a little more blue ash in this sky that the sunset tinged with dawn, a few more ritual phrases: “Well, well, ten o’clock already. Children, you don’t seem to realize that here one goes to bed at ten?” “And yet I haven’t done anything out of the ordinary, Madame Audebert; well, I feel as tired as if I hadn’t stopped...” A few more clinks of crockery, the hard clatter of dominoes on the bare table, one more moaning protest from Lisette who, three-quarters asleep, would refuse to go to bed... One more attempt to win back the gaze, the inward smile, the trust of the mysteriously wounded Vinca, and the hour would strike, the same hour that, the night before, had seen Philippe steal away... He thought of it without any precise desire, without any plan, and as though compelled by Vinca’s mood to retreat toward another refuge, another gentle shoulder, an efficacious warmth, urgently needed by this convalescent from pleasure, wounded besides by the passionate hostility of an adolescent...

The rites were performed, one by one; a servant carried away the whimpering Lisette, and Madame Ferret placed the double six on the gleaming table.

“Are you coming outside, Vinca? These silkworm moths banging into all the lamps are unbearable...”

She followed him without answering, and near the sea they still found that light which twilight leaves there for so long.

“Don’t you want me to go and fetch your scarf?”

“No, thank you.”

They walked together, bathed in a very light blue mist that rose from the salt meadow and smelled of wild thyme. Philippe restrained himself from taking his friend’s arm, and was appalled by his own discretion.

“My God, what is there between us? Are we lost to one another? Since she knows nothing of what happened over there, perhaps I have only to forget it, and we shall become happy again as before, unhappy as before, united as before?”

But he did not add hypnotic faith to his wish, since Vinca walked beside him, cold and gentle as though her great love had left her, and she did not perceive her companion’s anguish. Besides, Phil felt the hour drawing near and suffered from a quivering like the fever he had the day after, stung by a weever fish, he had felt in his bandaged arm the burning that the rising tide reawakened there...

He stopped and wiped his forehead:

“I’m suffocating. I don’t feel well, Vinca.”

“Oh! no, not well,” Vinca’s voice echoed.

He thought it a truce and eagerly reached toward her with voice and gesture:

“Oh! you’re so sweet! Oh! darling!...”

“No,” the voice interrupted, “I’m not sweet.”

The childish sentence left Philippe some hope, and he seized his friend’s bare arm.

“You’re angry with me, I know, for having cried today like a woman...”

“No, not like a woman...”

He blushed in the darkness and tried to explain himself:

“You understand, that conger eel you were tormenting in its hole... That creature’s blood on your lobster hook... It suddenly turned my stomach...”

“Ah! yes, your stomach... turned...”

The tone of her voice was so knowing that Philippe held his breath in fear. “She knows everything.” He waited for the crushing account and the explosion of tears and reproaches. But Vinca remained silent, and after a long while, as after the calm pause that follows a thunderbolt, he ventured a timid question:

“And is that weakness enough to make you seem as though you no longer love me?”

Vinca turned toward him the pale, hazy patch of her face, confined between the two rigid hedges of her hair:

“Oh! Phil, I still love you. Unfortunately, that changes nothing.”

He felt his leaping heart strike his throat:

“Yes? Then you’re going to forgive me for having been such a ‘little girl,’ so ridiculous?”

She hesitated for only a second:

“Why, yes. I’m going to forgive you, Phil. But that, too, changes nothing.”

“About what?”

“About us, Phil.”

She spoke with a sibylline gentleness which he did not dare question further and in which he did not dare rejoice. Vinca must have followed him in his mental retreat, for she added subtly:

“Do you remember the scenes you used to make with me, and the ones I made with you, not three weeks ago, because we were impatient at having four years, five years, to languish before getting married?... My poor Phil, I really think I would like to go backward and become a child again, today...”

He waited for her to emphasize, to comment upon that skillful, insidious “today” suspended before him in the pure blue air of the August night. But Vinca already knew how to arm herself with silence. He insisted:

“Then you’re not angry with me anymore? Tomorrow, we shall be... we shall be Vinca and Phil, as always? Forever?”

“Forever, if you want, Phil... Come. Let’s go back inside. It’s cool.”

She had not repeated “as always” after him. But he contented himself with that incomplete oath and with the cold little hand clasped for a moment in his own. For at that instant, the unwinding chain of the well, the alarm-bell clang of the empty bucket against the curb, the scraping of curtains along their rod in an open window—the day’s last human sounds—rang out the hour for Philippe, the same hour for which he had watched the night before, in order to reopen the villa door and dart out in secret... Ah! the muted red light of an unknown room... Ah! the dark happiness, death attained by degrees, life regained by slow beats of the wings...

As though, since the night before, he had been awaiting a sort of absolution from Vinca—an ambiguous absolution which she had just granted him with such sincerity in her tone, such reticence in her words—he suddenly assessed, as a man, the gift that a beautiful, imperious demoness had bestowed upon him.




XIV


“Has the date of your departure for Paris been settled?” Madame Dalleray asked.

“We are still due to go back on September twenty-fifth,” Philippe replied. “Sometimes, depending on where the Sundays fall in the month, our departure falls on the twenty-third or twenty-fourth, or the twenty-sixth. But it rarely varies by more than two days.”

“Yes... In short, you are leaving in a fortnight. In a fortnight, at this time...”

Philippe tore his gaze from the sea, flat and white near the sands, in the distance the color of a tuna’s back beneath the low clouds, and turned in astonishment toward Madame Dalleray. Wrapped in ample white cloth like the dress of the women of Tahiti, she smoked gravely, her hair impeccably arranged, powdered with a powder the same color as her skin, and nothing about her revealed that this young man seated not far from her, handsome and dark like her, was anything to her other than a younger brother.

Beside Vinca, a little sister, much like her, opened blue eyes in a round, sun-baked face beneath fair hair like stiff stubble, and rested the closed fists of a well-brought-up child on the tablecloth beside her plate. Two identical white dresses clothed the older and the younger girl, ironed, starched, of flounced organdy.

“A Sunday in Tahiti,” Philippe mocked inwardly, “I have never seen her look so ugly.”

Vinca’s mother, Vinca’s father, Vinca’s aunt, Phil and his parents, and the Parisian passing through encircled the table in green sweaters, striped blazers, and tussore jackets. The villa, rented every year by the two families of friends, smelled that morning of hot brioche and floor wax. The graying man, who had come from Paris, represented, among these brightly clad bathers and darkened children, the delicate, pale, well-dressed stranger.

“How you are changing, little Vinca!” he said to the girl.

“Tell me about it,” Phil muttered sourly.

The stranger leaned toward Vinca’s mother to confess to her in a low voice:

“She is becoming ravishing! Ravishing! In two years... you will see!”

Vinca heard, cast a quick feminine glance at the stranger, and smiled. Her crimson mouth parted over a blade of white teeth, her pupils, blue as the flower whose name she bore, were veiled by fair lashes, and Phil himself was dazzled. “Hey!... what has got into her?”

In the canvas-lined hall, Vinca served the coffee. She moved stiffly and without mishap, with a kind of acrobatic charm. When a gust of wind jostled the fragile table, Vinca caught an overturned chair with her foot and, with her chin, a lace mat that was flying away, and at the same time did not cease pouring a flawless stream of coffee into a cup.

“Look at her!” the stranger exclaimed rapturously.

He called her a “Tanagra,” made her taste some Chartreuse, asked her the names of the lovers she was driving to despair at the Cancale casino...

“Ha! Ha! The Cancale casino! But there is no casino in Cancale!”

She laughed, showing the solid semicircle of all her teeth, pivoting like a ballerina on the tips of her white shoes. Cunning was coming to her along with coquetry; she did not turn her gaze toward Philippe, who, gloomy behind the piano and the large bouquet of thistles planted in a copper bucket, was contemplating her.

“I was mistaken,” he admitted to himself. “She is very pretty. That is something new!”

As the stranger, to the sound of the phonograph, proposed teaching Vinca the _balancello_, Philippe slipped outside, ran toward the beach, and curled into a ball in a hollow in the dunes, where he put his head on his arms and his arms on his knees. A new Vinca, full of voluptuous insolence, persisted beneath his closed eyelids: Vinca coquettish, well armed, suddenly augmented by rounded flesh, Vinca wicked and as rebellious as one could wish...

“Phil! My Phil! I was looking for you... What is the matter?”

The seductress, breathless, was beside him, innocently pulling his hair by the handful to make him raise his head.

“There is nothing wrong with me,” he said hoarsely.

He opened his eyes fearfully. Kneeling in the sand, she was crumpling her ten organdy flounces and crawling like a squaw.

“Phil! Please, don’t be angry... You have something against me... Phil, you know very well that I love you more than anyone in the world. Speak to me, Phil!”

He searched her for the fleeting splendor that had irritated him. But now she was nothing more than a dismayed Vinca, an adolescent burdened too soon with the humility, the awkwardness, the dreary obstinacy of true love... He snatched his hand away from her as she kissed it:

“Leave me alone! You don’t understand, you never understand anything!... Get up, come on!”

And as he smoothed the crumpled dress, tied the sash at her waist, and calmed the stiff hair standing up in the wind, he sought to mold upon her once more the shape of the little idol he had glimpsed...




III


“The holidays, now, amount to a month and a half, that’s all!...”

“One month,” said Vinca. “You know very well that I shall be in Paris on September twentieth.”

“Why? Your father is free until October first every year.”

“Yes, but Mother and I, and Lisette, do not have too much time from September twentieth to October fourth for the autumn shopping—a dress for me to wear to class, a coat, a hat, and the same things for Lisette... I meant us, women, after all...”

Phil, lying on his back, tossed handfuls of sand into the air.

“Oh, honestly... ‘You women...’ What a fuss you make over all that!”

“It has to be done... You find your suit laid out on your bed. You concern yourself only with your shoes, because you buy them from a shop your father forbids you to go to; the rest takes care of itself. It is very convenient for you men!...”

Philippe sat up with a jerk of his loins, ready to answer the irony. But Vinca was not making fun of him. She was sewing, edging with pink scallops a crêpon dress the same blue as her eyes. Her fair hair, cut in the Joan of Arc style, was slowly growing longer. Sometimes she parted it at the nape and tied with blue ribbons two short wheat-colored brooms, one along each cheek. Since lunch she had lost one of her ribbons, and half her hair beat against half her face like a spread curtain.

Philippe frowned:

“God, how badly combed your hair is, Vinca!”

She blushed beneath her holiday tan and cast him a humble glance as she pushed her hair behind her ear:

“I know... my hair will look bad as long as it is too short. This hairstyle is just for the meantime...”

“You don’t care about temporary ugliness...” he said harshly.

“I swear I do, Phil.”

Ashamed of so much gentleness, he fell silent, and she raised astonished eyes to him, for she had not expected any leniency. He himself believed this was a temporary truce in his little companion’s touchiness and prepared himself for reproaches, childish sarcasms, for what he called her “greyhound temper.” But she smiled melancholyly, with a wandering smile addressed to the calm sea, to the sky where the high wind traced ferns of cloud.

“On the contrary, I very much want to be pretty, I assure you. Mother says I can still become pretty, but that I must be patient.”

Her proud and awkward fifteen years, trained by running, salted, hardened, thin and sturdy, often made her resemble a stinging, brittle riding switch, but her eyes of incomparable blue and her simple, healthy mouth were finished works of feminine grace.

“A few more days, three weeks,” Phil said to himself. He wiped the sand from his hands on a clump of wet wild thyme, laden with flowers and little hornets caught by the rain, which waited, numbed, for the next ray of sunlight. He breathed in from his palms the fresh, chaste fragrance, and resisted a wave of weakness, of tenderness, a ten-year-old child’s sadness. But through the windowpane, between the long tears of rain and the whirling corollas of the battered morning glories, he looked at Vinca’s face, that woman’s face which she showed only to him, and which she hid from everyone else behind her fifteen years as a sensible, cheerful young girl.

A break in the clouds held the downpour within the cloud, half-opened above the horizon a luminous wound, from which an inverted fan of rays blossomed, a sorrowful white. Philippe’s soul leapt forward to meet this respite, seeking the relief, the release that his tormented sixteen years naïvely demanded. But, facing the sea, he could feel behind him the closed window and Vinca leaning against the pane.

“A few more days,” he repeated to himself. “And we shall be separated. What are we to do?”

It did not even occur to him that the end of the holidays the year before had made him an unhappy boy, then one calmed by the return to Paris and day school, and resigned to Sunday consolations. The year before, Philippe had been fifteen; each birthday relegates to a murky, wretched past everything that is not Vinca and himself. Did he love her, then, to such an extent? He questioned himself, found no word other than the word love, and angrily flung his hair back from his forehead.

“Perhaps it isn’t that I love her all that much, but she is mine! That’s all!”

He turned toward the house and shouted into the wind:

“Vinca! Come! It isn’t raining anymore!”

She opened the door and stood on the threshold like an invalid, raising one shoulder toward her ear with a fearful air.

“Come on, come! The sea is ebbing; it will carry the rain away with it!”

She bound her hair with a white scarf tied at the nape of her neck and looked like a wounded woman.

“Come as far as the Nose, at least; it’s dry under the rock.”

She followed him without a word along the customs officers’ path, which ran like a ledge along the cliffside. They trod on peppery oregano and the last fragrances of sweet clover. Below them, the sea snapped like torn flags and unctuously licked the rocks. Its force drove warm gusts up toward the top of the cliff, bearing the smell of mussels and the earthy aroma of the little crevices where wind and bird sow seeds as they fly.

They reached their retreat, dry and well sheltered beneath a prow of rock, a rimless platform from which they seemed to be sailing toward the open sea. Philippe sat down beside Vinca, who rested her head on his shoulder. She seemed exhausted and immediately closed her eyes. Her brown, rosy, rounded cheeks, dusted with russet freckles, velvety with close down of a plantlike softness, had grown pale since morning, as had her fresh mouth, always a little cracked like a fruit bitten by the day’s heat.

After lunch, instead of meeting the complaints of her “childhood sweetheart” with her usual common sense as an intelligent, stubborn, gentle little bourgeois, she had burst into tears, into desperate confessions, into bitter declarations that hated their youth, the future beyond reach, flight made impossible, resignation unacceptable... She had cried, “I love you!” as one cries “Farewell!” and, “I can no longer leave you!” with eyes full of horror. Love, which had grown before they did, had enchanted their childhood and guarded their adolescence against dubious friendships. Less ignorant than Daphnis, Philippe revered and bullied Vinca like a brother, but cherished her as though, in the Eastern manner, they had been married from the cradle...

Vinca sighed and opened her eyes again without lifting her head:

“I’m not tiring you, am I, Phil?”

He shook his head, admiring, so close to his own, those blue eyes whose blue, each time gentler to his heart, quivered between lashes tipped with gold.

“You see,” he said, “the storm is moving down. The sea will still be rough at four in the morning... But we have the clearing now, and this evening a beautiful full-moonrise...”

Instinctively, he spoke of improving weather, of calm, leading Vinca toward serene images. But she did not answer.

“Will you come and play tennis at the Jallons’ tomorrow?”

She shook her head no, her eyes closed again, with sudden fury, as though she were refusing forever to drink, to eat, to live...

“Vinca!” Philippe pleaded sternly. “You must. We’ll go.”

She half-opened her mouth and swept the sea with the gaze of a condemned woman:

“Then we’ll go,” she repeated. “What is the use of not going? What is the use of going? Nothing will change anything.”

They both thought of the Jallons’ garden, of tennis, of afternoon tea. Pure and frenzied lovers, they thought of the game that would disguise them, for yet another day, as laughing children, and felt utterly exhausted.

“A few more days,” Philippe said to himself, “and we shall be separated. We shall no longer wake beneath the same roof, and I shall see Vinca only on Sundays, at her father’s, at mine, or at the cinema. And I am sixteen. Sixteen and five makes twenty-one. Hundreds and hundreds of days... A few months of holidays, it is true, but their ending is atrocious... And yet she is mine... She is mine...”

He then realized that Vinca was slipping from his shoulder. With a gentle, imperceptible, deliberate movement, she was sliding, her eyes closed, down the sloping shelf of rock, so narrow that Vinca’s feet were already dangling over empty space... He understood and did not tremble. He weighed the expediency of what his companion was attempting, and tightened his arm around Vinca’s waist so as not to part himself from her. As he pressed it against himself, he felt the very living, resilient reality, the vigorous perfection of that young girl’s body, ready to obey him in life, ready to draw him into death...

“To die? What is the use?... Not yet. Must I depart for the other world without having truly possessed all this, which was born for me?”

On that sloping rock, he dreamed of possession as a timid adolescent might dream of it, but also as a demanding man might, an heir grimly resolved to enjoy the goods destined for him by time and human laws. For the first time, he alone decided the fate of them as a couple, free either to abandon them to the waves or to cling to the rocky ledge, like the stubborn seed which, nourished by little, flowered there...

The Ripening Grain

A Novel

PARIS

ERNEST FLAMMARION, PUBLISHER

26, Rue Racine, 26





I


“Are you going fishing, Vinca?”

With a haughty nod of her head, the Periwinkle Vinca, whose eyes were the color of spring rain, replied that she was indeed going fishing. Her mended sweater bore witness to it, as did her espadrilles, stiffened by salt. Everyone knew that her blue-and-green checked skirt, which was three years old and left her knees bare, belonged to the shrimps and crabs. And did those two hand nets over her shoulder, and that bristling woolen beret, bluish like a dune thistle, constitute fishing gear, yes or no?

She passed the one who had hailed her. She went down toward the rocks, taking long strides on her thin, shapely, terra-cotta-colored spindle legs. Philippe watched her walk, comparing this year’s Vinca with the Vinca of previous holidays. Has she finished growing? It is time she stopped. She has no more flesh on her than last year. Her short hair scatters into stiff, richly golden straw; she has been letting it grow for four months, but it can neither be braided nor rolled up. Her cheeks and hands are dark with sunburn, her neck milk-white beneath her hair, her smile constrained, her laugh ringing; and though she fastens smocks and sweaters tightly over a nonexistent bosom, she hikes up skirt and drawers to go down into the water, as high as she can, with the serenity of a little boy...

The companion who was watching her, lying on the dune amid long-haired grass, cradled his dimple-cleft chin on his crossed arms. He is sixteen and a half, since Vinca has reached fifteen and a half. Their whole childhood united them; adolescence separates them. Last year already, they exchanged sour retorts and furtive blows; now silence falls between them at every moment, so heavily that they prefer sulking to the effort of conversation. But Philippe, subtle, born for hunting and deceit, cloaks his muteness in mystery and turns everything that troubles him into a weapon. He sketches disillusioned gestures, ventures remarks such as “What’s the use?... You can’t understand...,” while Vinca knows only how to remain silent, to suffer from what she keeps silent, from what she would like to learn, and to stiffen herself against the premature, imperious instinct to give everything, against the fear that Philippe, changed from day to day, stronger from hour to hour, may break the frail mooring that brings him back every year, from July to October, to the dense wood sloping toward the sea, to the rocks hairy with black bladder wrack. Already he has a disastrous way of staring fixedly at his friend without seeing her, as though Vinca were transparent, fluid, negligible...

Perhaps next year she will fall at his feet and say a woman’s words to him: “Phil! Don’t be unkind... I love you, Phil; do with me whatever you wish... Speak to me, Phil...” But this year she still retains the surly dignity of children; she resists, and Phil does not like that resistance.

He watched the slender, graceful girl who was now going down toward the sea. He had no more desire to caress her than to beat her, but he wanted her trusting, promised to him alone, and available like those treasures of which he was ashamed—dried petals, agate marbles, shells and seeds, pictures, a little silver watch...

“Wait for me, Vinca! I’m going fishing with you!” he cried.

She slowed her pace without turning around. He caught up with her in a few bounds and took possession of one of the hand nets.

“Why did you take two?”

“I took the little bag net for the narrow holes, and my own hand net, as usual.”

He plunged his gentlest dark gaze into her blue eyes:

“So it wasn’t for me?”

At the same time he offered her his hand to cross the difficult passage through the rocks, and blood rose beneath the tan of Vinca’s cheeks. A new gesture, a new look, were enough to disconcert her. Yesterday they had scoured the cliffs and probed the holes side by side—each at their own risk... As nimble as he, she could not remember ever having asked Phil for help...

“A little gentleness, Vinca!” he pleaded with a smile, for she had pulled her hand away with an overly broad, angular gesture. “What have you got against me?”

She bit her lips, cracked by her daily plunges, and made her way over the rocks bristling with barnacles. She was reflecting and felt full of doubt. What is the matter with him? Here he is, attentive and charming, and he has just offered her his hand as though she were a lady... She slowly lowered the net bag into a hollow where the motionless seawater revealed seaweed, sea cucumbers, “wolf-fish,” scorpionfish all head and fins, black crabs edged with red, and shrimps... Phil’s shadow darkened the sunlit pool.

“Move away! You’re casting your shadow over the shrimps, and besides, that big hole is mine!”

He did not insist, and she fished alone, impatient and less skillful than usual. Ten shrimps, twenty shrimps escaped her too-abrupt sweep of the net and hid in cracks from which their fine whiskers felt the water and mocked the implement...

“Phil! Come, Phil! It’s full of shrimps, and they won’t let themselves be caught!”

He came over nonchalantly and leaned above the teeming little abyss:

“Naturally! That’s because you don’t know how...”

“I know perfectly well,” Vinca cried sharply, “only I haven’t the patience.”

Phil plunged the hand net into the water and held it motionless.

“In the crack in the rock,” Vinca whispered behind his shoulder, “there are some beautiful, beautiful ones... Can’t you see their horns?”

“No. It doesn’t matter. They’ll come.”

“You think so!”

“Of course. Look.”

She leaned farther over, and her hair brushed her companion’s cheek like a short, captive wing. She drew back, then returned with an imperceptible movement, only to draw back again. He did not seem to notice, but his free hand drew Vinca’s bare, tanned, salt-covered arm toward him.

One day, I saw Ellénore agitated and trying to conceal from me an idea that preoccupied her. After much entreaty, she made me promise that I would not oppose the resolution she had taken, and confessed to me that M. de P** had written to her: he had won his lawsuit; he remembered with gratitude the services she had rendered him, and their relationship of ten years. He offered her half his fortune, not in order to reunite with her, which was no longer possible, but on condition that she leave the ungrateful and treacherous man who had separated them. “I have replied,” she told me, “and you can well guess that I refused.” I guessed it only too well. I was touched, but in despair at the new sacrifice Ellénore was making for me. Nevertheless, I dared raise no objection: my attempts in that direction had always been so fruitless! I withdrew to reflect on the course I had to take. It was clear to me that our bonds had to be broken. They were painful to me; they were becoming harmful to her; I was the sole obstacle preventing her from recovering a suitable position and the consideration which, in society, sooner or later follows opulence; I was the only barrier between her and her children: I no longer had any excuse in my own eyes. To yield to her in these circumstances was no longer generosity, but culpable weakness. I had promised my father that I would become free again as soon as I was no longer necessary to Ellénore. At last it was time to embark upon a career, to begin an active life, to acquire some claim to the esteem of men, to make noble use of my faculties. I returned to Ellénore, believing myself unshakable in my resolve to force her not to reject the Count de P**’s offers and, if necessary, to tell her that I no longer loved her. “Dear friend,” I said to her, “one struggles for a time against one’s destiny, but in the end one always yields. The laws of society are stronger than the wills of men; the most imperious feelings break against the fatality of circumstances. In vain does one persist in consulting only one’s heart; sooner or later one is condemned to listen to reason. I cannot keep you any longer in a position equally unworthy of you and of me; I cannot do so either for your sake or for my own.” As I spoke without looking at Ellénore, I felt my ideas becoming vaguer and my resolve weakening. I tried to summon my strength again, and continued in a hurried voice: “I shall always be your friend; I shall always feel the deepest affection for you. The two years of our relationship will not be erased from my memory; they will forever remain the finest period of my life. But love—that transport of the senses, that involuntary intoxication, that oblivion of all interests, of all duties—Ellénore, I no longer feel it.” I waited a long time for her reply without raising my eyes to her. When at last I looked at her, she was motionless; she gazed at everything around her as though she recognized none of it; I took her hand: I found it cold. She pushed me away. “What do you want of me?” she said. “Am I not alone, alone in the universe, alone without a single being who understands me? What more have you to say to me? Have you not told me everything? Is it not all over, over beyond recall? Leave me, go away; is that not what you desire?” She tried to move away; she staggered; I tried to hold her, and she fell unconscious at my feet; I lifted her up, embraced her, restored her to consciousness. “Ellénore,” I cried, “come back to yourself, come back to me; I love you with love, with the tenderest love; I deceived you so that you might be freer in your choice.” Credulities of the heart, you are inexplicable! These simple words, contradicted by so many words that had preceded them, restored Ellénore to life and trust; she made me repeat them several times: she seemed to breathe avidly. She believed me: she became intoxicated with her love, which she mistook for ours; she confirmed her reply to the Count de P**, and I found myself more deeply committed than ever.

Three months later, a new possibility of change appeared in Ellénore’s situation. One of those vicissitudes common in republics convulsed by factions recalled her father to Poland and restored him to his estates. Although he scarcely knew his daughter, whom her mother had taken to France at the age of three, he wished to have her settle near him. Only vague reports of Ellénore’s adventures had reached him in Russia, where he had lived throughout his exile. Ellénore was his only child: he feared isolation, and wanted to be cared for; he sought only to discover his daughter’s dwelling, and as soon as he learned where it was, he urged her to come and join him. She could feel no real attachment to a father whom she did not remember ever having seen. Nevertheless, she felt that it was her duty to obey; in this way she would secure a great fortune for her children, and would herself rise again to the rank of which her misfortunes and her conduct had deprived her; but she declared to me positively that she would go to Poland only if I accompanied her. “I am no longer,” she told me, “at the age when the soul opens itself to new impressions. My father is a stranger to me. If I remain here, others will hasten to surround him; he will be just as happy. My children will have M. de P**’s fortune. I know very well that I shall be generally blamed; I shall be regarded as an ungrateful daughter and an unfeeling mother: but I have suffered too much; I am no longer young enough for the opinion of the world to have great power over me. If there is something harsh in my resolution, it is you, Adolphe, whom you must blame. If I could deceive myself about you, I might perhaps consent to an absence whose bitterness would be lessened by the prospect of a sweet and lasting reunion; but you would like nothing better than to imagine me two hundred leagues away from you, contented and tranquil, amid my family and opulence. You would write me reasonable letters on that subject, which I can already foresee; they would tear my heart apart; I do not wish to expose myself to that. I do not have the consolation of telling myself that, by the sacrifice of my entire life, I have succeeded in inspiring in you the feeling I deserved; but after all, you accepted that sacrifice. I already suffer enough from the barrenness of your manner and the coldness of our relations; I endure these sufferings that you inflict on me; I do not wish to brave any voluntarily.”

There was in Ellénore’s voice and tone something harsh and violent that bespoke a firm determination rather than a deep or touching emotion. For some time she had grown angry in advance whenever she asked something of me, as though I had already refused it. She disposed of my actions, but she knew that my judgment repudiated them. She would have liked to penetrate the innermost sanctuary of my thoughts in order to shatter there a mute opposition that incensed her against me. I spoke to her of my situation, of my father’s wish, of my own desire; I pleaded, I became heated. Ellénore remained unshakable. I tried to reawaken her generosity, as though love were not the most selfish of all feelings and consequently, when wounded, the least generous. By a strange effort, I tried to move her to pity for the unhappiness I experienced in remaining near her; I succeeded only in exasperating her. I promised to go and see her in Poland; but in my promises, devoid of warmth and unreserve, she saw only my impatience to leave her.

From that day on, nothing more had been heard of him. Though Marguerite had dismissed her guests and changed her habits, the duke had sent no further word. What I had gained from this was that my mistress belonged to me more completely, and that my dream was at last coming true. Marguerite could no longer do without me. Without troubling herself about what might result from it, she openly displayed our liaison, and I had reached the point of never leaving her house. The servants called me Monsieur and officially regarded me as their master.

Prudence had strongly remonstrated with Marguerite about this new life; but Marguerite had replied that she loved me, that she could not live without me, and that, whatever might come of it, she would not renounce the happiness of having me constantly beside her, adding that all those whom it displeased were free not to return.

That was what I had heard one day when Prudence had told Marguerite that she had something very important to tell her, and I had listened at the door of the room in which they had shut themselves.

Some time later Prudence returned.

I was at the far end of the garden when she entered; she did not see me. From the way Marguerite had come forward to meet her, I suspected that a conversation like the one I had already overheard was about to take place again, and I wanted to hear it as I had the other.

The two women shut themselves in a boudoir, and I began to listen.

“Well?” Marguerite asked.

“Well! I saw the duke.”

“What did he say to you?”

“That he readily forgave you for the first scene, but that he had learned that you were living openly with Monsieur Armand Duval, and that he did not forgive you for that. ‘Let Marguerite leave this young man,’ he told me, ‘and, as in the past, I shall give her whatever she wants; otherwise, she must give up asking me for anything whatsoever.’”

“What did you answer?”

“That I would convey his decision to you, and I promised him that I would make you see reason. Consider, my dear child, the position you are losing, a position Armand will never be able to restore to you. He loves you with all his soul, but he does not have enough fortune to provide for all your needs, and one day you will inevitably have to part, when it is too late and the duke is no longer willing to do anything for you. Do you want me to speak to Armand?”

Marguerite seemed to be reflecting, for she did not answer. My heart was beating violently as I waited for her reply.

“No,” she resumed, “I shall not leave Armand, and I shall not hide the fact that I live with him. It may be madness, but I love him! What can you expect? And besides, by now he has grown accustomed to loving me without hindrance; he would suffer too much if he were forced to leave me, even for just one hour a day. Besides, I have not so much time left to live that I should make myself unhappy and do the bidding of an old man whose very sight makes me grow old. Let him keep his money; I shall do without it.”

“But how will you manage?”

“I do not know.”

Prudence was no doubt about to answer something, but I burst in and ran to throw myself at Marguerite’s feet, covering her hands with the tears that my joy at being loved in this way made me shed.

“My life is yours, Marguerite; you no longer need that man. Am I not here? Would I ever abandon you, and could I ever repay sufficiently the happiness you give me? No more constraint, my Marguerite; we love each other! What does the rest matter to us?”

“Oh! Yes, I love you, my Armand!” she murmured, winding both arms around my neck. “I love you as I would not have believed I could love. We shall be happy, we shall live quietly, and I shall bid an eternal farewell to this life of which I am now ashamed. You will never reproach me for the past, will you?”

Tears veiled my voice. I could answer only by pressing Marguerite to my heart.

“Come,” she said, turning back toward Prudence and speaking in an emotional voice, “you will report this scene to the duke, and you will add that we do not need him.”

From that day on, there was no more talk of the duke. Marguerite was no longer the woman I had known. She avoided everything that might have reminded me of the life amid which I had met her. No wife, no sister, ever had for her husband or brother the love and care that she had for me. That sickly nature was open to every impression, receptive to every feeling. She had broken with her friends as she had with her habits, with her manner of speaking as she had with her former expenditures. When people saw us leave the house to go for a ride in a charming little boat I had bought, they would never have believed that this woman, dressed in a white gown, wearing a large straw hat and carrying on her arm the simple silk cloak that was to protect her from the coolness of the water, was that same Marguerite Gautier who, four months earlier, had caused a stir with her luxury and her scandals.

Alas! We hastened to be happy, as though we had guessed that we could not be so for long.

For two months we had not even gone to Paris. No one had come to see us except Prudence and that Julie Duprat of whom I have told you, and to whom Marguerite was later to entrust the touching account I have here.

I spent whole days at my mistress’s feet. We opened the windows overlooking the garden, and, as we watched summer descend joyfully among the flowers it brings into bloom and beneath the shade of the trees, we breathed side by side that true life which neither Marguerite nor I had understood until then.

This woman displayed a child’s wonder at the slightest things. There were days when she ran through the garden like a ten-year-old girl, chasing a butterfly or a dragonfly. This courtesan, who had caused more money to be spent on bouquets than would be needed to keep an entire family living in happiness, would sometimes sit on the lawn for an hour to examine the simple flower whose name she bore.

It was during that time that she read Manon Lescaut so often. Many times I caught her making notes in that book, and she always told me that when a woman loves, she cannot do what Manon did.

Two or three times the duke wrote to her. She recognized the handwriting and gave me the letters without reading them.

Sometimes the words of those letters brought tears to my eyes.

I went and leaned against the mantelpiece, directly opposite Marguerite, and watched her dance. No sooner had she noticed me than she became flustered. I saw it, and greeted her distractedly with a gesture of my hand and a glance.

When I thought that after the ball she would leave not with me, but with that rich fool, when I pictured to myself what would probably follow their return to her home, the blood rushed to my face, and I felt the urge to disrupt their lovemaking.

After the country dance, I went to pay my respects to the mistress of the house, who was displaying to the guests’ eyes magnificent shoulders and half of a dazzling bosom.

That woman was beautiful and, in terms of figure, more beautiful than Marguerite. I understood this even better from certain glances Marguerite cast at Olympe while I was speaking to her. The man who became this woman’s lover could be as proud as M. de N... was, and she was beautiful enough to inspire a passion equal to the one Marguerite had inspired in me.

She had no lover at that time. It would not be difficult to become one. All that was needed was to display enough gold to make her take notice.

My mind was made up. This woman would be my mistress.

I began playing the part of a suitor by dancing with Olympe.

Half an hour later, Marguerite, pale as a corpse, put on her fur-lined cloak and left the ball.




Chapter XXIV


That was something already, but it was not enough. I understood the power I had over this woman, and I abused it like a coward.

When I think that she is dead now, I wonder whether God will ever forgive me for the harm I did.

After supper, which was extremely boisterous, we began to gamble.

I sat down beside Olympe and staked my money with such boldness that she could not help noticing. In an instant, I won a hundred and fifty or two hundred louis, which I spread out before me and upon which she fixed ardent eyes.

I was the only person who was not wholly absorbed in the game and who paid attention to her. I went on winning for the rest of the night, and it was I who gave her money with which to play, for she had lost everything she had with her and probably everything she had at home.

At five in the morning, everyone left.

I had won three hundred louis.

All the gamblers were already downstairs; I alone had remained behind without anyone noticing, for I was not a friend of any of those gentlemen.

Olympe herself was lighting the staircase, and I was about to go down like the others when, turning back toward her, I said:

“I must speak to you.”

“Tomorrow,” she said to me.

“No, now.”

“What do you have to say to me?”

“You will see.”

And I went back into the apartment.

“You lost, didn’t you?” I said to her.

“Yes.”

“Everything you had at home?”

She hesitated.

“Be frank.”

“Well, it is true.”

“I have won three hundred louis. Here they are, if you are willing to keep me here.”

And at the same time, I threw the gold onto the table.

“And why this proposal?”

“Because I love you, by God!”

“No, but because you are in love with Marguerite and want to take revenge on her by becoming my lover. A woman like me is not so easily deceived, my dear friend; unfortunately, I am still too young and too beautiful to accept the role you are offering me.”

“So you refuse?”

“Yes.”

“Would you rather love me for nothing? In that case, I would be the one to refuse. Think it over, my dear Olympe. If I had sent some third party to offer you these three hundred louis on my behalf, on the conditions I attach to them, you would have accepted. I preferred to deal with you directly. Accept without trying to discover the reasons that make me act; tell yourself that you are beautiful, and that there is nothing surprising about my being in love with you.”

Marguerite was a kept woman like Olympe, and yet, the first time I saw her, I would never have dared say to her what I had just said to this woman. That was because I loved Marguerite, because I had discerned in her instincts that this other creature lacked, and because, at the very moment when I was proposing this bargain, despite her extreme beauty, the woman with whom I was about to conclude it disgusted me.

She ended by accepting, of course, and at noon I left her home as her lover; but I left her bed without carrying away any memory of the caresses and words of love she had believed herself obliged to lavish on me in return for the six thousand francs I left her.

And yet men had ruined themselves over that woman.

From that day onward, I subjected Marguerite to unremitting persecution. Olympe and she ceased seeing one another; you can easily understand why. I gave my new mistress a carriage and jewels, I gambled—in short, I committed every extravagance befitting a man in love with a woman like Olympe. Word of my new passion spread at once.

Even Prudence was taken in by it and ended by believing that I had completely forgotten Marguerite. Marguerite, whether she had guessed the motive behind my actions or was mistaken like the others, responded with great dignity to the wounds I inflicted on her every day. Only, she appeared to be suffering, for wherever I encountered her, each time I saw her she was paler and sadder than before. My love for her, exalted to such a pitch that it believed itself to have become hatred, rejoiced at the sight of this daily suffering. Several times, in circumstances in which I behaved with vile cruelty, Marguerite raised such pleading eyes to me that I blushed at the role I had assumed and came close to asking her forgiveness for it.

But these fits of repentance lasted no longer than a flash of lightning, and Olympe, who had ended by setting aside every kind of pride and had understood that by hurting Marguerite she would obtain from me whatever she wanted, constantly incited me against her and insulted her whenever she found an opportunity, with the persistent cowardice of a woman given license by a man.

The last time she had come to my rooms, she had sat down in the place where she had just seated herself; only, since that time, she had been another man's mistress; kisses other than mine had touched her lips, toward which, despite myself, my own were reaching, and yet I felt that I loved this woman as much as, and perhaps more than, I had ever loved her.

Nevertheless, it was difficult for me to begin the conversation on the subject that had brought her. Marguerite doubtless understood this, for she resumed:

“I have come to trouble you, Armand, because I have two things to ask of you: forgiveness for what I said yesterday to Mademoiselle Olympe, and mercy for what you may perhaps be ready to do to me still. Willingly or not, since your return you have caused me so much pain that I would now be incapable of enduring a quarter of the emotions I endured up until this morning. You will take pity on me, will you not? And you will understand that there are nobler things for a man of heart to do than to take revenge on a sick and sorrowful woman such as I am. Here, take my hand. I have a fever; I left my bed to come and ask you, not for your friendship, but for your indifference.”

Indeed, I took Marguerite's hand. It was burning hot, and the poor woman was shivering beneath her velvet cloak.

I rolled the armchair in which she was sitting nearer the fire.

“Do you then believe that I did not suffer,” I replied, “on the night when, after waiting for you in the country, I came to look for you in Paris, where I found nothing but that letter which nearly drove me mad? How could you deceive me, Marguerite—me, who loved you so much?”

“Let us not speak of that, Armand; I did not come to speak of it. I wanted to see you as something other than an enemy, that is all, and I wanted to press your hand once more. You have a young, pretty mistress whom you love, they say: be happy with her and forget me.”

“And you, you are happy, no doubt?”

“Do I have the face of a happy woman, Armand? Do not mock my sorrow, you who know better than anyone its cause and its extent.”

“It depended only on you never to be unhappy—if indeed you are, as you say.”

“No, my friend, circumstances were stronger than my will. I obeyed, not my instincts as a fallen woman, as you seem to suggest, but a grave necessity and reasons that you will learn one day, and that will make you forgive me.”

“Why do you not tell me those reasons today?”

“Because they would not bring about an impossible reconciliation between us, and because they might estrange you from people from whom you must not become estranged.”

“Who are these people?”

“I cannot tell you.”

“Then you are lying.”

Marguerite rose and made her way toward the door.

I could not witness this mute and expressive sorrow without being moved, when I compared within myself this pale, weeping woman with the madcap girl who had mocked me at the Opéra-Comique.

“Thou shalt not go,” I said, placing myself in front of the door.

“Why?”

“Because, despite what thou hast done to me, I still love thee, and I want to keep thee here.”

“To turn me out tomorrow, is that it? No, it is impossible! Our two destinies are separate; let us not try to reunite them. You might despise me, whereas now you can only hate me.”

“No, Marguerite,” I cried, feeling all my love and all my desires awaken at the touch of this woman. “No, I shall forget everything, and we shall be happy as we had promised ourselves we would be.”

Marguerite shook her head as a sign of doubt and said:

“Am I not your slave, your dog? Do with me whatever you will; take me, I am yours.”

And, removing her cloak and hat, she threw them onto the sofa and began abruptly unfastening the bodice of her dress, for, through one of those reactions so frequent in her illness, the blood was rushing from her heart to her head and choking her.

A dry, hoarse cough followed.

“Have my coachman told,” she resumed, “to take my carriage back.”

I went downstairs myself to dismiss the man.

When I returned, Marguerite was lying in front of the fire, and her teeth were chattering with cold.

I took her in my arms, undressed her without her making a movement, and carried her, icy cold, to my bed.

Then I sat down beside her and tried to warm her beneath my caresses. She did not say a word to me, but she smiled at me.

Oh! It was a strange night. Marguerite's whole life seemed to have passed into the kisses with which she covered me, and I loved her so much that, in the midst of the transports of her feverish love, I wondered whether I was not going to kill her so that she might never belong to another.

A month of a love like that, in body as in heart, and one would be nothing but a corpse.

Daylight found us both awake.

Marguerite was livid. She did not say a word. Large tears flowed from her eyes from time to time and stopped upon her cheek, shining like diamonds. Her exhausted arms opened from time to time to grasp me, then fell back strengthless upon the bed.

For a moment I believed that I might be able to forget what had happened since my departure from Bougival, and I said to Marguerite:

“Wilt thou have us leave, abandon Paris?”

“No, no,” she said to me, almost in terror, “we should be too unhappy. I can no longer contribute to thy happiness, but as long as I have a breath left, I shall be the slave of thy whims. At whatever hour of the day or night thou mayst want me, come; I shall be thine. But no longer link thy future with mine; thou wouldst be too unhappy, and thou wouldst make me too unhappy.

“For a little while yet I am a pretty girl; take advantage of it, but do not ask anything else of me.”

When she had gone, I was terrified by the solitude in which she left me. Two hours after her departure, I was still sitting on the bed she had just left, looking at the pillow that retained the impressions of her form, and wondering what was to become of me between my love and my jealousy.

At five o'clock, without knowing what I was going there to do, I made my way to the Rue d'Antin.

“Well, Father, I cannot promise you anything,” I said at last; “what you are asking of me is beyond my strength. Believe me,” I continued, seeing him make an impatient movement, “you exaggerate the consequences of this liaison. Marguerite is not the sort of girl you believe her to be. This love, far from leading me down a bad path, is capable, on the contrary, of developing the most honorable feelings in me. True love always makes one better, whoever the woman who inspires it may be. If you knew Marguerite, you would understand that I am exposing myself to no danger. She is as noble as the noblest women. As much greed as there is in others, there is just as much selflessness in her.”

“Which does not prevent her from accepting your entire fortune, for the sixty thousand francs that come to you from your mother, and that you are giving her, are—remember well what I am telling you—your only fortune.”

My father had probably saved this peroration and this threat to deal me the final blow.

I was stronger in the face of his threats than in the face of his entreaties.

“Who told you that I was going to hand that sum over to her?” I replied.

“My notary. Would an honest man have drawn up such a deed without warning me? Well, I have come to Paris to prevent you from ruining yourself for the sake of a girl. When your mother died, she left you enough to live honorably, not enough to lavish gifts upon your mistresses.”

“I swear to you, Father, Marguerite knew nothing of this gift.”

“Then why were you making it?”

“Because Marguerite, this woman whom you slander and whom you want me to abandon, is sacrificing everything she possesses in order to live with me.”

“And you accept that sacrifice? What sort of man are you, sir, to allow a Mademoiselle Marguerite to sacrifice anything for you? Come, that is enough. You will leave this woman. A moment ago I was asking you; now I order you. I will not have such filth in my family. Pack your trunks and prepare to follow me.”

“Forgive me, Father,” I then said, “but I will not leave.”

“Because?…”

“Because I have already reached the age when one no longer obeys an order.”

My father turned pale at this reply.

“Very well, sir,” he resumed; “I know what remains for me to do.”

He rang.

Joseph appeared.

“Have my trunks taken to the Hôtel de Paris,” he said to my servant. At the same time, he went into his room, where he finished dressing.

When he reappeared, I went to meet him.

“Will you promise me, Father,” I said to him, “not to do anything that might cause Marguerite pain?”

My father stopped, looked at me disdainfully, and contented himself with replying:

“You are mad, I believe.”

After which he went out, violently closing the door behind him.

I went downstairs in my turn, took a cabriolet, and left for Bougival.

Marguerite was waiting for me at the window.




Chapter XXI


“At last!” she cried, throwing her arms around my neck. “Here you are! How pale you are!”

Then I told her about my scene with my father.

“Oh, my God! I suspected as much,” she said. “When Joseph came to tell us that your father had arrived, I shuddered as though at the news of some misfortune. Poor darling! And it is I who am causing you all this sorrow. Perhaps you would do better to leave me than to fall out with your father. Yet I have done nothing to him. We live very quietly, and we are going to live more quietly still. He knows very well that you must have a mistress, and he ought to be glad that it is I, since I love you and aspire to no more than your means allow. Did you tell him how we have arranged our future?”

“Yes, and that is what irritated him most, for he saw in that decision proof of our mutual love.”

“What are we to do, then?”

“Remain together, my dear Marguerite, and let this storm pass.”

“Will it pass?”

“It will have to.”

“But your father will not leave it at that.”

“What do you expect him to do?”

“How should I know? Everything a father can do to make his son obey him. He will remind you of my past life and will perhaps do me the honor of inventing a few new stories to make you abandon me.”

“You know very well that I love you.”

“Yes, but what I also know is that sooner or later one must obey one’s father, and perhaps you will end by allowing yourself to be persuaded.”
