“No, Marguerite, it is I who will persuade him. It is the gossip of some of his friends that is causing this great anger; but he is good, he is just, and he will reconsider his first impression. Besides, after all, what do I care!”

“Do not say that, Armand; I would rather endure anything than let it be thought that I am setting you against your family. Let today pass, and tomorrow return to Paris. Your father will have reflected on his side, as you have on yours, and perhaps you will understand one another better. Do not clash with his principles; appear to make a few concessions to his wishes; seem not to care quite so much for me, and he will leave things as they are. Hope, my darling, and be quite certain of one thing: whatever happens, your Marguerite will remain yours.”

“Do you swear it to me?”

“Do I need to swear it to you?”

How sweet it is to let oneself be persuaded by a voice one loves! Marguerite and I spent the whole day repeating our plans to each other, as though we had understood the need to carry them out more quickly. At every moment we expected some event, but fortunately the day passed without bringing anything new.

The next day, I left at ten o’clock and reached the hotel around noon.

My father had already gone out.

I went to my rooms, where I hoped he might perhaps have gone. No one had come. I went to my notary’s. No one!

I returned to the hotel and waited until six o’clock. Monsieur Duval did not return.

I set off again for Bougival.

I found Marguerite no longer waiting for me as on the previous day, but seated by the fire, which the season already made necessary.

She was sufficiently absorbed in her thoughts to let me approach her armchair without hearing me and without turning around. When I placed my lips on her forehead, she started as though that kiss had awakened her with a jolt.

“You frightened me,” she said to me. “And your father?”

“I did not see him. I do not know what this means. I found him neither at his hotel nor in any of the places where there was a possibility that he might be.”

“Well, it will have to be done again tomorrow.”

“I am strongly inclined to wait until he sends for me. I believe I have done everything I ought to do.”

“No, my darling, that is not enough; you must go back to your father, especially tomorrow.”

“But I assure you,” I added in a cold tone, as though I had wished to prove that I was forever cured of my passion, “I assure you that I am not angry. It was perfectly natural that someone should be waiting for you, just as it is perfectly natural for me to leave at three in the morning.”

“Do you also have someone waiting for you at home?”

“No, but I must go.”

“Goodbye, then.”

“You are sending me away?”

“Not in the least.”

“Why are you hurting me?”

“How have I hurt you?”

“You tell me that someone was waiting for you.”

“I could not help laughing at the thought that you had been so happy to see me come home alone, when there was such a good reason for it.”

“One often takes childish delight in a trifle, and it is cruel to destroy that delight when, by allowing it to remain, one can make the person who finds it happier still.”

“But whom do you think you are dealing with? I am neither a virgin nor a duchess. I have known you only since today, and I owe you no account of my actions. Even supposing that one day I become your mistress, you must understand clearly that I have had other lovers besides you. If you are already making jealous scenes before it happens, what will it be like afterward, if there ever is an afterward! I have never seen a man like you.”

“That is because no one has ever loved you as I love you.”

“Come now, honestly, do you really love me so much?”

“As much as it is possible to love, I believe.”

“And this has been going on since...?”

“Since a day when I saw you step down from a carriage and enter Susse’s, three years ago.”

“Do you know that is very beautiful? Well then, what must I do to acknowledge this great love?”

“You must love me a little,” I said, with a pounding heart that almost prevented me from speaking; for, despite the half-mocking smiles with which she had accompanied this entire conversation, it seemed to me that Marguerite was beginning to share my agitation, and that I was approaching the hour I had awaited for so long.

“Well, and the duke?”

“What duke?”

“My jealous old man.”

“He will know nothing about it.”

“And if he does find out?”

“He will forgive you.”

“Oh, no! He will abandon me, and what will become of me?”

“You certainly risk his abandoning you for another man.”

“How do you know?”

“From the instruction you gave that no one was to be admitted tonight.”

“That is true; but that man is a serious lover.”

“One for whom you care very little, since you have your door barred to him at such an hour.”

“You are hardly the person to reproach me for that, since it was in order to receive you, you and your friend.”

Little by little I had moved closer to Marguerite; I had put my hands around her waist, and I could feel her supple body resting lightly upon my clasped hands.

“If you only knew how I love you!” I said to her softly.

“Is that really true?”

“I swear it to you.”

“Well, if you promise to do everything I wish without saying a word, without raising an objection, without questioning me, I may love you.”

“Anything you wish!”

“But I warn you: I want to be free to do whatever I please, without giving you the slightest detail about my life. For a long time I have been looking for a young lover, with no will of his own, loving without suspicion, loved without rights. I have never been able to find one. Men, instead of being satisfied that one grants them for a long time what they would scarcely have hoped to obtain once, demand from their mistress an account of the present, the past, and even the future. As they grow accustomed to her, they want to dominate her, and they become all the more demanding the more one gives them everything they want. If I decide to take a new lover now, I want him to possess three very rare qualities: I want him to be trusting, submissive, and discreet.”

“Well, I shall be anything you wish.”

“We shall see.”

“And when shall we see?”

“Later.”

“Why?”

“Because,” said Marguerite, freeing herself from my arms and taking from a large bouquet of red camellias brought that morning a camellia which she placed in my buttonhole, “because treaties cannot always be carried out on the day they are signed. It is easy to understand.”

“And when shall I see you again?” I said, pressing her in my arms.

“When this camellia changes color.”

“And when will it change color?”

“Tomorrow, from eleven until midnight. Are you satisfied?”

“You ask me that?”

“Not a word about any of this to your friend, or to Prudence, or to anyone at all.”

“I promise you.”

“Now kiss me, and let us go back into the dining room.”

She offered me her lips, smoothed her hair once more, and we left that room, she singing, I half mad.

In the drawing room she stopped and said softly to me:

“It must seem strange to you that I appear ready to accept you like this, at once; do you know what causes it? It is because,” she continued, taking my hand and placing it against her heart, whose violent, repeated throbbing I felt, “it is because, as I am destined to live less long than others, I have promised myself to live more quickly.”

“Do not speak to me like that again, I beg you.”

“Oh! Take comfort,” she continued, laughing. “However little time I may have to live, I shall live longer than you will love me.”

And she went into the dining room singing.

“Where is Nanine?” she said when she saw Gaston and Prudence alone.

“She is asleep in your bedroom, waiting for you to go to bed,” Prudence replied.

“The poor creature! I am killing her! Come, gentlemen, be off; it is time.”

Ten minutes later, Gaston and I went out. Marguerite squeezed my hand as she said goodbye to me and remained with Prudence.

“Well,” Gaston asked me when we were outside, “what do you say of Marguerite?”

“She is an angel, and I am mad about her.”

“I suspected as much; did you tell her?”

“Yes.”

“And did she promise to believe you?”

“No.”

“That is not how it was with Prudence.”

“She promised you?”

“She did better than that, my dear fellow! One would never believe it, but that fat Duvernoy is still very fine!”

“Come, come,” she said to me, “drive away those bad theories and laugh; life is delightful, my dear, depending on the glass through which one looks at it. Here, consult your friend Gaston; there is a man who strikes me as understanding love as I understand it. What you must be convinced of, unless you want to become an insipid young man, is that next door there is a beautiful girl who is impatiently waiting for the man who is with her to leave, who is thinking of you, who is reserving her night for you, and who loves you—I am certain of it. Now come and stand at the window with me, and let us watch the count leave; he will not be long in making room for us.”

Prudence opened a window, and we leaned side by side on the balcony.

She watched the few passersby; I dreamed.

Everything she had said was buzzing in my head, and I could not help admitting that she was right; but the genuine love I felt for Marguerite had difficulty accommodating itself to that reasoning. And so, from time to time, I heaved sighs that made Prudence turn around and shrug her shoulders like a doctor who has despaired of a patient.

“How clearly one perceives that life must be short,” I said to myself, “from the rapidity of its sensations! I have known Marguerite for only two days, she has been my mistress only since yesterday, and she has already so completely taken possession of my thoughts, my heart, and my life that this visit from the Count de G... is a calamity for me.”

At last the count came out, got back into his carriage, and disappeared. Prudence closed her window.

At that same moment Marguerite called us.

“Come quickly, they are setting the table,” she said. “We are going to have supper.”

When I entered her rooms, Marguerite ran to me, threw herself upon my neck, and kissed me with all her might.

“Are we still sulking?” she asked me.

“No, it is over,” Prudence replied. “I gave him a moral lecture, and he promised to behave.”

“That is more like it!”

In spite of myself, I glanced at the bed; it was still made. As for Marguerite, she was already wearing a white dressing gown.

We sat down at table.

Charm, sweetness, openness—Marguerite had them all, and from time to time I was forced to acknowledge that I had no right to ask anything more of her; that many people would have been happy in my place; and that, like Virgil’s shepherd, I had only to enjoy the leisure a god—or rather a goddess—afforded me.

I tried to put Prudence’s theories into practice and to be as cheerful as my two companions; but what was natural in them was an effort in me, and my nervous laughter, which deceived them, came very close to tears.

At last supper came to an end, and I was left alone with Marguerite. As was her habit, she went and sat on her rug before the fire and gazed sadly at the flame in the hearth.

She was musing! About what? I do not know. I watched her lovingly and almost fearfully as I thought of what I was ready to suffer for her.

“Dost thou know what I was thinking about?”

“No.”

“About a plan I have devised.”

“And what is this plan?”

“I cannot confide it to thee yet, but I can tell thee what would result from it. The result would be that a month from now I should be free, I should no longer owe anything, and we should go and spend the summer together in the country.”

“And you cannot tell me by what means?”

“No; thou needst only love me as I love thee, and everything will succeed.”

“And did you devise this plan entirely by yourself?”

“Yes.”

“And will you carry it out by yourself?”

“I alone shall have the troubles,” Marguerite said to me with a smile I shall never forget, “but we shall share the profits.”

I could not help blushing at the word “profits”; I remembered Manon Lescaut and Des Grieux living on M. de B...’s money.

I replied in a rather harsh tone, rising as I did so:

“You will permit me, my dear Marguerite, to share only in the profits of ventures that I devise and carry out myself.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means that I strongly suspect the Count de G... of being your partner in this happy plan, whose liabilities and profits I accept neither.”

“You are a child. I thought you loved me; I was mistaken. Very well.”

At the same time, she rose, opened her piano, and began playing the Invitation to the Dance again, up to that famous passage in the major key that always stopped her.

Was it from habit, or to remind me of the day on which we had met? All I know is that with that melody my memories returned, and, going over to her, I took her head between my hands and kissed her.

“Do you forgive me?” I asked her.

“You can plainly see that I do,” she replied; “but take note that this is only our second day, and already I have something to forgive you for. You keep your promises of blind obedience very badly.”

“What can I do, Marguerite? I love you too much, and I am jealous of your slightest thought. What you proposed to me just now would drive me wild with joy, but the mystery preceding the execution of this plan constricts my heart.”

“Come, let us reason a little,” she resumed, taking both my hands and looking at me with a charming smile that I found impossible to resist. “You love me, do you not? And you would be happy to spend three or four months in the country alone with me. I too would be happy in that solitude together; not only would I be happy in it, but I need it for my health. I cannot leave Paris for so long without putting my affairs in order, and the affairs of a woman like me are always very tangled. Well, I have found the means of reconciling everything—my affairs and my love for you; yes, for you, do not laugh: I am mad enough to love you! And now you put on your grand airs and say grand words to me. Child, child three times over, remember only that I love you, and do not worry about anything.—Is it agreed, then?”

“Whatever you want is agreed; you know that very well.”

“Then, before a month has passed, we shall be in some village, walking beside the water and drinking milk. It seems strange to you that I, Marguerite Gautier, should speak in this way. That is because, my friend, when this Parisian life, which seems to make me so happy, does not consume me, it bores me, and then I have sudden yearnings for a quieter existence that would remind me of my childhood. One has always had a childhood, whatever one may have become. Oh! Do not worry, I am not going to tell you that I am the daughter of a retired colonel and that I was educated at Saint-Denis. I am a poor country girl, and six years ago I did not know how to write my name. That reassures you, does it not? Why are you the first person to whom I turn to share the joy of the desire that came over me? No doubt because I recognized that you loved me for my sake and not for yours, whereas the others have never loved me except for their own.”

“You are young, you are beautiful; life will console you. You are noble, and the memory of a good deed will redeem many things from the past for you. In the six months he has known you, Armand has forgotten me. Four times I have written to him without his once thinking of answering me. I could have died without his knowing it!

“Whatever your resolve to live differently from the way you have lived, Armand, who loves you, will not consent to the seclusion to which his modest position would condemn you, and which is not suited to your beauty. Who knows what he might then do! He has gambled; I found out. Without your telling me anything about it, I know it still; but, in a moment of intoxication, he might have lost part of what I have been amassing for many years for my daughter’s dowry, for him, and for the peace of my old age. What might have happened may still happen.

“Are you certain, moreover, that the life you would leave for him would not attract you again? Are you certain, you who have loved him, that you will not love another? Will you not, in the end, suffer from the obstacles your relationship will place in your lover’s life, and for which you may be unable to console him if, with age, thoughts of ambition succeed dreams of love? Reflect on all this, madame: you love Armand; prove it to him by the only means still left to you of proving it to him—by sacrificing your love to his future. No misfortune has yet occurred, but misfortunes would occur, and perhaps greater ones than those I foresee. Armand may become jealous of a man who has loved you; he may challenge him, he may fight, he may finally be killed; and think what you would suffer before the father who would demand an accounting from you for his son’s life.

“Lastly, my child, know everything, for I have not told you everything; know, then, what brought me to Paris. I have a daughter, as I have just told you, young, beautiful, pure as an angel. She is in love, and she too has made that love the dream of her life. I had written all this to Armand, but, wholly absorbed in you, he did not answer me. Well, my daughter is going to marry. She is marrying the man she loves; she is entering an honorable family that wants everything in mine to be honorable. The family of the man who is to become my son-in-law has learned how Armand lives in Paris and has declared to me that it will withdraw its word if Armand continues this life. The future of a girl who has done you no harm, and who has the right to count on the future, is in your hands.

“Have you the right, and do you feel you have the strength, to shatter it? In the name of your love and your repentance, Marguerite, grant me my daughter’s happiness.

“I wept silently, my friend, before all these reflections, which I had often made myself and which, in your father’s mouth, acquired an even graver reality. I told myself everything your father did not dare tell me and which had come to his lips twenty times: that, after all, I was nothing but a kept woman, and that whatever reason I might give for our relationship, it would always have the appearance of a calculation; that my past life left me no right to dream of such a future, and that I was accepting responsibilities for which my habits and my reputation afforded no guarantee. Lastly, I loved you, Armand. The paternal manner in which Monsieur Duval spoke to me, the chaste sentiments he evoked in me, the esteem of that loyal old man which I was about to win, and yours, which I was certain of having later—all this awakened noble thoughts in my heart that raised me in my own eyes and gave voice to holy vanities until then unknown to me. When I thought that one day this old man, who was imploring me for his son’s future, would tell his daughter to mingle my name with her prayers, like the name of a mysterious friend, I was transformed, and I was proud of myself.

“The exaltation of the moment perhaps exaggerated the truth of these impressions; but that is what I felt, my friend, and these new feelings silenced the counsels given me by the memory of the happy days spent with you.”

“—Very well, monsieur, I said to your father as I wiped away my tears. Do you believe that I love your son?

“—Yes, Monsieur Duval said to me.

“—With a selfless love?

“—Yes.

“—Do you believe that I had made this love the hope, the dream, and the pardon of my life?

“—Firmly.

“—Well, monsieur, embrace me once as you would embrace your daughter, and I swear to you that this kiss, the only truly chaste one I have ever received, will make me strong against my love, and that within a week your son will have returned to you, perhaps unhappy for a time, but cured forever.

“—You are a noble girl, your father replied, kissing me on the forehead, and you are attempting something for which God will give you credit; but I greatly fear that you will achieve nothing with my son.

“—Oh! Do not worry, monsieur; he will hate me.

“There had to be an insurmountable barrier between us, for one as well as for the other.

“I wrote to Prudence that I accepted Monsieur le Comte de N…’s proposals, and that she should go and tell him that I would have supper with her and with him.

“I sealed the letter and, without telling him what it contained, asked your father to have it delivered to its address upon arriving in Paris.

“He nevertheless asked me what it contained.

“—It is your son’s happiness, I answered him.

“Your father embraced me one last time. I felt on my forehead two tears of gratitude that were like the baptism of my former sins, and at the very moment when I had just consented to give myself to another man, I shone with pride at the thought of what I was redeeming through this new sin.

“It was only natural, Armand; you had told me that your father was the most honorable man one could ever meet.

“Monsieur Duval got back into his carriage and left.

“But I was a woman, and when I saw you again, I could not keep from weeping; yet I did not weaken.

“Did I do right? That is what I ask myself today, as I take, ill, to a bed that I may leave only when dead.

“You witnessed what I felt as the hour of our inevitable separation drew nearer; your father was no longer there to sustain me, and there was a moment when I came very close to confessing everything to you, so terrified was I by the thought that you were going to hate and despise me.

I had gone too far to turn back, and besides, this girl overwhelmed me. This mixture of gaiety, sadness, innocence, prostitution, even this illness, which was bound to heighten in her the sensitivity of her impressions as well as the irritability of her nerves—everything made me understand that if, from the very first, I did not gain some hold over this forgetful and flighty nature, she was lost to me.

“Come now, is what you are saying really serious?” she said.

“Very serious.”

“But why did you not tell me this sooner?”

“When could I have told you?”

“The day after you were introduced to me at the Opéra-Comique.”

“I think you would have received me very badly if I had come to see you.”

“Why?”

“Because I had been stupid the night before.”

“That is true. But even so, you already loved me then?”

“Yes.”

“Which did not prevent you from going to bed and sleeping quite peacefully after the performance. We know what these great loves are like.”

“Well, that is where you are mistaken. Do you know what I did on the evening of the Opéra-Comique?”

“No.”

“I waited for you at the door of the Café Anglais. I followed the carriage that took you and your three friends away, and when I saw you alight alone and go into your home alone, I was very happy.”

Marguerite began to laugh.

“What are you laughing at?”

“Nothing.”

“Tell me, I beg you, or I shall think that you are making fun of me again.”

“You will not be angry?”

“What right would I have to be angry?”

“Well, there was a good reason why I went home alone.”

“What was it?”

“Someone was waiting for me here.”

Had she stabbed me with a knife, she could not have hurt me more. I rose and, holding out my hand to her, said:

“Goodbye.”

“I knew you would be angry,” she said. “Men have a mania for wanting to learn what is bound to cause them pain.”

“But I assure you,” I added in a cold tone, as though I had wished to prove that I was forever cured of my passion, “I assure you that I am not angry. It was perfectly natural for someone to be waiting for you, just as it is perfectly natural for me to leave at three in the morning.”

“Do you too have someone waiting for you at home?”

“No, but I must go.”

“Goodbye, then.”

“Are you sending me away?”

“Not in the least.”

“Why are you hurting me?”

“How have I hurt you?”

“You tell me that someone was waiting for you.”

“I could not help laughing at the thought that you had been so happy to see me go home alone, when there was such a good reason for it.”

“We often make a joy of some childish trifle, and it is cruel to destroy that joy when, by allowing it to remain, one can make the person who finds it happier still.”

“But who do you think you are dealing with? I am neither a virgin nor a duchess. I have known you only since today, and I owe you no account of my actions. Even supposing that one day I become your mistress, you must understand that I have had other lovers besides you. If you are already making jealous scenes before then, what will it be afterward, if there ever is an afterward? I have never seen a man like you.”

“That is because no one has ever loved you as I love you.”

“Come now, honestly, do you really love me so much?”

“As much as it is possible to love, I believe.”

“And this has lasted since...?”

“Since a day when I saw you alight from a carriage and enter Susse’s, three years ago.”

“Do you know that that is very beautiful? Well, what must I do to acknowledge this great love?”

“You must love me a little,” I said, with a pounding heart that almost prevented me from speaking; for, despite the half-mocking smiles with which she had accompanied this entire conversation, it seemed to me that Marguerite was beginning to share my agitation and that I was approaching the hour I had awaited for so long.

“Well, and the duke?”

“What duke?”

“My jealous old man.”

“He will know nothing about it.”

“And if he does find out?”

“He will forgive you.”

“Oh, no! He will abandon me, and what will become of me?”

“You do risk his abandoning you for someone else.”

“How do you know?”

“From the instruction you gave that no one was to be admitted tonight.”

“That is true; but that man is a serious friend.”

“One for whom you care very little, since you have your door barred to him at such an hour.”

“You are hardly the one to reproach me for that, since it was in order to receive you and your friend.”

Little by little I had drawn closer to Marguerite; I had put my hands around her waist, and I could feel her supple body resting lightly upon my clasped hands.

“If you only knew how I love you!” I said to her in a low voice.

“Truly?”

“I swear it to you.”

“Well, if you promise to do everything I wish without saying a word, without raising an objection, without questioning me, perhaps I shall love you.”

“Anything you wish!”

“But I warn you, I want to be free to do whatever I please, without giving you the slightest detail about my life. For a long time I have been looking for a young lover, without a will of his own, loving without mistrust, loved without rights. I have never been able to find one. Men, instead of being satisfied that they are granted for a long time what they would scarcely have hoped to obtain once, demand from their mistress an account of the present, the past, and even the future. As they grow accustomed to her, they want to dominate her, and they become all the more demanding the more they are given everything they want. If I decide to take a new lover now, I want him to possess three very rare qualities: I want him to be trusting, submissive, and discreet.”

“Well, I shall be everything you wish.”

“We shall see.”

“And when shall we see?”

“Later.”

“Why?”

“Because,” said Marguerite, freeing herself from my arms and taking from a large bouquet of red camellias brought that morning a camellia which she put in my buttonhole, “because treaties cannot always be carried out on the day they are signed. That is easy to understand.”

“And when shall I see you again?” I said, clasping her in my arms.

“When this camellia changes color.”

“And when will it change color?”

“Tomorrow, between eleven and midnight. Are you satisfied?”

“That is true,” I said, letting my head fall onto Marguerite’s knees; “but I love you like a madman.”

“Well, my friend, you should have loved me a little less or understood me a little better. Your letter caused me a great deal of pain. If I had been free, in the first place I would not have received the count the day before yesterday, or, having received him, I would have come to ask you for the forgiveness you were asking of me just now, and from then on I would have had no lover but you. For a moment I thought I could grant myself that happiness for six months; you did not want it; you insisted on knowing the means, and, good God, the means were easy enough to guess. In making use of them, I was making a greater sacrifice than you think. I could have said to you: I need twenty thousand francs; you were in love with me, and you would have found them, at the risk of reproaching me for them later. I preferred to owe you nothing; you did not understand that delicacy, for it is one. We women, when we still have a little heart left, give words and things a breadth and a significance unknown to other women; and so I repeat that, on Marguerite Gautier’s part, the means she found of paying her debts without asking you for the money needed to do so were a delicacy from which you ought to benefit without saying a word. If you had met me only today, you would be only too happy with what I would promise you, and you would not ask me what I did the day before yesterday. We are sometimes forced to purchase satisfaction for our soul at the expense of our body, and we suffer far more when, afterward, that satisfaction eludes us.”

I listened to Marguerite and gazed at her in admiration. When I reflected that this marvelous creature, whose feet I would once have longed to kiss, was consenting to let me count for something in her thoughts, to give me a role in her life, and that I was still not content with what she was giving me, I wondered whether man’s desire has any bounds when, having been satisfied as quickly as mine had been, it still reaches for something else.

“It is true,” she resumed; “we creatures of chance have fanciful desires and inconceivable loves. We give ourselves for one thing one day and for another the next. There are people who would ruin themselves without obtaining anything from us, and there are others who can have us for a bouquet. Our heart has its whims; that is its only diversion and its only excuse. I gave myself to you more quickly than to any man, I swear it; why? Because, seeing me cough blood, you took my hand, because you wept, because you are the only human being who was willing to pity me. I am going to tell you something foolish, but I once had a little dog that looked at me very sadly when I coughed; it is the only being I have ever loved.

“When it died, I wept more than I did at my mother’s death. It is true that she had beaten me for twelve years of her life. Well, I loved you at once as much as I loved my dog. If men knew what can be had with a tear, they would be loved more and we would be less ruinous.

“Your letter belied you; it revealed to me that you did not possess all the insights of the heart; it harmed you more in the love I had for you than anything you could have done to me. It was jealousy, it is true, but ironic and impertinent jealousy. I was already sad when I received that letter; I expected to see you at noon, to have lunch with you, to erase, by the sight of you, a persistent thought I had, one that before knowing you I accepted without difficulty.

“Besides,” Marguerite continued, “you were the only person before whom I had immediately believed I could think and speak freely. Everyone who surrounds women like me has an interest in scrutinizing their slightest words and drawing conclusions from their most insignificant actions. Naturally, we have no friends. We have selfish lovers who spend their fortunes not for us, as they say, but for their vanity.

“For those people, we must be cheerful when they are joyful, in good health when they want supper, and as skeptical as they are. We are forbidden to have a heart, on pain of being jeered at and ruining our credit.

“We no longer belong to ourselves. We are no longer beings, but things. We come first in their self-love and last in their esteem. We have female friends, but they are friends like Prudence, women who were once kept and who still have expensive tastes that their age no longer allows them to indulge. Then they become our friends, or rather our table companions. Their friendship goes as far as servitude, never as far as disinterestedness. They will never give you anything but profitable advice. It matters little to them if we have ten more lovers, provided they gain dresses or a bracelet from it, and can from time to time ride in our carriage and come to the theater in our box. They take our bouquets from the day before and borrow our cashmere shawls. They never do us a service, however small, without making us pay twice what it is worth. You saw it yourself on the evening when Prudence brought me the six thousand francs I had asked her to go and request from the duke on my behalf: she borrowed five hundred francs from me, which she will never repay, or which she will pay back in hats that will never leave their boxes.

“And so we cannot have—or rather, I could not have—but one happiness: sad as I sometimes am, ill as I always am, to find a man superior enough not to demand an account of my life from me, and to be the lover of my feelings far more than of my body. I had found that man in the duke, but the duke is old, and old age neither protects nor consoles. I had thought I could accept the life he provided for me; but what can I say? I was perishing from boredom, and if I had to be consumed, I might as well throw myself into a blaze as suffocate myself with charcoal.”

—My notary. Would an honest man have done such a thing without warning me? Well, it is to prevent you from ruining yourself over a girl that I have come to Paris. When your mother died, she left you enough to live honorably, not enough to lavish gifts on your mistresses.

—I swear to you, Father, Marguerite knew nothing of this gift.

—Then why were you making it?

—Because Marguerite, this woman whom you slander and whom you want me to abandon, is sacrificing everything she possesses in order to live with me.

—And you accept this sacrifice? What kind of man are you, sir, to allow a Mademoiselle Marguerite to sacrifice anything for you? Come now, that is enough. You will leave this woman. A moment ago I was asking you; now I am ordering you. I will have no such filth in my family. Pack your bags and prepare to come with me.

—Forgive me, Father, I then said, but I will not leave.

—Because?...

—Because I have already reached the age when one no longer obeys an order.

My father turned pale at this reply.

—Very well, sir, he resumed; I know what remains for me to do.

He rang.

Joseph appeared.

—Have my bags taken to the Hôtel de Paris, he said to my servant. At the same time, he went into his room, where he finished dressing.

When he reappeared, I went to meet him.

—Will you promise me, Father, I said to him, not to do anything that might cause Marguerite pain?

My father stopped, looked at me disdainfully, and merely replied:

—I believe you are mad.

After which he went out, violently slamming the door behind him.

I went downstairs in my turn, took a cabriolet, and left for Bougival.

Marguerite was waiting for me at the window.




Chapter XXI


—At last! she exclaimed, throwing her arms around my neck. Here you are! How pale you are!

Then I told her about my confrontation with my father.

—Oh, my God! I suspected as much, she said. When Joseph came to tell us of your father’s arrival, I shuddered as though at news of some calamity. Poor darling! And it is I who am causing you all this sorrow. Perhaps you would do better to leave me than to fall out with your father. And yet I have done nothing to him. We are living very quietly, and we are going to live more quietly still. He knows very well that you must have a mistress, and he ought to be happy that it is I, since I love you and desire no more than your position allows. Did you tell him how we have arranged our future?

—Yes, and that is what irritated him most, for he saw in that decision proof of our mutual love.

—What are we to do, then?

—Stay together, my dear Marguerite, and let this storm pass.

—Will it pass?

—It will have to.

—But your father will not leave it at that.

—What do you expect him to do?

—How should I know? Everything a father can do to make his son obey him. He will remind you of my past life and perhaps do me the honor of inventing a few new stories so that you will abandon me.

—You know very well that I love you.

—Yes, but what I also know is that sooner or later one must obey one’s father, and perhaps in the end you will allow yourself to be persuaded.

—No, Marguerite, it is I who will persuade him. It is the gossip of some of his friends that is causing this great anger; but he is good, he is just, and he will reconsider his first impression. Besides, after all, what do I care!

—Do not say that, Armand; I would prefer anything to letting people think that I am making you fall out with your family. Let today pass, and tomorrow go back to Paris. Your father will have reflected on his side, as you have on yours, and perhaps you will understand each other better. Do not clash with his principles; appear to make a few concessions to his wishes; seem not to care quite so much for me, and he will leave things as they are. Have hope, my darling, and be quite certain of one thing: whatever happens, your Marguerite will remain yours.

—Do you swear it to me?

—Do I need to swear it to you?

How sweet it is to let oneself be persuaded by a voice one loves! Marguerite and I spent the whole day repeating our plans to each other, as though we had understood the need to carry them out more quickly. At every moment we expected some event, but fortunately the day passed without bringing anything new.

The next day, I left at ten o’clock and arrived at the hotel around noon.

My father had already gone out.

I went to my own home, where I hoped he might perhaps have gone. No one had come. I went to my notary’s. No one!

I returned to the hotel and waited until six o’clock. Monsieur Duval did not return.

I set out again for Bougival.

I found Marguerite no longer waiting for me as she had the day before, but sitting by the fire, which the season already made necessary.

She was so deeply absorbed in thought that she allowed me to approach her armchair without hearing me and without turning around. When I pressed my lips to her forehead, she started as though the kiss had awakened her with a jolt.

—You frightened me, she said. And your father?

—I did not see him. I do not know what this means. I found him neither at his place nor in any of the places where there was a possibility that he might be.

—Well, you will have to try again tomorrow.

—I am strongly inclined to wait until he sends for me. I believe I have done everything I ought to do.

—No, my darling, that is not enough; you must go back to your father, especially tomorrow.

—Why tomorrow rather than another day?

—Because, said Marguerite, who seemed to blush a little at this question, because your insistence will appear more earnest, and we shall be forgiven sooner as a result.

For the rest of the day, Marguerite was preoccupied, distracted, sad. I was obliged to repeat what I said to her twice in order to obtain an answer. She attributed this preoccupation to the fears for the future inspired in her by the events of the past two days.

I spent the night reassuring her, and the next day she made me leave with an anxious insistence that I could not explain.

Had she stabbed me, she could not have hurt me more. I rose and, holding out my hand to her:

“Goodbye,” I said.

“I knew you would get angry,” she said. “Men have a mania for wanting to learn what is bound to cause them pain.”

“But I assure you,” I added in a cold tone, as though I had wished to prove that I was forever cured of my passion, “I assure you that I am not angry. It was perfectly natural that someone should be waiting for you, just as it is perfectly natural for me to leave at three in the morning.”

“Do you also have someone waiting for you at home?”

“No, but I must go.”

“Goodbye, then.”

“You are sending me away?”

“Not in the least.”

“Why are you causing me pain?”

“What pain have I caused you?”

“You tell me that someone was waiting for you.”

“I could not help laughing at the thought that you had been so happy to see me come home alone, when there was such a good reason for it.”

“We often take childish delight in something, and it is cruel to destroy that delight when, by allowing it to remain, one can make the person who finds it happier still.”

“But who do you think you are dealing with? I am neither a virgin nor a duchess. I have known you only since today and owe you no account of my actions. Even supposing that I should one day become your mistress, you must understand that I have had other lovers besides you. If you are already making jealous scenes before it happens, what will it be like afterward, if there ever is an afterward! I have never seen a man like you.”

“That is because no one has ever loved you as I love you.”

“Come now, honestly, do you really love me so much?”

“As much as it is possible to love, I believe.”

“And this has lasted since...?”

“Since a day when I saw you step down from a carriage and enter Susse’s, three years ago.”

“Do you know that is very beautiful? Well then, what must I do to acknowledge this great love?”

“You must love me a little,” I said, with my heart beating so hard that I could scarcely speak; for, despite the half-mocking smiles with which she had accompanied this entire conversation, it seemed to me that Marguerite was beginning to share my agitation, and that I was approaching the hour I had awaited for so long.

“Well, and the duke?”

“What duke?”

“My jealous old man.”

“He will know nothing about it.”

“And if he finds out?”

“He will forgive you.”

“Oh, no! He will abandon me, and what will become of me?”

“You do risk being abandoned by him for another man.”

“How do you know?”

“From the instruction you gave that no one was to be let in tonight.”

“That is true; but that man is a serious friend.”

“One for whom you care very little, since you have your door barred to him at such an hour.”

“You are hardly the one to reproach me for that, since it was in order to receive you, you and your friend.”

Little by little I had drawn closer to Marguerite, had put my hands around her waist, and could feel her supple body resting lightly on my clasped hands.

“If you only knew how I love you!” I said to her in a low voice.

“Is that really true?”

“I swear it to you.”

“Well, if you promise to do everything I wish without saying a word, without raising an objection, without questioning me, perhaps I shall love you.”

“Anything you wish!”

“But I warn you, I want to be free to do whatever I please, without giving you the slightest detail about my life. For a long time I have been looking for a young lover, without a will of his own, loving without mistrust, loved without rights. I have never been able to find one. Instead of being satisfied that they are granted for a long time what they would scarcely have hoped to obtain once, men demand from their mistress an account of the present, the past, and even the future. As they grow accustomed to her, they want to dominate her, and they become all the more demanding the more they are given everything they want. If I decide to take a new lover now, I want him to possess three very rare qualities: I want him to be trusting, submissive, and discreet.”

“Well, I shall be anything you wish.”

“We shall see.”

“And when shall we see?”

“Later.”

“Why?”

“Because,” said Marguerite, freeing herself from my arms and taking from a large bouquet of red camellias brought that morning a camellia which she slipped into my buttonhole, “because treaties cannot always be carried out on the day they are signed. That is easy to understand.”

“And when shall I see you again?” I said, clasping her in my arms.

“When this camellia changes color.”

“And when will it change color?”

“Tomorrow, between eleven and midnight. Are you satisfied?”

“You have to ask?”

“Not a word about any of this to your friend, or to Prudence, or to anyone at all.”

“I promise you.”

“Now kiss me, and let us go back into the dining room.”

She offered me her lips, smoothed her hair once more, and we left that room, she singing, I half mad.

In the drawing room she said to me in a low voice, stopping:

“It must seem strange to you that I appear ready to accept you so immediately; do you know what causes it? It is because,” she continued, taking my hand and placing it against her heart, whose violent, repeated throbbing I felt, “it is because, since I am destined to live less long than others, I have promised myself to live more quickly.”

“Do not speak to me like that anymore, I beg you.”

“Oh! Take comfort,” she continued, laughing. “However little time I may have to live, I shall live longer than you will love me.”

And she went into the dining room singing.

“Where is Nanine?” she said when she saw Gaston and Prudence alone.

“She is sleeping in your room, waiting for you to go to bed,” Prudence replied.

“The poor creature! I am killing her! Come, gentlemen, leave; it is time.”

Ten minutes later, Gaston and I went out. Marguerite squeezed my hand as she said goodbye to me and remained with Prudence.

“Well,” Gaston asked me when we were outside, “what do you say to Marguerite?”

“She is an angel, and I am mad about her.”

“What do you expect, Marguerite? I love you too much, and I am jealous of the least of your thoughts. What you proposed to me just now would drive me mad with joy, but the mystery that precedes the execution of this plan constricts my heart.”

“Come, let us reason a little,” she resumed, taking both my hands and looking at me with a charming smile which it was impossible for me to resist; “you love me, do you not? And you would be happy to spend three or four months in the country alone with me; I too would be happy with this solitude for two; not only would I be happy with it, but I need it for my health. I cannot leave Paris for so long without putting my affairs in order, and the affairs of a woman like me are always very tangled; well, I have found a way to reconcile everything, my affairs and my love for you—yes, for you, do not laugh, I am mad enough to love you! And now you put on your grand airs and say grand things to me. Child, three times a child, just remember that I love you, and do not worry about anything. Is it agreed, then?”

“Whatever you wish is agreed; you know that very well.”

“Then, before a month has passed, we shall be in some village, walking along the water’s edge and drinking milk. It seems strange to you to hear me talk this way, me, Marguerite Gautier; that is because, my friend, when this Parisian life, which seems to make me so happy, does not burn me, it wearies me, and then I have sudden longings for a quieter existence that would remind me of my childhood. One has always had a childhood, whatever one may have become. Oh! Do not worry, I am not going to tell you that I am the daughter of a retired colonel and that I was educated at Saint-Denis. I am a poor country girl, and six years ago I did not know how to write my name. There, you are reassured, are you not? Why are you the first person to whom I turn to share the joy of the desire that has come over me? No doubt because I have recognized that you loved me for myself and not for yourself, whereas the others have never loved me except for themselves.

“I have very often been to the country, but never as I would have wished to go there. I am counting on you for this simple happiness, so do not be unkind, and grant it to me. Tell yourself this: she is not destined to live to old age, and one day I would regret not having done for her the first thing she asked of me, when it was so easy to do.”

What could one answer to such words, especially with the memory of a first night of love, and in expectation of a second?

An hour later, I held Marguerite in my arms, and had she asked me to commit a crime, I would have obeyed her.

At six in the morning I left, and before leaving I said to her:

“Until this evening?”

She embraced me more tightly, but did not answer me.

During the day, I received a letter containing these words:

“Dear child, I am a little unwell, and the doctor orders me to rest. I shall go to bed early this evening and shall not see you. But, to reward you, I shall expect you tomorrow at noon. I love you.”

My first words were: “She is deceiving me!”

An icy sweat passed over my brow, for I already loved this woman too much for that suspicion not to overwhelm me.

And yet, with Marguerite, I ought to have expected such an occurrence almost every day, and it had often happened to me with my other mistresses without my troubling much about it. Whence, then, came the power this woman was gaining over my life?

Then I thought that, since I had the key to her apartment, I would go and see her as usual. In that way I would very soon know the truth, and if I found a man there, I would slap his face.

In the meantime, I went to the Champs-Élysées. I remained there for four hours. She did not appear. In the evening, I went into every theater she habitually attended. She was in none of them.

At eleven o’clock, I went to the Rue d’Antin.

There was no light in Marguerite’s windows. Nevertheless, I rang. The porter asked me where I was going.

“To Mademoiselle Gautier’s,” I told him.

“She has not come home.”

“I shall go upstairs and wait for her.”

“There is no one at her apartment.”

Clearly, these were instructions that I could override, since I had the key, but I feared a ridiculous scene, and I left.

Only, I did not go home; I could not leave the street, and I did not take my eyes off Marguerite’s house. It seemed to me that I still had something to learn, or at least that my suspicions were going to be confirmed.

Around midnight, a coupé that I knew well stopped near number 9.

The Comte de G... stepped out of it and entered the house, after dismissing his carriage.

For a moment I hoped that, as with me, he would be told that Marguerite was not at home, and that I would see him come out again; but at four in the morning I was still waiting.

I have suffered greatly during the past three weeks, but it is nothing, I believe, compared with what I suffered that night.




Chapter XIV


Once home, I began to weep like a child. There is no man who has not been deceived at least once, and who does not know what one suffers.

Under the weight of those feverish resolutions which one always believes one will have the strength to keep, I told myself that I must break off this love immediately, and I waited impatiently for daylight so that I could go and book my seat and return to my father and my sister, a twofold love of which I was certain, and which would not deceive me.

However, I did not wish to leave without Marguerite knowing clearly why I was leaving. Only a man who has definitively ceased to love his mistress leaves her without writing to her.

I composed and recomposed twenty letters in my head.

I had been dealing with a girl like all kept women; I had idealized her far too much; she had treated me like a schoolboy, using, in order to deceive me, a ruse of insulting simplicity; it was clear. My pride then gained the upper hand. I had to leave this woman without giving her the satisfaction of knowing how much this break was making me suffer, and this is what I wrote to her, in my most elegant handwriting and with tears of rage and grief in my eyes:

Prudence had indeed brought all her moral influence to bear upon Marguerite concerning this new life; but Marguerite had replied that she loved me, that she could not live without me, and that, whatever might come of it, she would not give up the happiness of having me constantly beside her, adding that all those whom it displeased were free not to return.

That was what I had heard one day when Prudence had told Marguerite that she had something very important to tell her, and when I had listened at the door of the room in which they had shut themselves away.

Some time later Prudence returned.

I was at the far end of the garden when she came in; she did not see me. From the way Marguerite had gone to meet her, I suspected that a conversation like the one I had already overheard was about to take place again, and I wanted to hear it as I had the other.

The two women shut themselves in a boudoir, and I began listening.

“Well?” asked Marguerite.

“Well! I have seen the duke.”

“What did he say to you?”

“That he willingly forgave you for the first scene, but that he had learned that you were living openly with M. Armand Duval, and that he did not forgive you for that. ‘Let Marguerite leave this young man,’ he told me, ‘and, as in the past, I shall give her everything she wants; otherwise, she must give up asking me for anything whatsoever.’”

“And what did you answer?”

“That I would convey his decision to you, and I promised him that I would make you listen to reason. Think, my dear child, of the position you are losing, and which Armand will never be able to restore to you. He loves you with all his soul, but he does not have enough money to provide for all your needs, and one day he will indeed have to leave you, when it is too late and the duke is no longer willing to do anything for you. Would you like me to speak to Armand?”

Marguerite seemed to be thinking, for she did not answer. My heart was beating violently as I awaited her reply.

“No,” she resumed, “I shall not leave Armand, and I shall not hide in order to live with him. Perhaps it is madness, but I love him! What can you expect? And besides, by now he has grown accustomed to loving me without hindrance; he would suffer too much if he were forced to leave me, even for only an hour a day. Moreover, I do not have so much time left to live that I should make myself unhappy and do the bidding of an old man whose mere sight makes me grow old. Let him keep his money; I shall do without it.”

“But how will you manage?”

“I do not know.”

Prudence was doubtless about to answer something, but I burst in and ran to throw myself at Marguerite’s feet, covering her hands with the tears that the joy of being loved in this way made me shed.

“My life is yours, Marguerite; you no longer need that man—am I not here? Would I ever abandon you, and could I ever pay enough for the happiness you give me? No more constraint, my Marguerite; we love each other! What does the rest matter to us?”

“Oh! Yes, I love you, my Armand!” she murmured, winding both arms around my neck. “I love you as I would not have believed I was capable of loving. We shall be happy, we shall live peacefully, and I shall bid an eternal farewell to this life of which I am now ashamed. You will never reproach me for the past, will you?”

Tears veiled my voice. I could answer only by clasping Marguerite to my heart.

“Very well,” she said, turning back toward Prudence and speaking in an emotional voice, “you will report this scene to the duke, and you will add that we do not need him.”

From that day onward, there was no more talk of the duke. Marguerite was no longer the woman I had known. She avoided everything that might have reminded me of the life amid which I had met her. No wife, no sister ever showed her husband or her brother the love and care that she showed me. That sickly nature was open to every impression, receptive to every feeling. She had broken with her friends as she had with her habits, with her way of speaking as she had with her former expenditures. When people saw us leave the house to go for an outing in a charming little boat I had bought, they would never have believed that this woman, dressed in a white gown, shaded by a large straw hat, and carrying on her arm the simple silk cloak that was to protect her from the coolness of the water, was that same Marguerite Gautier who, four months earlier, had caused a stir with her luxury and her scandals.

Alas! We hastened to be happy, as though we had guessed that we could not be so for long.

For two months we had not even gone to Paris. No one had come to see us except Prudence and that Julie Duprat of whom I have spoken to you, and to whom Marguerite was later to entrust the touching account I have here.

I spent entire days at my mistress’s feet. We opened the windows overlooking the garden, and, watching summer alight joyfully upon the flowers it causes to bloom and beneath the shade of the trees, we breathed side by side that true life which neither Marguerite nor I had understood until then.

This woman displayed a child’s wonder at the smallest things. There were days when she ran through the garden, like a ten-year-old girl, chasing a butterfly or a dragonfly. This courtesan, who had caused more money to be spent on bouquets than would be needed to keep an entire family living happily, would sometimes sit on the lawn for an hour to examine the simple flower whose name she bore.

It was during that time that she so often read Manon Lescaut. Many times I caught her making notes in that book, and she always told me that when a woman loves, she cannot do what Manon did.

Two or three times the duke wrote to her. She recognized the handwriting and gave me the letters without reading them.

Sometimes the wording of those letters brought tears to my eyes.

He had believed that, by closing his purse to Marguerite, he would bring her back to him; but when he had seen how useless that means was, he had been unable to bear it. He had written, asking once again, as in the past, for permission to return, whatever conditions might be imposed upon that return.

In spite of myself, I glanced at the bed; it had not been disturbed. As for Marguerite, she was already wearing a white dressing gown.

We sat down at the table.

Charm, gentleness, openness—Marguerite had everything, and from time to time I was forced to acknowledge that I had no right to ask anything more of her; that many people would have been happy in my place, and that, like Virgil’s shepherd, I had only to enjoy the leisure that a god—or rather, a goddess—was granting me.

I tried to put Prudence’s theories into practice and to be as cheerful as my two companions; but what came naturally to them was an effort for me, and the nervous laughter by which they were deceived came very close to tears.

At last supper ended, and I was left alone with Marguerite. As was her custom, she went and sat on her rug before the fire and gazed sadly at the flame in the hearth.

She was thinking! Of what? I do not know; for my part, I watched her with love and almost with terror as I thought of what I was ready to suffer for her.

“Knowest thou what I was thinking about?”

“No.”

“About a plan I have devised.”

“And what is this plan?”

“I cannot confide it to thee yet, but I can tell thee what would result from it. The result would be that a month from now I should be free, I should no longer owe anything, and we should go and spend the summer together in the country.”

“And you cannot tell me by what means?”

“No; thou needst only love me as I love thee, and everything will succeed.”

“And did you devise this plan all by yourself?”

“Yes.”

“And will you carry it out alone?”

“I alone shall have the troubles,” Marguerite said to me with a smile I shall never forget, “but we shall share the profits.”

I could not help blushing at the word profits; I remembered Manon Lescaut and Des Grieux living on M. de B.’s money.

I replied in a somewhat harsh tone as I rose:

“You will permit me, my dear Marguerite, to share only in the profits of ventures that I devise and conduct myself.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means that I strongly suspect Monsieur le Comte de G. of being your partner in this fortunate plan, whose liabilities and profits alike I decline to share.”

“You are a child. I thought you loved me; I was mistaken. Very well.”

At the same time, she rose, opened her piano, and began once more to play the Invitation to the Dance, up to that famous passage in the major key at which she always stopped.

Was it out of habit, or to remind me of the day when we had met? All I know is that the melody brought my memories back, and, going up to her, I took her head between my hands and kissed her.

“Do you forgive me?” I said to her.

“You can see that I do,” she replied; “but bear in mind that this is only our second day, and already I have something to forgive you for. You keep your promises of blind obedience very poorly.”

“What do you expect, Marguerite? I love you too much, and I am jealous of your slightest thought. What you proposed to me just now would drive me mad with joy, but the mystery preceding the execution of this plan constricts my heart.”

“Come, let us reason a little,” she resumed, taking both my hands and looking at me with a charming smile that I found it impossible to resist. “You love me, do you not? And you would be happy to spend three or four months in the country alone with me. I too should be happy in that solitude together; not only should I be happy in it, but I need it for my health. I cannot leave Paris for so long without putting my affairs in order, and the affairs of a woman like me are always very tangled. Well, I have found a way to reconcile everything—my affairs and my love for you; yes, for you, do not laugh: I am mad enough to love you! And now you put on your grand airs and make grand pronouncements to me. Child, child three times over, remember only that I love you, and do not worry about anything. Is it agreed, then?”

“Whatever you wish is agreed; you know that very well.”

“Then, within a month, we shall be in some village, strolling along the water’s edge and drinking milk. It seems strange to you to hear me speak this way, me, Marguerite Gautier. It is because, my friend, when this Parisian life, which seems to make me so happy, is not burning me, it wearies me, and then I am suddenly filled with longings for a calmer existence that would remind me of my childhood. One has always had a childhood, whatever one may have become. Oh, do not worry; I am not going to tell you that I am the daughter of a retired colonel and that I was educated at Saint-Denis. I am a poor country girl, and six years ago I did not know how to write my own name. You are reassured now, are you not? Why are you the first person to whom I turn to share the joy of the longing that has come over me? No doubt because I recognized that you loved me for myself and not for yourself, whereas the others have never loved me except for themselves.

“I have very often been to the country, but never as I should have liked to go. I am counting on you for this simple happiness, so do not be unkind; grant it to me. Tell yourself this: she is not destined to live to old age, and one day I should regret not having done for her the first thing she asked of me, when it was so easy to do.”

What could one reply to such words, especially with the memory of a first night of love and in anticipation of a second?

An hour later, I held Marguerite in my arms, and had she asked me to commit a crime, I would have obeyed her.

At six in the morning I left, and before leaving I said to her:

“Tonight?”

She kissed me more tightly, but did not answer.

During the day, I received a letter containing these words:

“Dear child, I am a little unwell, and the doctor has ordered me to rest. I shall go to bed early tonight and shall not see you. But, to reward you, I shall expect you tomorrow at noon. I love you.”

I had therefore read those urgent and repeated letters, and I had torn them up without telling Marguerite what they contained, and without advising her to see the old man again, although a feeling of pity for the poor man's grief inclined me to do so; but I feared that in this advice she might see a desire, by having the duke resume his former visits, to make him resume the expenses of the household; above all, I dreaded that she might think me capable of denying responsibility for her life in all the consequences into which her love for me might lead her.

The result was that the duke, receiving no reply, ceased writing, and that Marguerite and I continued to live together without concerning ourselves with the future.




Chapter XVIII


It would be difficult to give you details of our new life. It consisted of a series of childish pastimes that were delightful to us, but insignificant to those to whom I might recount them.

You know what it is to love a woman; you know how the days grow shorter, and with what amorous indolence one lets oneself be carried into the morrow. You are familiar with that forgetfulness of all things which springs from a violent, trusting, and reciprocated love. Every being who is not the beloved woman seems a useless being in creation. One regrets having already cast fragments of one's heart to other women, and one cannot conceive the possibility of ever clasping any hand other than the one one holds in one's own. The mind admits neither work nor memory, nothing, in short, that might distract it from the one thought constantly offered to it. Every day one discovers in one's mistress a new charm, an unknown delight. Existence is nothing more than the repeated fulfillment of a continuous desire; the soul is nothing more than the vestal charged with tending the sacred fire of love.

Often, when night had fallen, we would go and sit beneath the little wood overlooking the house. There we listened to the cheerful harmonies of the evening, both thinking of the approaching hour that would leave us in each other's arms until the next day. At other times we remained in bed all day, without even letting the sun enter our room. The curtains were tightly closed, and the outside world stopped for a while for us. Nanine alone had the right to open our door, but only to bring us our meals; and even those we ate without getting up, constantly interrupting them with laughter and wild antics. This was followed by a few moments' sleep, for, vanishing into our love, we were like two persistent divers who return to the surface only to draw breath.

Nevertheless, I caught moments of sadness, and sometimes even tears, in Marguerite; I asked her where this sudden sorrow came from, and she would reply:

“Our love is not an ordinary love, my dear Armand. You love me as though I had never belonged to anyone, and I tremble lest later, repenting of your love and holding my past against me as a crime, you force me to cast myself back into the life in the midst of which you found me. Remember that now that I have tasted a new life, I would die if I returned to the other one. Tell me, then, that you will never leave me.”

“I swear it to you!”

At these words, she would look at me as though to read in my eyes whether my oath was sincere; then she would throw herself into my arms and, hiding her head against my breast, say to me:

“It is because you do not know how much I love you!”

One evening, we were leaning on the window balcony; we were watching the moon, which seemed to be emerging with difficulty from its bed of clouds, and listening to the wind noisily stirring the trees. We were holding hands and had not spoken for a good quarter of an hour when Marguerite said to me:

“Winter is here; would you like us to leave?”

“And for where?”

“For Italy.”

“Are you bored, then?”

“I am afraid of winter; above all, I am afraid of our return to Paris.”

“Why?”

“For many reasons.”

And she abruptly went on, without giving me the reasons for her fears:

“Will you leave? I will sell everything I have; we will go and live over there; nothing will remain to me of what I was; no one will know who I am. Will you do it?”

“Let us leave, if that would please you, Marguerite; let us take a journey,” I said to her; “but what need is there to sell things you will be glad to find upon our return? I do not have a large enough fortune to accept such a sacrifice, but I have enough for us to travel in fine style for five or six months, if that appeals to you in the slightest.”

“Actually, no,” she continued, leaving the window and going to sit on the sofa in the shadow of the room; “what is the use of going to spend money over there? I already cost you quite enough here.”

“You reproach me with it, Marguerite; that is not generous.”

“Forgive me, my friend,” she said, holding out her hand to me; “this stormy weather is bad for my nerves; I do not say what I mean to say.”

And, after kissing me, she fell into a long reverie.

Similar scenes took place several times, and although I did not know what gave rise to them, I nonetheless perceived in Marguerite a feeling of anxiety about the future. She could not doubt my love, for it grew each day, and yet I often saw her sad without her ever explaining the cause of her sadness to me except by attributing it to a physical cause.

Fearing that she might grow weary of a life that was too monotonous, I suggested that she return to Paris, but she always rejected this suggestion and assured me that she could not be as happy anywhere as she was in the country.

Prudence now came only rarely, but in return she wrote letters that I had never asked to see, although each time they plunged Marguerite into deep preoccupation. I did not know what to think.

One day Marguerite remained in her room.

I entered. She was writing.

“To whom are you writing?” I asked her.

“To Prudence. Would you like me to read you what I am writing?”

I abhorred anything that might appear to be suspicion, so I replied to Marguerite that I had no need to know what she was writing; and yet, I was certain of it, that letter would have revealed to me the true cause of her sadness.

The next day the weather was splendid. Marguerite suggested that we go for a boat ride and visit the island of Croissy. She seemed very cheerful; it was five o'clock when we returned.

“Open the door,” I told him, wondering who could be coming to my home at such an hour, and not daring to believe that it might be Marguerite.

“Sir,” Joseph said to me when he returned, “it is two ladies.”

“It is we, Armand,” a voice called out to me, which I recognized as Prudence’s.

I came out of my bedroom.

Prudence, standing, was looking at the few curiosities in my drawing room; Marguerite, seated on the sofa, was deep in thought.

When I entered, I went over to her, knelt down, took both her hands, and, deeply moved, said to her:

“Forgive me.”

She kissed me on the forehead and said:

“That makes three times already that I have forgiven you.”

“I was going to leave tomorrow.”

“How can my visit change your decision? I have not come to prevent you from leaving Paris. I have come because I did not have time during the day to answer you, and because I did not want to leave you thinking that I was angry with you. Besides, Prudence did not want me to come; she said that I might be disturbing you.”

“You disturb me—you, Marguerite! How could you?”

“Well! You might have had a woman here with you,” Prudence replied, “and it would not have been amusing for her to see two more arrive.”

During this observation of Prudence’s, Marguerite was watching me attentively.

“My dear Prudence,” I replied, “you do not know what you are saying.”

“The thing is, your apartment is very charming,” Prudence retorted; “may one see the bedroom?”

“Yes.”

Prudence went into my bedroom, less to inspect it than to make amends for the foolish thing she had just said and to leave Marguerite and me alone.

“Why did you bring Prudence?” I then asked her.

“Because she was with me at the theatre, and because, when I left here, I wanted to have someone to accompany me.”

“Was I not here?”

“Yes; but apart from the fact that I did not want to disturb you, I was quite sure that, on coming as far as my door, you would ask to come up to my rooms, and, as I could not grant you that, I did not want you to leave with the right to reproach me for a refusal.”

“And why could you not receive me?”

“Because I am watched very closely, and the slightest suspicion could do me the greatest harm.”

“Is that truly the only reason?”

“If there were another, I would tell you; we are past keeping secrets from one another.”

“Come now, Marguerite, I do not want to take several paths to arrive at what I want to say to you. Frankly, do you love me a little?”

“Very much.”

“Then why did you deceive me?”

“My friend, if I were the Duchess So-and-so, if I had an income of two hundred thousand livres, if I were your mistress and had another lover besides you, you would have the right to ask me why I deceive you; but I am Mademoiselle Marguerite Gautier, I have debts of forty thousand francs, not a penny to my name, and I spend a hundred thousand francs a year; your question becomes pointless and my answer unnecessary.”

“That is fair,” I said, letting my head fall upon Marguerite’s knees; “but I love you like a madman.”

“Well then, my friend, you should have loved me a little less or understood me a little better. Your letter caused me a great deal of pain. If I had been free, to begin with I would not have received the count the day before yesterday, or, having received him, I would have come to ask you for the forgiveness you were asking of me just now, and from then on I would have had no lover but you. For a moment I thought I might grant myself that happiness for six months; you would not have it; you insisted on knowing the means, and, good God, the means were easy enough to guess. In employing them, I was making a greater sacrifice than you think. I could have said to you: I need twenty thousand francs; you were in love with me, and you would have found them, at the risk of reproaching me for them later. I preferred to owe you nothing; you did not understand that delicacy, for it is one. Women like us, when we still have a little heart left, give words and things a scope and significance unknown to other women; I therefore repeat to you that, on Marguerite Gautier’s part, the means she found of paying her debts without asking you for the money needed to do so was an act of delicacy from which you ought to benefit without saying anything. If you had only met me today, you would be only too happy with what I was promising you, and you would not ask me what I did the day before yesterday. We are sometimes forced to purchase satisfaction for our souls at the expense of our bodies, and we suffer far more when, afterward, that satisfaction escapes us.”

I listened to Marguerite and gazed at her with admiration. When I thought that this marvelous creature, whose feet I would once have longed to kiss, was consenting to let me count for something in her thoughts, to give me a part in her life, and that I was still not content with what she gave me, I wondered whether man’s desire has any bounds when, having been satisfied as swiftly as mine had been, it still reaches for something else.

“It is true,” she continued; “we creatures of chance have capricious desires and inconceivable loves. We give ourselves now for one thing, now for another. There are men who would ruin themselves without obtaining anything from us, and there are others who have us for a bouquet. Our heart has its whims; they are its only diversion and its only excuse. I gave myself to thee more quickly than to any man, I swear it to thee; why? Because, seeing me spit blood, thou tookest my hand, because thou wept, because thou art the only human creature who was willing to pity me. I am going to tell thee something foolish, but I once had a little dog that looked at me very sadly when I coughed; it is the only being I have ever loved.

“When it died, I wept more than at my mother’s death. It is true that she had beaten me for twelve years of her life. Well, I loved thee at once as much as my dog. If men knew what they could obtain with a tear, they would be loved more, and we would be less ruinous to them.”

She was pondering! What about? I do not know; as for me, I was looking at her with love and almost with terror, thinking of what I was prepared to suffer for her.

My first words were: “She is cheating on me!”

An icy sweat passed over my brow, for I already loved this woman too much for such a suspicion not to overwhelm me.

Then, since I had the key to her home, I thought of going to see her as usual. In that way I would very quickly learn the truth, and if I found a man there, I would slap his face.

In the meantime, I went to the Champs-Élysées. I remained there for four hours. She did not appear. That evening, I went into every theater she habitually attended. She was in none of them.

At eleven o'clock, I went to the Rue d'Antin.

There was no light in Marguerite's windows. Nevertheless, I rang. The porter asked me where I was going.

“How the sight of other people’s life and happiness makes those wish to live who, the day before, in the solitude of their souls and in the shadows of their sickrooms, wished to die quickly!”

It seems to me that, if you came, I would recover. What would be the use of recovering?”

Chapter XII


At five in the morning, when daylight began to show through the curtains, Marguerite said to me:

“Forgive me for sending you away, but I must. The duke comes every morning; when he comes, he will be told that I am asleep, and he may wait for me to wake up.”

I took Marguerite’s head in my hands, her loosened hair streaming around her, and gave her one last kiss, saying:

“When shall I see you again?”

“Listen,” she went on, “take that little gold key on the mantelpiece, go and open that door, bring the key back here, and leave. During the day, you will receive a letter and my instructions, for you know that you must obey blindly.”

“Yes, and what if I were to ask for something already?”

“What?”

“That you let me keep this key.”

“I have never done for anyone what you are asking of me.”

“Well, do it for me, for I swear to you that I do not love you as the others loved you.”

“Very well, keep it; but I warn you that it rests solely with me to make that key of no use to you.”

“Why?”

“There are bolts on the inside of the door.”

“Wicked woman!”

“I shall have them removed.”

“So you love me a little?”

“I do not know how it has happened, but it seems to me that I do. Now go; I am falling asleep.”

We remained in each other’s arms for a few seconds, and I left.

The streets were deserted; the great city was still asleep; a gentle coolness ran through those districts that the noise of men would invade a few hours later.

It seemed to me that this sleeping city belonged to me; I searched my memory for the names of those whose happiness I had envied until then, and I could not recall a single one without finding myself happier than he.

To be loved by a chaste young girl, to be the first to reveal to her that strange mystery of love, is certainly a great joy, but it is the simplest thing in the world. To take possession of a heart unaccustomed to attack is to enter an open and ungarrisoned city. Education, a sense of duty, and family are very strong sentinels; but no sentinels are so vigilant that they cannot be deceived by a sixteen-year-old girl to whom nature, through the voice of the man she loves, gives its first counsels of love, all the more ardent because they seem all the purer.

The more the young girl believes in goodness, the more readily she surrenders herself, if not to the lover, at least to love; for, being without mistrust, she is without strength, and to make oneself loved by her is a triumph that any man of twenty-five may grant himself whenever he wishes.
