“Go away. This carpet you are walking on is no longer ours. In your house you do not own a piece of furniture, a pin, or a wisp of straw, and it is I who have ruined you, poor man!”

Then there would be a great sob, after which he would weep profusely, and at last, once the surprise had passed, he would forgive her.

“Yes,” she murmured through clenched teeth, “he will forgive me, he who could offer me a million and still not have enough for me to forgive him for having known me... Never! Never!”

The idea of Bovary’s superiority over her exasperated her. Then, whether she confessed or did not confess, in a moment, later, tomorrow, he would nevertheless learn of the catastrophe; so she would have to await that horrible scene and bear the weight of his magnanimity. She felt the urge to return to Lheureux: what good would it do? To write to her father; it was too late; and perhaps she was now regretting not having yielded to the other man when she heard the trot of a horse in the lane. It was he; he opened the gate; he was paler than the plaster wall. Bounding up the stairs, she quickly escaped across the square; and the mayor’s wife, who was talking in front of the church with Lestiboudois, saw her enter the tax collector’s house.

She ran to tell Madame Caron. The two ladies went up into the attic; and, concealed by linen spread over poles, they settled themselves comfortably so as to see the entire interior of Binet’s house.

She kept repeating to herself: “I have a lover! a lover!” delighting in the idea as though in that of another puberty that had come upon her. So at last she was going to possess those joys of love, that fever of happiness of which she had despaired. She was entering into something marvelous where everything would be passion, ecstasy, delirium; a bluish immensity surrounded her, the summits of feeling sparkled beneath her thoughts, and ordinary existence appeared only far away, down below, in the shadows, between those heights.

Then she remembered the heroines of the books she had read, and the lyrical legion of those adulterous women began singing in her memory with the voices of sisters that enchanted her. She herself was becoming like a real part of those imaginings and fulfilling the long daydream of her youth, seeing herself as that type of woman in love whom she had envied so much. Besides, Emma felt the satisfaction of revenge. Had she not suffered enough! But now she was triumphant, and love, so long held back, burst forth in its entirety with joyful seethings. She savored it without remorse, without anxiety, without uneasiness.

The following day passed in a new sweetness. They made vows to each other. She told him of her sorrows. Rodolphe interrupted her with his kisses; and, gazing at him through half-closed eyelids, she asked him to call her by her name again and to repeat that he loved her. It was in the forest, as on the previous day, beneath a clog-makers’ hut. Its walls were of straw and the roof came down so low that they had to remain bent over. They were sitting close against each other on a bed of dry leaves.

From that day on, they wrote to each other regularly every evening. Emma took her letter to the end of the garden, near the river, and placed it in a crack in the terrace. Rodolphe came to fetch it and put another there, which she always complained was too short.

One morning, when Charles had gone out before dawn, she was seized by the fancy to see Rodolphe that very instant. She could reach La Huchette quickly, stay there for an hour, and be back in Yonville while everyone was still asleep. The idea made her pant with longing, and she soon found herself in the middle of the meadow, where she walked with rapid steps without looking behind her.

Day was beginning to break. From a distance, Emma recognized her lover’s house, its two swallow-tailed weather vanes standing out black against the pale twilight.

Beyond the farmyard stood a main building that must be the château. She entered it as though the walls had parted of their own accord at her approach. A broad, straight staircase led up to a corridor. Emma turned the latch of a door, and suddenly, at the back of the room, she saw a man sleeping. It was Rodolphe. She gave a cry.

“There you are! There you are!” he kept saying. “How did you manage to come?... Ah! Your dress is wet!”

“I love you!” she replied, putting her arms around his neck.

This first act of daring having succeeded, now, whenever Charles went out early, Emma dressed quickly and crept down the steps leading to the water’s edge.

But when the cattle plank had been raised, she had to follow the walls running alongside the river; the bank was slippery, and to keep from falling she clung with one hand to clumps of withered wallflowers. Then she cut across plowed fields, where she sank in, stumbled, and entangled her thin boots. Her scarf, tied over her head, fluttered in the wind above the grasslands; she was afraid of the oxen and began to run; she arrived breathless, her cheeks rosy, her whole person giving off a fresh scent of sap, greenery, and open air. At that hour, Rodolphe was still asleep. It was like a spring morning entering his room.

The yellow curtains along the windows softly let through a heavy golden light. Emma groped her way, blinking, while the dewdrops hanging from the bands of her hair formed what looked like a halo of topazes all around her face. Laughing, Rodolphe drew her to him and clasped her to his heart.

Then she examined the room, opened the drawers of the furniture, combed her hair with his comb, and looked at herself in the shaving mirror. Often she even put between her teeth the stem of a large pipe that lay on the bedside table among some lemons and lumps of sugar, beside a carafe of water.

They needed a good quarter of an hour to say goodbye. Then Emma wept; she wished she never had to leave Rodolphe. Something stronger than herself drove her toward him, so much so that one day, seeing her arrive unexpectedly, he frowned like someone annoyed.

“What is the matter with you?” she said. “Are you suffering? Talk to me!”

At last, with a serious air, he declared that her visits were becoming reckless and that she was compromising herself.




X


Little by little, Rodolphe’s fears took hold of her. At first, love had intoxicated her, and she had thought of nothing beyond it. But now that he was indispensable to her life, she feared losing some part of it, or even that it might be disturbed. When she returned from his house, she cast anxious glances all around, watching every shape that passed along the horizon and every village dormer from which she might be seen. She listened to the footsteps, the shouts, the sound of the plows; and she stopped, paler and more trembling than the leaves of the poplars swaying above her head.

One morning, as she was returning in this way, she suddenly thought she could make out the long barrel of a rifle that seemed to be aimed at her. It protruded obliquely over the rim of a small barrel, half buried among the grass at the edge of a ditch. Emma, on the verge of fainting with terror, nevertheless went forward, and a man emerged from the barrel like those spring-loaded devils that leap up from the bottoms of boxes. He wore gaiters buckled up to his knees, his cap pulled down over his eyes; his lips were chattering and his nose was red. It was Captain Binet, lying in wait for wild ducks.

“I learned from a peddler who, while traveling through your part of the country this winter, had a tooth pulled, that Bovary was still working hard. That does not surprise me, and he showed me his tooth; we had coffee together. I asked him whether he had seen you; he told me he had not, but that he had seen two animals in the stable, from which I conclude that business is going well. So much the better, my dear children, and may the good Lord send you every imaginable happiness.

“It grieves me that I still do not know my beloved little granddaughter Berthe Bovary. I have planted an oat-plum tree for her in the garden, beneath your room, and I do not want anyone to touch it, except to make preserves for her later, which I shall keep in the cupboard for her, when she comes.

“Farewell, my dear children. I embrace you, my daughter; you too, my son-in-law, and the little one, on both cheeks.

“I remain, with many compliments,

“Your affectionate father,

“THEODORE ROUAULT.”

For several minutes she remained holding the thick paper between her fingers. The spelling mistakes intertwined with one another, and Emma followed the sweet thought that chattered all through it like a hen half hidden in a thorn hedge. The writing had been dried with ashes from the hearth, for a little gray dust slipped from the letter onto her dress, and she almost thought she could see her father bending toward the fireplace to take up the tongs. How long it had been since she had sat beside him, on the footstool, in the chimney corner, when she would burn the end of a stick in the tall flame of the crackling sea rushes!...

She remembered summer evenings filled with sunlight. The foals neighed when anyone passed and galloped, galloped... Beneath her window there was a beehive, and sometimes the bees, wheeling in the light, struck the windowpanes like rebounding balls of gold. What happiness there had been then! What freedom! What hope! What an abundance of illusions! None remained now! She had spent them on all the adventures of her soul, through all her successive states, in virginity, in marriage, and in love—thus losing them continually throughout her life, like a traveler who leaves some of his wealth at every inn along the road.

But what, then, was making her so unhappy? Where was the extraordinary catastrophe that had devastated her? And she raised her head, looking around her as though searching for the cause of what was making her suffer.

A ray of April light shimmered on the porcelain on the shelf; the fire was burning; beneath her slippers she felt the softness of the carpet; the daylight was white, the air warm, and she heard her child bursting into peals of laughter.

Indeed, the little girl was then rolling about on the lawn, amid the grass that was being turned for hay. She was lying flat on her stomach at the top of a haystack. Her nurse was holding her by the skirt. Lestiboudois was raking nearby, and every time he came close, she leaned over, beating the air with both arms.

“Bring her to me!” said her mother, rushing forward to embrace her. “How I love you, my poor child! How I love you!”

Then, noticing that the tips of her ears were a little dirty, she quickly rang for hot water and cleaned her, changed her underclothes, stockings, and shoes, asked a thousand questions about her health, as though she had just returned from a journey, and finally, kissing her again and shedding a few tears, she handed her back to the servant, who remained utterly astonished at this excess of tenderness.

That evening, Rodolphe found her more serious than usual.

“It will pass,” he decided. “It is a whim.”

And he failed to keep three appointments in succession. When he returned, she was cold and almost disdainful toward him.

“Ah! You are wasting your time, my pretty one...”

And he appeared not to notice either her melancholy sighs or the handkerchief she was pulling out.

It was then that Emma repented!

She even wondered why she detested Charles, and whether it would not have been better if she could have loved him. But he offered little purchase for such revivals of feeling, so that she remained greatly perplexed in her half-formed impulse toward sacrifice, when the apothecary happened to provide her with an opportunity.




XI


He had recently read a eulogy of a new method for curing clubfeet; and as he was a supporter of progress, he conceived the patriotic idea that Yonville, in order to keep abreast, ought to have operations for strephopodia.

“For,” he said to Emma, “what is there to risk? Consider”—and he counted the advantages of the attempt on his fingers—“almost certain success, relief and improved appearance for the patient, fame quickly acquired by the operator. Why, for example, should your husband not wish to rid poor Hippolyte, from the Golden Lion, of his affliction? Bear in mind that he would not fail to tell all the travelers about his cure, and then”—Homais lowered his voice and looked around him—“who could prevent me from sending a short notice about it to the newspaper? Good Lord! An article circulates... people talk about it... it ends by snowballing! And who knows? Who knows?”

Indeed, Bovary might succeed; nothing assured Emma that he was not skillful, and what satisfaction it would be for her to have encouraged him to take a step by which his reputation and fortune would be increased! All she asked was to lean on something more solid than love.

Urged by the apothecary and by her, Charles allowed himself to be persuaded. He sent to Rouen for Doctor Duval’s volume, and every evening, his head in his hands, he immersed himself in his reading.

While he studied equinus, varus, and valgus—that is, strephocatopodia, strephendopodia, and strephexopodia (or, to put it more clearly, the different deviations of the foot, whether downward, inward, or outward)—together with strephyopodia and strephanopodia (in other words, twisting underneath and straightening upward), Monsieur Homais, with all manner of arguments, exhorted the inn servant to submit to the operation.

“You will perhaps feel scarcely more than a slight pain; it is merely a prick, like a minor bloodletting, less than the removal of certain corns.”

At the gallop of four horses, she had been carried away for eight days toward a new country, from which they would never return. On they went, on they went, their arms entwined, without speaking. Often, from the top of a mountain, they would suddenly glimpse some splendid city with domes, bridges, ships, forests of lemon trees, and cathedrals of white marble, whose pointed steeples bore storks’ nests. They would proceed at a walk because of the great paving stones, and on the ground there were bouquets of flowers offered to you by women dressed in red bodices. Bells could be heard ringing, mules neighing, together with the murmur of guitars and the sound of fountains, whose drifting spray cooled heaps of fruit arranged in pyramids at the feet of pale statues that smiled beneath the jets of water. And then, one evening, they would arrive in a fishing village, where brown nets dried in the wind along the cliff and the huts. It was there that they would stop to live; they would inhabit a low house with a flat roof, shaded by a palm tree, at the end of a gulf, on the seashore. They would go boating in a gondola, they would sway in a hammock; and their existence would be easy and ample like their silk garments, all warm and starry like the balmy nights they would contemplate. Yet across the immensity of this future she conjured up for herself, nothing particular emerged; the days, all magnificent, resembled one another like waves; and it swayed on the horizon, infinite, harmonious, bluish, and flooded with sunlight.
But the child would begin to cough in her cradle, or Bovary would snore more loudly, and Emma would not fall asleep until morning, when dawn whitened the windowpanes and little Justin was already opening the shutters of the pharmacy on the square.

She had sent for Monsieur Lheureux and had said to him:

“I would need a cloak, a large cloak, with a long cape collar, lined.”

“Are you going on a journey?” he asked.

“No! But... no matter, I am counting on you, am I not? And quickly!”

He bowed.

“I would also need,” she continued, “a trunk... not too heavy... convenient.”

“Yes, yes, I understand, about ninety-two centimeters by fifty, as they make them nowadays.”

“With an overnight bag.”

“There is definitely trouble behind all this,” Lheureux thought.

“And here,” Madame Bovary said, drawing her watch from her waistband, “take this; you can pay yourself out of it.”

But the merchant exclaimed that she was wrong; they knew each other; did he doubt her? What childishness! She nevertheless insisted that he take at least the chain, and Lheureux had already put it in his pocket and was leaving when she called him back.

“You will leave everything at your house. As for the cloak”—she appeared to reflect—“do not bring that either; just give me the workman’s address and tell him to keep it at my disposal.”

It was the following month that they were to run away. She would leave Yonville as though going to Rouen to do some shopping. Rodolphe would have reserved the seats, obtained passports, and even written to Paris so as to have the whole coach compartment to themselves as far as Marseilles, where they would buy a carriage and, from there, continue without stopping by way of Genoa. She would have taken care to send her luggage to Lheureux’s, from where it would be carried directly to the Hirondelle, so that in this way no one would have any suspicions; and in all of this, her child was never mentioned. Rodolphe avoided speaking of her; perhaps Emma did not think of her.

He wanted another two weeks before him to finish making some arrangements; then, after a week, he asked for another fortnight; then he said he was ill; next he took a trip; the month of August passed, and after all these delays they decided that it would irrevocably be September 4, a Monday.

At last Saturday, the day before the day before, arrived.

Rodolphe came in the evening, earlier than usual.

“Is everything ready?” she asked him.

“Yes.”

Then they walked around a flower bed and went to sit near the terrace, on the coping of the wall.

“You are sad,” Emma said.

“No, why?”

And yet he was looking at her strangely, tenderly.

“Is it because you are going away?” she continued. “Because you are leaving your loved ones, your life? Ah! I understand... But I have nothing in the world! You are everything to me. And so I shall be everything to you; I shall be a family to you, a homeland; I shall care for you, I shall love you.”

“How charming you are!” he said, seizing her in his arms.

“Truly?” she said with a voluptuous laugh. “Do you love me? Then swear it!”

“If I love you! If I love you! Why, I adore you, my love!”

The moon, perfectly round and purple in color, was rising level with the ground at the far end of the meadow. It rose quickly among the branches of the poplars, which hid it here and there like a black curtain pierced with holes. Then it appeared, dazzlingly white, in the empty sky that it illuminated; and then, slowing down, it cast upon the river a broad patch that made an infinity of stars; and that silvery light seemed to writhe there down to the depths, like a headless serpent covered with luminous scales. It also resembled some monstrous candelabrum from which drops of molten diamond streamed all along its length. The balmy night spread out around them; sheets of shadow filled the foliage. Emma, her eyes half closed, breathed in with deep sighs the fresh wind that was blowing. They did not speak, so lost were they in the inrush of their reverie. The tenderness of former days returned to their hearts, abundant and silent like the flowing river, with as much softness as the fragrance of the mock orange brought, and cast across their memories shadows more immense and melancholy than those of the motionless willows stretching over the grass. Often some nocturnal creature, hedgehog or weasel, setting out to hunt, disturbed the leaves, or at moments they would hear a ripe peach fall by itself from the espalier.

“Ah! What a beautiful night!” Rodolphe said.

“We shall have others!” Emma replied.

And, as though speaking to herself:

“Yes, it will be delightful to travel... Why is my heart sad, though? Is it apprehension of the unknown... the effect of leaving familiar habits behind... or rather...? No, it is an excess of happiness! How weak I am, am I not? Forgive me!”

“There is still time!” he exclaimed. “Think it over; perhaps you will regret it.”

“Never!” she said impetuously.

And, moving closer to him:

“What misfortune could possibly befall me? There is no desert, no precipice, no ocean that I would not cross with you. As we go on living together, it will be like an embrace growing tighter, more complete, each day! We shall have nothing to trouble us, no worries, no obstacle! We shall be alone, wholly each other’s, eternally... Speak, answer me.”

At regular intervals he answered, “Yes... yes!...” She had run her hands through his hair, and she kept repeating in a childish voice, despite the large tears flowing down her cheeks:

“Rodolphe! Rodolphe!... Ah! Rodolphe, dear little Rodolphe!”

Midnight struck.

“Midnight!” she said. “Come, it is tomorrow! Only one more day!”

He rose to leave; and, as though the gesture he made had been the signal for their flight, Emma suddenly assumed a cheerful air:

“You have the passports?”

“Yes.”

“You are not forgetting anything?”

“No.”

“You are sure?”

“Certainly.”

“It is at the Hôtel de Provence, is it not, that you will wait for me?... at noon?”

He nodded.

“Until tomorrow, then!” Emma said in a final caress.

And now Effi detached the wafer seal and read: “Most highly honored madam,
most gracious Baroness! Permit me to add a most humble request to my most respectful morning greetings. A dear friend of mine of many years’ standing, a daughter of our Good Town of Kessin, Miss Marietta Trippelli, will arrive here on the midday train and remain among us until tomorrow morning. She intends to be in Petersburg on the seventeenth, to give concerts there until the middle of January. Prince Kotschukoff is once again opening his hospitable house to her. In her unfailing kindness toward me, Trippelli has promised to spend this evening at my home and to perform several songs entirely of my choosing (for she knows no difficulties). Might the Baroness be prevailed upon to attend this musical evening? Seven o’clock. Your husband, on whose appearance I confidently rely, will support my most humble request. Present will be only Pastor Lindequist (who will accompany her) and, of course, the widowed Pastor’s wife Trippel. With the most distinguished devotion, A. Gieshübler.”

“Well—,” said Innstetten, “yes or no?”

“Of course yes. That will take me out of myself. And besides, I cannot turn down my dear Gieshübler at his very first invitation.”

“Agreed. So, Friedrich, tell Mirambo, who presumably brought the note, that we would have the honor.” Friedrich left.

When he had gone, Effi asked: “Who is Mirambo?”

“The real Mirambo is a robber chieftain in Africa—Lake Tanganyika, if your geography extends that far—but ours is merely Gieshübler’s coal-yard manager and factotum, and will very probably wait upon us this evening in tails and cotton gloves.”

It was quite evident that the little incident had had a favorable effect on Effi and restored a good deal of her lightheartedness, but Innstetten wished to do his part to advance this convalescence. “I am glad that you said yes, and so quickly and without hesitation, and now I should like to make you another suggestion, to set you entirely to rights again. I can see that something from last night is still haunting you, something that does not suit my Effi, something that simply must go away again, and there is nothing better for that than fresh air. The weather is magnificent, fresh and mild at the same time, with scarcely a breath of wind; what do you say to our taking a drive, but a long one, not merely through the plantation, and in the sleigh, of course, with the bells on and the white snow blankets, and then, when we are back at four, you can rest, and at seven we shall be at Gieshübler’s and hear Trippelli.”

Effi took his hand. “How good you are, Geert, and how forbearing. For I must have seemed childish to you, or at least very childlike; first with my fear, and then afterward, asking you to sell the house and, what is worse still, that business with the Prince. You are to put his chair outside the door—it is laughable. For after all, he is the man who decides our fate. Mine too. You cannot imagine how ambitious I am. I really married you solely out of ambition. But you must not look so serious at that. I do love you . . . what is it called again, when one breaks off a twig and plucks off the leaves? With all my heart, with all its smart, beyond all measure.”

And she laughed brightly. “And now tell me,” she continued, when Innstetten still remained silent, “where are we to go?” “I had thought to the railway station, but by a roundabout route, and then back along the highway. And we shall eat at the station, or better still at Golchowski’s, at the ‘Prince Bismarck’ inn, which we passed on the day of our arrival, if you perhaps remember. Making such an appearance always has a good effect, and then I shall have an election talk with the starosta by Effi’s grace, and though he is not worth much personally, he keeps his establishment in order and his kitchen in even better order. The people here know about eating and drinking.”

It was close to eleven when they had this conversation. At twelve Kruse drew up before the door with the sleigh, and Effi got in. Johanna wanted to bring the foot muff and furs, but after everything that still weighed upon her, Effi felt such a need for fresh air that she refused them all and took only a double blanket. Innstetten, however, said to Kruse: “Kruse, we are now going to the railway station, where the two of us have already been once this morning. People will be surprised, but that does no harm. I think we shall drive along the plantation here and then turn left toward the Kroschentin church tower. Let the horses run. We must be at the station by one.”

And so the drive began. Smoke hung above the town’s white roofs, for there was little movement in the air. Utpatel’s mill too was turning only slowly, and they sped past it, close beside the churchyard, whose barberry bushes grew out over the railings and brushed Effi with their tips, so that snow fell onto her carriage rug. On the other side of the road was an enclosed plot, not much larger than a garden bed, and within it nothing was visible but a young pine rising from its center.

“Is someone buried there too?” Effi asked. “Yes, the Chinaman.”

Effi started; it felt like a stab. But she still had enough strength to control herself and asked with apparent calm:

“Ours?”

“Yes, ours. Naturally, he could not be accommodated in the municipal churchyard, and so Captain Thomsen, who was something like a friend of his, bought this plot and had him buried here. There is also a stone with an inscription. All before my time, of course. But people still talk about it.”

“So there is something to it after all. A story. You said something like that earlier this morning. And in the end it will be best if I hear what it is. As long as I do not know, despite all my good intentions, I am still a victim of my imaginings. Tell me what really happened. Reality cannot torment me as much as my imagination.”

“Bravo, Effi. I did not want to speak of it. But now it has come about of its own accord, and that is good. Besides, it is really nothing at all.”

“Oh, Mama, how can you say such a thing? Of course, when our dear relations drive up in winter and stay for six hours, or perhaps even longer, and Aunt Gundel and Aunt Olga scrutinize me and find me pert—and Aunt Gundel once told me so, too—yes, then things are sometimes not very pleasant, I must admit. But otherwise I have always been happy here, so happy.”

And as she said this, she flung herself, weeping violently, onto her knees before Mama and kissed both her hands.

“Get up, Effi. Those are moods that come over one when one is as young as you are and is facing marriage and the unknown. But now read me the letter, unless it contains something quite exceptional, or perhaps secrets.”

“Secrets,” Effi laughed, and sprang up again, her mood suddenly transformed. “Secrets! Yes, he is always making a start at them, but most of it I could have posted at the mayor’s office, where the district administrator’s ordinances are always displayed. Well, Geert is a district administrator, after all.”

“Read, read.”

“Dear Effi! ... That is how it always begins, you see, and sometimes he also calls me his ‘little Eve.’”

“Read, read ... You are supposed to be reading.”

“Very well: Dear Effi! The nearer we come to our wedding day, the more sparing your letters become. When the post arrives, I always look first for your handwriting, but, as you know (and indeed I did not wish it otherwise), usually in vain. The workmen are now in the house, preparing the rooms—only a few of them, to be sure—for your arrival. The best of it will probably not be done until we are away on our journey. Madelung, the upholsterer, who supplies everything, is a character, and I shall tell you about him next time, but above all about how happy I am because of you, because of my sweet little Effi. The ground here is burning beneath my feet, and meanwhile our good town is growing ever quieter and lonelier. The last bathing visitor left yesterday; toward the end he bathed in nine-degree water, and the bathing attendants were always glad when he emerged unscathed. For they feared he might have a stroke, which would then bring the resort into disrepute, as though the waves here were worse than elsewhere. I rejoice when I think that in only four weeks I shall be sailing with you from the Piazzetta to the Lido, or over to Murano, where they make glass beads and beautiful jewelry. And may the most beautiful be for you. Many greetings to your parents, and the tenderest kiss to you from your Geert.” Effi folded the letter again to put it into the envelope.

“That is a very nice letter,” said Frau von Briest, “and the fact that he maintains the proper measure in everything is one merit more.”

“Yes, the proper measure—he maintains that.”

“My dear Effi, let me ask you a question: would you wish that the letter did not maintain the proper measure; would you wish it were more tender, perhaps effusively tender?”

“No, no, Mama. Truly and honestly, no; I do not wish that. It is better this way, after all.”

“It is better this way, after all. Just listen to how that sounds. You are so peculiar. And then you were crying earlier. Is there something weighing on your heart? There is still time. Do you not love Geert?”

“Why should I not love him? I love Hulda, and I love Bertha, and I love Hertha. And I love old Niemeyer too. And that I love you both goes without saying. I love everyone who means well by me and is kind to me and spoils me. And Geert will probably spoil me too. In his own way, of course. He already intends to give me jewelry in Venice. He has no idea that I care nothing for jewelry. I would rather climb, and I would rather swing, and best of all always with the fear that something somewhere might tear or break and that I might fall. It will hardly cost me my head straightaway.”

“And perhaps you also love your cousin Briest?”

“Yes, very much. He always cheers me up.”

“And would you have liked to marry Cousin Briest?”

“Marry him? For heaven’s sake, no. He is still half a boy. Geert is a man, a handsome man, a man with whom I can make an impression and who will amount to something in the world. Whatever are you thinking, Mama?”

“Well, that is good, Effi; that pleases me. But there is still something on your mind.”

“Perhaps.”

“Well, speak.”

“Look, Mama, that he is older than I am does no harm; perhaps it is quite a good thing. He is not old, after all, and he is healthy and vigorous and so soldierly and so dashing. And I could almost say that I was entirely and utterly for him, if only he ... yes, if only he were a little different.”

“In what way, Effi?”

“Yes, in what way. Well, you must not laugh at me. It is something I first pricked up my ears at quite recently, over at the parsonage. We were talking about Innstetten, and all at once old Niemeyer furrowed his brow—but with furrows of respect and admiration—and said: ‘Yes, the Baron! He is a man of character, a man of principles.’”

“And so he is, Effi.”

“Certainly. And I believe Niemeyer even said afterward that he was also a man of firm convictions. And that, I think, is something more still. Oh, and I ... I have none. Look, Mama, there is something in that which torments and frightens me. He is so loving and good to me, and so indulgent, but ... I am afraid of him.”



Chapter Five

The Hohen-Cremmen festivities were over; everyone had departed, including the young couple, who had left on the very evening of the wedding day.

The wedding-eve party had satisfied everyone, especially those taking part in the performance, and Hulda had been the delight of all the young officers, both the Rathenow Hussars and their somewhat more critically disposed comrades from the Alexander Regiment. Yes, everything had gone well and smoothly, almost beyond expectation. Only Bertha and Hertha had sobbed so violently that Jahnke’s Low German verses were as good as lost. But even that had done little harm. Some discerning connoisseurs had even been of the opinion that this was the real thing: faltering, sobbing, and incomprehensibility—under this sign (and especially when the performers were such pretty, red-blond curly heads) the most decisive victories were always won. Cousin Briest had been able to pride himself on a very special triumph in a role of his own composition. He had appeared as a clerk from Demuth’s who, having learned that the young bride intended to travel to Italy immediately after the wedding, wished to deliver a traveling trunk. This trunk naturally proved to be an enormous bonbonnière from Hövel. There had been dancing until three o’clock, during which old Briest, talking himself more and more into a state of supreme champagne exhilaration, had made all manner of remarks about the torch dance still customary at many courts and the curious custom of dancing for the bride’s garter—remarks that showed no sign of ending and, growing more and more extreme, finally went so far that they absolutely had to be stopped. “Pull yourself together, Briest,” his wife had whispered to him in a rather serious tone; “you are not standing here to make double entendres, but to do the honors of the house. We are holding a wedding, not a hunting party.” To which Briest had replied that he saw no such great difference between the two; besides, he was happy.

The wedding day itself had also gone well. Niemeyer had spoken superbly, and one of the old gentlemen from Berlin, who more or less belonged to court society, had remarked on the way back from the church to the wedding house that it was indeed remarkable how richly talents were sown in a state such as ours. “I see in that a triumph of our schools, and perhaps even more of our philosophy. When I consider that this Niemeyer, an old village pastor who at first looked like an almshouse inmate ... yes, my friend, tell me yourself, did he not speak like a court preacher? That tact and that art of antithesis, exactly like Kögel, and in feeling superior to him. Kögel is too cold. To be sure, a man in his position must be cold. What is it that causes one to founder in life, after all? Always warmth alone.” The dignitary to whom these words had been addressed—still unmarried, but perhaps for that very reason involved in a “liaison” for the fourth time—naturally agreed. “Only too true, my dear friend,” he said. “Too much warmth! ... quite superb ... By the way, I must tell you a story later.”

“For the last time, then, for the last time I open these eyes.
They shall, alas, see the sun no more; a gloomy, misty day keeps it veiled from them. Mourn, then, Nature! Your son, your friend, your beloved draws near his end. Lotte, it is a feeling beyond compare, and yet it comes closest to a dawning dream, to say to oneself: this is the last morning. The last! Lotte, I have no sense of the word: the last! Do I not stand here in all my strength, and tomorrow I shall lie stretched out and limp upon the ground. To die! What does that mean? See, we dream when we speak of death. I have seen many a person die; but humanity is so limited that it has no sense of the beginning and end of its existence. Now still mine, yours! Yours, O beloved! And in an instant—separated, parted—perhaps forever?—No, Lotte, no—how can I cease to be? How can you cease to be? We are!—cease to be!—What does that mean? It is yet another word, an empty sound, without feeling for my heart.—Dead, Lotte! Buried in the cold earth, so confined! So dark!—I had a female friend who was my all in my helpless youth; she died, and I followed her corpse and stood at the grave as they lowered the coffin and the ropes, whirring, slipped out from beneath it and darted back up, then the first shovelful rattled down, and the fearful chest gave back a dull sound, and duller and ever duller, and at last was covered!—I fell down beside the grave—seized, shaken, terrified, my innermost being torn apart, but I did not know what was happening to me—what will happen to me—To die! Grave! I do not understand the words!

O forgive me! Forgive me! Yesterday! It should have been the last moment of my life. O you angel! For the first time, for the first time wholly without doubt, the blissful feeling glowed through my inmost being: she loves me! She loves me! The holy fire that streamed from your lips still burns upon mine; new, warm bliss is in my heart. Forgive me! Forgive me!

Ah, I knew that you loved me, knew it from the first soulful glances, from the first pressure of the hand, and yet, whenever I was away again, whenever I saw Albert at your side, I despaired again amid feverish doubts.

Do you remember the flowers you sent me when, in that fatal company, you could not say a word to me or offer me your hand? O, I knelt before them half the night, and they sealed your love to me. But alas! These impressions passed away, just as the feeling of his God’s grace gradually withdraws again from the believer’s soul, though it was bestowed upon him in sacred, visible signs with all the fullness of heaven.

All that is transitory, but no eternity shall extinguish the glowing life that I savored yesterday upon your lips, that I feel within me! She loves me! This arm embraced her, these lips trembled upon her lips, this mouth stammered against hers. She is mine! You are mine! Yes, Lotte, forever.

And what does it matter that Albert is your husband? Husband! That would be for this world, then—and for this world it would be a sin that I love you, that I would like to tear you from his arms into mine? Sin? Good, and I punish myself for it; I have tasted that sin in all its heavenly bliss, have drawn the balm and strength of life into my heart. From this moment you are mine! Mine, O Lotte! I go before you! I go to my Father, to your Father. To Him I shall lament it, and He will comfort me until you come, and I shall fly to meet you and clasp you and remain with you before the countenance of the Infinite in eternal embraces.

I am not dreaming, I am not deluding myself! Near the grave, things grow clearer to me.

We shall be! We shall see each other again! See your mother!

I shall see her, shall find her, ah, and pour out my whole

heart before her! Your mother, your very image.”

Toward eleven Werther asked his servant whether Albert had returned. The servant said: yes, he had seen Albert’s horse being led there. Thereupon his master gives him an open note containing the following: “Would you be so kind as to lend me your pistols for a journey I intend to make? Fare you very well!”

The dear woman had slept little the previous night; what she had feared was decided, decided in a manner she could neither have foreseen nor feared. Her blood, otherwise so pure and flowing so easily, was in a feverish tumult; a thousand different sensations distracted her beautiful heart. Was it the fire of Werther’s embraces that she felt in her breast? Was it resentment at his audacity? Was it a vexed comparison of her present state with those days of wholly ingenuous, free innocence and carefree confidence in herself? How was she to face her husband, how confess to him a scene that she might so properly acknowledge, and that she nevertheless did not dare acknowledge to herself? They had remained silent toward each other for so long, and was she to be the first to break the silence and, at precisely the wrong time, make so unexpected a disclosure to her husband? She already feared that the mere news of Werther’s visit would make an unpleasant impression upon him, and now this unexpected catastrophe besides! Could she hope that her husband would see it entirely in the proper light, would receive it wholly without prejudice? And could she wish him to read her soul? And yet again, could she dissemble before the man to whom she had always stood open and free like a crystal-clear glass, and from whom she had never concealed, nor had ever been able to conceal, any of her feelings? The one and the other caused her anxiety and placed her in a quandary; and again and again her thoughts returned to Werther, who was lost to her, whom she could not let go, whom—alas!—she had to leave to himself, and who, once he had lost her, had nothing left.

How heavily now the estrangement that had taken root between them weighed upon her, though in that moment she could not clearly account for it to herself! Such sensible, such good people began, because of certain secret differences, to remain silent with each other; each reflected upon his own right and the other’s wrong, and their relations became so entangled and embittered that it became impossible to untie the knot at the very critical moment upon which everything depended. Had a fortunate intimacy brought them closer to each other again sooner, had love and forbearance come alive between them in mutual exchange and opened their hearts, perhaps our friend might still have been saved.”

Every day, every day I met her. I confess the truth,
I was glad to meet her, yes, my heart took flight. This year it is two
years ago; now I think of it only when I wish, the whole adventure
amuses and distracts me. And as for the two green bird feathers,
I shall explain that shortly.
We had several places where we could meet, by the mill, on the road,
yes, even in my hut; she came wherever I wished. Good day! she always
called first, and I answered good day.

You are happy today, you are singing, she says, and her eyes sparkle.

Yes, I am happy, I answer. You have a spot there on your shoulder;
it is dust, perhaps it is mud from the road; I want to kiss that spot,
oh, do let me kiss it. Everything about you affects me tenderly,
I am so distraught over you. Last night I did not sleep.

And it was true; for more than one night I lay sleepless.

We walk side by side along the road.

What do you think, am I behaving as you like? she says. Perhaps
I talk too much? No? Yes, but you must tell me what you think.
Sometimes I think to myself that this can never turn out well....

What is it that will not turn out well? I ask.

This thing between us. That it will not turn out well. Whether you
believe it or not, I am walking here shivering now; a chill runs
down my back merely when I come near you. It is from happiness.

Yes, the same with me, I answer; a chill also runs through me merely
when I see you. Oh, it will surely turn out well. Besides, I shall pat
you a little on the back to warm you.

She reluctantly lets me do it; I pat a little harder, only in jest;
I laugh and ask whether it does not help.

Oh no, do not be so kind as to thump me on the back anymore, she says.

Those few words! It sounded so helpless to me when she said:
do not be so kind.

Then we went on along the road. Is she displeased with me because
of my jest? I asked myself, and I thought: let us see.
I said:

I happen to remember something. Once, on a sleigh ride, there was
a young lady who took a white silk handkerchief from around her own neck
and tied it around mine. In the evening I said to the lady: You shall
have Your handkerchief back tomorrow; I shall have it washed. No,
she answered, let me have it now; I want to keep it as it is,
just as You have worn it. And she was given the handkerchief. Three years
later I met the young lady again. The handkerchief? I said. She
brought the handkerchief. It lay in its paper, still unwashed; I saw it myself.

Edvarda glanced up at me.

Yes? What happened then?

No, there was no more, I said. But I thought it was a
lovely gesture.

Pause.

Where is that lady now?

Abroad.

23 — Hamsun: II
We spoke no more about it. But when she was going home, she said:

Good night, then. Do not go on thinking about that lady, will you?
I think of no one but you.

I believed her; I saw that she meant what she said, and it was enough
for me for all eternity if only she thought of me. I followed her.

Thank you, Edvarda, I said. Later I added with all my heart: You
are far too good for me, but I am grateful that you want me;
God will reward you for it. I may not be as splendid as
many others you could have; but I am so entirely yours, so violently
yours, by my immortal soul. What are you thinking about? There are
tears in your eyes.

It was nothing, she answered. It sounded so strange that
God would reward me for it. You say such things as.... I
love you so much!

She suddenly threw her arms around my neck right in the middle of the road
and kissed me passionately.

When she had gone, I turned aside and slipped into the forest to hide
and be alone with my joy. And, deeply moved, I ran back
to the road again and looked to see whether anyone might have noticed that
I went in there. But I saw no one.

XIII

Summer nights and still water and endlessly still forests. No
cry, no footstep from the roads; my heart was full as though with
dark wine.

Moths and hawk moths come flying soundlessly in through my
window, lured here by the glow from the hearth and by the smell of my
roasted bird. They strike the ceiling with a dull sound, whir
past my ears so that a chill passes through me, and settle
on my white powder horn on the wall. I observe them; they sit
trembling and look at me; they are spinners, borers, and moths. I
think some of them are like flying pansies.

I step outside the hut and listen. Nothing, no mountain farm,
everything sleeps. The air glows with flying insects, with myriads of
whirring wings. Over at the edge of the forest stand ferns and monkshood;
the bearberry is in bloom, and I love its little flowers. Thank
You, my God, for every heather blossom I have seen; they have been like little
roses on my path, and I weep for love of them. Somewhere
nearby there are wild pinks; I do not see them, but I
sense their fragrance.

But now, in the hours of night, great white flowers have suddenly
unfolded in the forest; their stigmas stand open, they breathe. And shaggy
hawk moths descend into their petals and make the whole
plant tremble. I go from one flower to another;
they are intoxicated, they are sexually intoxicated flowers, and I see
how they become intoxicated.

Light footsteps, a human being’s breath, a cheerful good evening.

I answer and throw myself down on the road and embrace the two knees
and the poor dress.

Good evening, Edvarda! I say once again, exhausted with happiness.

How you love me! she whispers.

How grateful I can be! I answer. You are mine, and
all day my heart lies still within me and thinks of you. You
are the most beautiful girl on this earth, and I have kissed you.
Often I blush with joy merely when I remember that I have
kissed you.

Why have you come to love me so much this very evening? she asks.

And I had for countless reasons; I had only needed
to think of her for it to happen. That gaze beneath the arched eyebrows
high upon her forehead, and that dark, lovely skin!

Should I not love you! I say. I go about thanking
every tree because you are well and in good health. Once, at a ball,
there was a young lady who sat out dance after dance, and everyone left
her sitting. I did not know her, but her face made
an impression on me, and I bowed to her. Well? No, she shook
her head. Does the young lady not dance? I said. Can You understand it,
she answered; my father was so handsome and my mother was a perfect
beauty, and my father swept my mother off her feet. But I
became lame.

Edvarda looked at me.

Let us sit down, she said.

We sat down in the heather.

Do you know what my friend says about you? she began. You
have the eyes of an animal, she says, and when you look at her you drive her
mad. It is as though you were touching her, she says.

I rowed out to my fishing ground. The weather had turned oppressive, the mosquitoes gathered in swarms, and I had to smoke tobacco the whole time to save myself. The haddock were biting; I hauled in the two-hook line; I made a good catch. On the way home I shot two auks.

When I reached the pier, the smith was standing there. He was at work. A thought passes through me, and I ask him:

May I go home with you?
No, he answers, Mr. Mack has given me work until midnight.

I nodded and thought to myself that this was good.

I took my catch with me and went, taking the road past the smith’s house. Eva was home alone.

I have longed for you so dearly, I said to her. And I was moved at the sight of her; she could scarcely look at me for astonishment. I love your youth and your good eyes, I said. Punish me today because I have thought more of another than of you. Listen, I come to you only to look at you; you do me good, I am in love with you. Did you hear me calling for you last night?

No, she answered in alarm.

I called for Edvarda, Miss Edvarda, but I meant you. It woke me. Yes, I meant you; I was excused—I misspoke when I said Edvarda. But let us speak no more of her. God, how you are my dearest girl, Eva! Your mouth is so red today. You have prettier feet than Edvarda; just look for yourself. — I lifted her dress and showed her her own legs.

A joy I had never yet seen in her flew across her face; she is about to turn away, but thinks better of it and puts one arm around my neck.

Some time passes. We talk together, sit all the while on a long bench, and talk to each other about many things. I said:

Would you believe it, Miss Edvarda has not yet learned to speak; she talks like a child, she says “more happier”; I have heard it myself. Do you think she has a beautiful forehead? I do not. She has a devilish forehead. Nor does she wash her hands.

Were we not supposed to speak no more of her?

Quite right. I merely forgot.

Some time passes again. I am thinking of something; I am silent.

Why are your eyes growing wet? Eva asks.

She has a beautiful forehead, by the way, I say, and her hands are always clean. It was only by chance that they were dirty once. I did not mean to say otherwise. — But now I continue heatedly and through clenched teeth: I sit constantly thinking of you, Eva; but it occurs to me that perhaps you have not heard what I am about to tell you. The first time Edvarda saw Aesop, she said: Aesop, why, he was a wise man; he was a Phrygian. Is that not ridiculous? She had read it in a book that same day, I am certain of it.

Yes, says Eva, but what of it?

As far as I remember, she also spoke of Aesop having had Xanthus as his teacher. Hahaha.

I see.
What the devil is the point of telling a gathering that Aesop had Xanthus as his teacher? I am merely asking. Ah, you are not in the mood today, Eva, otherwise you would laugh yourself sick over it.

Yes, I think it is amusing too, says Eva, and begins to laugh with effort and astonishment. But I do not understand it as well as you do.

I am silent and think, silent and thinking.

Would you rather that we sit quietly and say nothing? Eva asks softly. Goodness shone from her eyes; she stroked my hair with her hand.

You good, good soul! I exclaim, pressing her fiercely to me. I am certain I shall perish from love for you; I love you more and more; in the end you will come with me when I leave. You will see. Could you come with me?

Yes, she answers.

I scarcely hear this yes, but I feel it in her breath, I sense it in her; we hold each other wildly, and she gives herself to me so senselessly.

An hour later I kiss Eva farewell and leave. I meet Mr. Mack in the doorway.

Mr. Mack himself.

He starts and stares into the room, remains standing there on the threshold and staring. Well! he says, and cannot manage to say more; he is as though struck senseless.

You had not expected to find me here? I say, greeting him.

Eva does not move.

Mr. Mack collects himself; a remarkable assurance settles over him, and he answers:

You are mistaken; it is precisely you I am looking for. I wish to make you aware that from the first of April until the fifteenth of August, it is forbidden to fire shots within one eighth of a mile of an egg-and-down nesting ground. Today you shot two birds by the island; there are people who saw you.

I shot two auks, I said, stricken. It dawned on me on the spot that the man was within his rights.

Two auks or two eider ducks, it is all the same. You were within the protected area.

I acknowledge it, I said. It had not occurred to me until now.

But it ought to have occurred to you before now.

I also fired both barrels in roughly the same place in the month of May. It was on an island excursion. It happened at your own request.

That is another matter, Mr. Mack said curtly.
But then, for the devil’s sake, you surely know what you have to do?

Very well indeed, he answered.

Eva had held herself in readiness; when I went out, she followed, having put on a kerchief, and walked away from the house; I saw her take the road down to the piers. Mr. Mack walked home.

I thought it over. What agility in contriving a way out—how his eyes stabbed! One shot, two shots, a couple of auks, a fine, a payment. And then everything, everything was settled with Mr. Mack and his house. Fundamentally, it all went so exceedingly smoothly and quickly....

It had already begun to rain in large, soft drops. The magpies flew close to the ground, and when I came home and let Aesop loose, it ate grass. The wind began to sigh.

XXIII

A mile below me I see the sea. It is raining, and I am up in the mountains; a rock overhang shelters me from the rain. I smoke my short pipe, smoke one pipe after another, and each time I light it, the tobacco crawls upward like tiny glowing worms out of the ash. Thus, too, the thoughts swarm in my head. Before me on the ground lies a bundle of dry twigs from a ruined bird’s nest. And as this bird’s nest is, so too is my soul.

I remember every smallest trifle of the experiences of this day and the next. Hoho, how badly I was mauled....

I sit here up in the mountains, and the sea and the air roar; wind and weather seethe and lament horribly in my ears. Freighters and yachts can be seen far out with reefed sails; there are people aboard, they must be going somewhere, and God knows where all these lives are going, I think. The sea rises foaming into the air and tumbles, tumbles; it is as though peopled by great, raging figures that fling out their limbs and roar at one another—no, it is a revel among ten thousand shrieking devils who duck their heads between their shoulders and wheel around, whipping the sea white with the tips of their wings. Far, far out lies a submerged reef; from this reef a white merman rises and shakes his head after a leaking square-rigger running before the wind out to sea—hoho, out to sea, out into the desolate sea....

But that does not matter. Nothing matters now.

And quite like a little trembling song, her voice sounded in the forest.

And the foliage turns even yellower, autumn is drawing on, a few more stars have appeared in the sky, and from now on the moon looks like a shadow of silver dipped in gold. There was no cold, nothing, only a cool stillness and a streaming life in the forest. Every tree stood thinking. The berries were ripe.

Then came the twenty-second of August and the three iron nights.

XXVI
The first iron night.
At nine o’clock the sun goes down. A dim darkness settles over the earth, a couple of stars can be seen; two hours later, a gleam of the moon can be seen. I wander into the forest with my gun and my dog, I kindle a campfire, and the light from my fire shines in among the pine trunks. There is no frost.

The first iron night, I say. And a bewilderingly fierce joy in the time and the place thrills through me strangely....

A toast, you men and beasts and birds, to the solitary night in forests, in forests! A toast to the darkness and God’s murmuring among the trees, to the sweet, simple harmony of the silence against my ears, to green foliage and yellow foliage! A toast to the sound of life I hear, a snuffling muzzle against the grass, a dog sniffing across the ground! A tempestuous toast to the wildcat lying flat on its throat, taking aim and preparing to spring upon a sparrow in the dark, in the dark! A toast to the merciful stillness on earth, to the stars and to the half-moon, yes, to them and to it!

I rise and listen. No one has heard me. I sit down again.

Thanks for the solitary night, for the mountains, for the sighing of the darkness and the sea; it sighs through my heart! Thanks for my life, for my breath, for the grace of being alive tonight; for that I give thanks from my heart! Listen in the east and listen in the west—no, listen! It is the eternal God! This stillness murmuring against my ear is the blood of all nature seething, God interweaving the world and me. I see a gleaming spider’s thread in the light of my campfire, I hear a boat being rowed in the harbor, an aurora glides up across the sky in the north. Oh, by my immortal soul, I also give great thanks that it is I who am sitting here!

Silence. A pine cone falls dully to the ground. A pine cone fell! I think. The moon is high, the fire flickers on the half-burned firebrands and is about to go out. And late in the night I wander home.

The second iron night, the same stillness and the mild weather.
My soul broods. I walk mechanically over to a tree, pull my cap low over my forehead, and lean with my back against this tree, my hands clasped behind my neck. I stare and think; the flame from my campfire dazzles my eyes, and I do not feel it. I stand in this senseless position for a good while, looking at the fire; my legs are the first to give way and grow tired, and quite stiff-legged I sit down. Only now do I reflect upon what I have done. Why stare at the fire for so long?

Aesop raises his head and listens; he hears footsteps; Eva appears among the trees.

I am exceedingly pensive and sorrowful tonight, I say.

And out of compassion she makes no reply.

I love three things, I then say. I love a dream of love I once had. I love you, and I love this patch of earth. And which do you love most?

The dream.

It grows quiet again. Aesop knows Eva and tilts his head to one side and looks at her. I murmur:

I saw a girl on the road today; she was walking arm in arm with her lover. The girl pointed me out with her eyes and could hardly keep from laughing when I passed.

What was she laughing at?

I do not know. I suppose she was laughing at me. Why do you ask about it?

Did you know her?

Yes. I bowed to her.

And did she not know you?

No, she pretended not to know me.... But why are you sitting there cross-questioning me? It is ugly of you. You will not get me to say her name.

Pause.

I murmur again:

What was she laughing at? She is a flighty creature; but what was she laughing at? In the name of Jesus Christ, what have I ever done to her?

Eva replies:

It was ugly of her to laugh at you.

No, it was not ugly of her! I scream. You are not to sit here and censure her; she does nothing ugly; it was right of her to laugh at me. For Satan’s sake, be quiet and leave me alone, do you hear!

And Eva, frightened, leaves me alone. I look at her and at that very moment regret my harsh words; I fall down before her and wring my hands.

Go home, Eva. It is you I love most; how could I love a dream? It was only a joke; it is you I love. But go home now; I shall come to you tomorrow. Remember that I am yours, yes, do not forget it. Good night.

And Eva goes home.

The third iron night, a night of the utmost tension. If only there had been a little frost! Instead of frost, stagnant warmth after the day’s sun; the night was like a lukewarm morass. I kindled my campfire....

Eva, at times there can be a certain pleasure in being dragged by the hair. So perverse can a human mind become. One may be dragged by the hair down valleys and up mountains, and if someone asks what is going on, one may answer in utter rapture: I am being dragged by the hair! And if one is asked: But shall I not help you, free you? then one answers: No. And if one is asked: But can you endure it? then one answers: Yes, I can endure it, for I love the hand that is dragging me.... Do you know, Eva, what it is to hope?

Yes, I think so.

You see, Eva, to hope is something strange, yes, something very peculiar. One may walk along a road one morning and hope to meet upon that road a person one holds dear. And does one meet this person? No. Why not? Because the person is occupied that morning and is somewhere else altogether.... I came to know an old blind Lapp up in the mountains. For fifty-eight years he had seen nothing, and now he was over seventy. It seemed to him that he saw better and better as time went on; there was steady improvement, he thought. If nothing intervened, he would be able to glimpse the sun in a few years. His hair was still black, but his eyes were quite white. When we sat together in his hut and smoked, he told me about everything he had seen before he became blind. He was hardy and healthy, without feeling, indefatigable, and he preserved his hope. When I was about to leave, he followed me out and began pointing in different directions. There is south, he said, and there is north. First you go in that direction, and when you have gone some way down the mountain, you turn in that direction, he said. Quite right! I answered. And then the Lapp laughed contentedly and said: See, I did not know that forty or fifty years ago, so I do see better now than I did then; it is steadily improving. Then he ducked down and crept back into the hut, the eternal hut, his home on earth. And he sat down before the fire again, as before, full of hope that in a few years he would surely be able to glimpse the sun.... Eva, hope is exceedingly remarkable. I, for example, am now going about hoping to forget the person whom I did not meet on the road this morning.

But now take the doctor, as I tell you. Heed a friend’s advice; that prince is, after all, a half-old fool. — And in my agitation I lied about him, exaggerated his age, said that he was bald, that he was almost completely blind; I also claimed that he wore that crown on his shirt buttons solely and entirely to flaunt his nobility. — Besides, I have not bothered to get to know him, I said. There is nothing in him that marks him out in any way, he lacks the main lines, he is nothing.

But he is something, he is something! she screamed, and her voice cracked with anger. He is much more than you think, you forest creature! But just you wait, oh, he will speak to you, I shall ask him to. You do not believe that I love him, but you shall see that you are wrong. I will marry him, I shall think of him night and day. Remember that I say: I love him. Just let Eva come, ha-ha, God in heaven, just let her come, it is so unspeakably indifferent to me. Yes, I must see about getting away from here +++. She began to walk down the path from the hut, she took a few small, eager steps, turned around, still deathly pale in the face, and groaned: And never come before my eyes again.

XXV

The leaves are turning yellow, the potato tops had grown tall and were in bloom, hunting season came again, I shot ptarmigan, black grouse, and hares; one day I shot an eagle. Still, high sky, cool nights, many clear notes and piercing sounds in forest and field. Great and peaceful, the world rested ....

I have heard nothing further from Mr. Mack concerning the two auks I shot, I said to the doctor.

You may thank Edvarda for that, he replied. I know it; I heard that she opposed it.

I do not thank her, I said ....

Indian summer, Indian summer. The paths lay like belts through the yellowing forest, a new star appeared each day, the moon could be glimpsed like a shadow, a shadow of gold dipped in silver ....

God help you, you are married, Eva?

Did you not know?

No, I did not know.

Silently, she clasped my hand.

God help you, child, what are we to do now?

Whatever you wish. Perhaps you are not leaving yet; I will be happy as long as you are here.

No, Eva.

Yes, yes, only as long as you are here!

She looks forsaken and keeps clasping my hand.

No, Eva, go! Never again!

And nights pass and days come. It is already the third day since this conversation. Eva walks along the road carrying a load. How much firewood this child has carried home from the forest this summer! Put down your load, Eva, and let me see whether your eyes are still as blue.

Her eyes were red.

No, smile again, Eva! I resist you no longer, I am yours, I am yours ....

Evening. Eva sings; I hear her song, and a heat passes through me.

You are singing tonight, Eva?

Yes, I am happy.

And because she is shorter than I am, she jumps up a little to put her arms around my neck.

But Eva, you have torn your hands? Dear God, if only you had not torn them!

It does not matter.

Her face shines so wondrously.

Eva, have you spoken with Mr. Mack?

Once.

What did he say, and what did you say?

He has become very harsh toward us; he makes my husband work night and day on the wharf, and he sets me to all kinds of work as well. He has ordered me to do men’s work.

Why does he do that?

Eva looks down.

Why does he do that, Eva?

Because I love you.

But how can he know that?

I have told him.

Pause.

God grant that he were not so harsh toward you, Eva!

But it does not matter. Nothing matters now.

And her voice sounded in the forest exactly like a little trembling song.

And the leaves turn yellower still, it is drawing toward autumn, a few more stars have appeared in the sky, and from now on the moon looks like a shadow of silver dipped in gold. There was no cold, nothing, only a cool stillness and a streaming life in the forest. Every tree stood thinking. The berries were ripe.

Then came the twenty-second of August and the three iron nights.

XXVI

The first iron night.

At nine o’clock the sun goes down. A dim darkness settles over the earth, a couple of stars can be seen; two hours later, a gleam of the moon can be seen. I wander into the forest with my gun and my dog, I make a fire, and the light from my fire shines in among the pine trunks. There is no frost.

The first iron night, I say. And a bewilderingly intense joy at the time and the place strangely shakes me through and through ....

A toast, you human beings and animals and birds, to the solitary night in forests, in forests! A toast to the darkness and God’s murmuring among the trees, to the sweet, simple harmony of silence against my ears, to green leaves and yellow leaves! A toast to the sound of life that I hear, a snuffling muzzle against the grass, a dog sniffing over the ground! A resounding toast to the wildcat that lies with its throat to the ground, taking aim and preparing to spring upon a sparrow in the dark, in the dark! A toast to the merciful stillness on earth, to the stars and to the half-moon, yes, to them and to it! .

I rise and listen. No one has heard me. I sit down again.

Thanks for the solitary night, for the mountains, for the soughing of the darkness and the sea; it soughs through my heart! Thanks for my life, for my breath, for the grace of being alive tonight; for that I give thanks from my heart! Listen in the east and listen in the west, no, listen! It is the eternal God! This stillness that murmurs against my ear is the blood of all Nature seething, God weaving through the world and me. I see a shining strand of spiderweb in the light of my fire, I hear a boat being rowed in the harbor, a northern light glides upward across the sky in the north. Oh, by my immortal soul, I also give much thanks because it is I who am sitting here!

Silence. A pinecone falls dully to the ground. A pinecone fell! I think. The moon is high, the fire flickers on the half-burned brands and is about to go out. And late in the night I walk home.

The second iron night, the same stillness and the mild weather.

My soul broods. I walk mechanically over to a tree, pull my cap low over my forehead, and lean with my back against this tree, my hands clasped behind my neck. I stare and think; the flame from my fire dazzles my eyes, and I do not feel it. I stand in this senseless posture for quite some time and look at the fire; my legs are the first to fail and grow tired, and quite stiff-legged I sit down. Only now do I think about what I have done. Why stare at the fire for so long?

Aesop raises his head and listens; he hears footsteps, and Eva appears among the trees.

I am deeply pensive and sorrowful tonight, I say.

Johannes looked bewilderedly at the man, at his gate, wondering whether he should go in through it or remain standing there, then at the man again, at his long coat, his hat; he smiled in confusion and pain, like someone in distress.

The old tutor continued threateningly:

Another example; can you deny it? Nor did she get the man she was to have, her beloved since childhood, a young, splendid lieutenant. He went hunting one evening, a shot struck him squarely in the forehead and split his head in two. There he lay, a victim of the little caprice God wished to indulge in with him. Victoria, his bride, began to waste away; a worm ate at her, riddled her heart like a sieve; we, her friends, saw it. Then, a few days ago, she went to a gathering at the home of a family named Seier; incidentally, she told me that you too were to have been there, but did not come. In short, at this gathering she exerts herself beyond her strength; memories of her beloved come storming in upon her and make her lively out of defiance; she dances, dances all evening, dances like a mad person. Then she collapses, the floor turns red beneath her; they lift her up, carry her out, drive her home. She did not last long.

The tutor stepped close to Johannes and said harshly:

Victoria is dead.

Just like a blind man, Johannes began to fend the words off with his hands.

Dead? When did she die? Oh, so Victoria is dead?

She is dead, the tutor replied. She died this morning, this very forenoon. He thrust his hand into his pocket and drew out a thick letter. And she entrusted this letter to me to deliver to you. Here it is. After my death, she said. She is dead. I am delivering the letter to you. My mission is ended.

And without a greeting, without saying anything more, the tutor turned around and drifted slowly down the street and disappeared.

Johannes remained standing with the letter in his hand. Victoria was dead. Again and again he spoke her name aloud, and his voice was numb, almost hardened. He looked down at the letter and recognized the handwriting; there were capital and lowercase letters, the lines were straight, and she who had written them was dead!

Then he went in through his gate, up the stairs, found the right key to insert into the door lock, and opened it. His room was cold and dark. He sat down by the window and read Victoria’s letter in the last remnant of daylight.

Dear Johannes! she wrote. When you read this letter, I shall be dead! Everything is so strange to me now; I am no longer ashamed before you, and I am writing to you again, as though there were nothing to prevent it. Before, while I was still fully alive, I would rather have suffered night and day than written to you again; but now my soul has begun to leave my body, and I no longer think that way. Strangers have seen me bleed, the doctor has examined me and seen that I have only a remnant of one lung left; what more have I to be bashful about?

I have lain here in bed thinking over the last words I said to you. It was in the woods that evening. At the time I did not think they would be my last words, for then I would have said farewell to you at once and thanked you. Now I shall never see you again, so now I regret that I did not throw myself down before you and kiss your shoes and the ground you walked on, and show you how inexpressibly I have loved you. I have lain here, both yesterday and today, wishing that I were not too ill to make my way home again and go into the woods and find the place where we sat when you held both my hands; for then I could lie down there and see whether I could find some trace of you and kiss all the heather around it. But I cannot come home now unless perhaps I get a little better, as Mama believes.

Dear Johannes! It is strange to think that I have done nothing but come to earth and love you, and now say farewell to life. You may believe that it is strange to lie here and wait for the day and the hour. Step by step I am moving away from life and the people in the street and the clatter of carriages; I suppose I shall never see spring again either, and these houses and the streets and the trees in the park will remain after me. Today I was allowed to sit up in bed and look out of the window for a little while. Down on the corner there were two people who met; they greeted each other and took each other’s hands and laughed at what they said; but then it was so strange to me that I, who lay watching this, was to die. I found myself thinking: those two down there do not know that I am lying here waiting for my hour; but if they knew it, they would surely still greet each other and speak to each other just as they do now. Last night, when it was dark, I thought it was to be my final moment; my heart began to stand still, and it was as though I could already hear eternity rushing toward me from far away. But the next moment I returned from far away and began to breathe again. It was an utterly indescribable feeling. But Mama thinks that perhaps it was only the river and the waterfall back home that I remembered.

Good God, if only you knew how I have loved you, Johannes. I have not been able to show you; so much has placed itself in my way, first and foremost my own nature. Papa too was so cruel to himself, and I am his daughter. But now, when I am going to die and everything is too late, I write to you once more and tell you so. I ask myself why I do it, since it is of no consequence to you, especially when I shall not even be alive anymore; but I wanted so much to be close to you until the end, so that at least I would not feel more forsaken than before. When you read this, it is as though I can see your shoulders and hands and see all your movements with the letter as you hold it before you and read it. Then we are not so far apart, I think. I cannot send for you; I have no right to do so. Mama wanted to send for you as early as two days ago, but I preferred to write. I would also prefer you to remember me as I once was, when I had not yet been ill. I remember that you .... (Here some words have been omitted) .... my eyes and eyebrows; but they too are no longer as they were. For that reason as well, I did not want you to come. And I also want to ask you not to see me in my coffin. I am probably much as I was when I lived, only somewhat paler, and I am lying in a yellow dress; but even so, you would regret it if you came and saw me.

Now I have written on this letter many times today, and still I have not managed to tell you one thousandth of what I wanted to say. It is so terrible for me to die; I do not want to; I still hope so fervently in God that perhaps I might get a little better, if only until spring. Then the days are bright and there are leaves on the trees. If I were to recover now, I would certainly never be cruel to you again, Johannes. How I have wept and thought about it! Oh, I would go out and pat all the paving stones and stop and thank every stair I passed, and be good to everyone. It would not matter how badly I suffered, if only I were allowed to live. I would never complain about anything again; no, I would smile at whoever attacked and struck me, and thank and praise God if I were allowed to live. My life is so unlived; I have done nothing for anyone, and this failed life is to end now. If you knew how unwilling I am to die, then perhaps you would do something, do everything in your power. You probably cannot do anything; but I thought that if you and the whole world prayed for me and would not let me go, then God would grant me life. Oh, how grateful I would be then, and never again do harm to anyone, but smile at everything ordained for me, if only I were allowed to live.

I once did you a wrong, Johannes; I wanted to make amends for it, put it right. I really have a surprise that I think ... that is to say, that I hope you will be pleased by. I cannot say any more. But this time I will ask you to be present.

If it can give you any pleasure, then I shall come.

Will you?

Yes, I thank you for your kindness.

When he had gone down into the forest, he turned around and looked back. She had seated herself; the basket stood beside her. He did not go home, but continued wandering along the road and back again. A thousand thoughts struggled within him. A surprise? She had said it just now, only a moment ago; her voice had trembled. A hot and nervous joy arose within him, made his heart pound violently, and he felt himself lifted from the road on which he walked. And was it merely chance that she was dressed in yellow today as well? He had looked at her hand where the ring had once been—she wore no ring.

An hour passed. The vapors of the forest and the fields surrounded him, entered into his breath, into his heart. He sat down, lay back with his hands clasped beneath his neck, and listened for a time to the cuckoo’s piping on the other side of the inlet. Passionate birdsong quivered in the air around him.

So he had experienced it again! When she came up to him in the quarry in her yellow dress and with her blood-red hat, she looked like a wandering butterfly stepping from stone to stone and stopping before him. I did not want to disturb you, she had said, smiling; her smile was red, her whole face lit up, she scattered stars. Some fine blue veins had appeared on her neck, and the few freckles beneath her eyes gave her a warm color. She was in her twentieth summer.

A surprise? What was her intention? Did she perhaps mean to show him his books, to lay out those two or three volumes and please him by telling him that she had bought them all and cut open their pages? There you are, one tiny little token of attention and gentle consolation! Do not disdain my modest contribution!

He rose abruptly and remained standing. Victoria came back; her basket was empty.

You found no flowers? he asked absently.

No, I gave it up. Nor did I look; I merely sat there.

He said:

While I remember it: you must not go about thinking that you have done me any wrong. You have nothing to make amends for with any kind of gentle consolation.

No? she answered, taken aback. She thought further about it, looked at him, and pondered. No? I thought that at the time
«+++ I did not want you to go on bearing a grudge against me all the time for what happened.

No, I bear you no grudge.
