There is a great deal of philosophy, believe me, in my apparent lightness; life must be taken that way.”—“You may be right,” Oswald replied; “but it is by nature, and not through reflection, that you are so, and that is why your way of being suits no one but you.”

The Count d’Erfeuil heard Corinne's name mentioned in the ballroom, and he went in to find out what was happening. Lord Nelvil advanced as far as the door and saw the Prince of Amalfi, a Neapolitan of the handsomest appearance, asking Corinne to dance the Tarantella with him, a dance from Naples, full of grace and originality. Corinne's friends were asking her to do so as well. She accepted without waiting to be pressed, which greatly surprised the Count d’Erfeuil, accustomed as he was to the refusals with which it is customary to preface consent. But in Italy, that kind of affectation is unknown, and everyone quite simply believes that one pleases society more by readily doing what it desires. Corinne would have invented this natural manner had it not already been customary. The dress she had put on for the ball was elegant and light; her hair was gathered into a silk net in the Italian fashion, and her eyes expressed a keen pleasure that made her more alluring than ever. Oswald was troubled by it; he struggled against himself; he was indignant at being captivated by charms of which he ought to complain, since, far from thinking of pleasing him, it was almost in order to escape his sway that Corinne showed herself so ravishing. But who can resist the seductions of grace? Even were it disdainful, it would still be all-powerful; and that was assuredly not Corinne's disposition. She caught sight of Lord Nelvil, blushed, and, as she looked at him, her eyes held an enchanting tenderness.

A profound silence reigned around Oswald and Corinne; the guides themselves had withdrawn into the distance; and since near the crater there is neither animal, nor insect, nor plant, nothing could be heard there but the hissing of the agitated flame. Nevertheless, a sound from the city reached even that place; it was the sound of bells making themselves heard through the air: perhaps they were celebrating a death; perhaps they were announcing a birth; no matter, they caused a gentle emotion in the travelers. “Dear Oswald,” said Corinne, “let us leave this desert, let us go back down toward the living; my soul is ill at ease here. All other mountains, in bringing us nearer to heaven, seem to raise us above earthly life; but here I feel only turmoil and terror: I seem to see nature treated like a criminal, and condemned, like a depraved being, no longer to feel the beneficent breath of its Creator. This is surely not the abode of the good; let us go away.”

Heavy rain was falling while Corinne and Lord Nelvil went back down toward the plain. At every moment their torches were on the verge of going out. The lazzaroni accompanied them, uttering continual cries that might inspire terror in anyone who did not know that this was their habitual manner. But these men are sometimes stirred by a surplus of life with which they do not know what to do, because they combine idleness and violence in equal measure. Their physiognomy, more strongly marked than their character, seems to indicate a kind of vivacity in which the mind and the heart play no part. Oswald, anxious lest the rain should harm Corinne, lest their light should fail them, and, finally, lest she should be exposed to some danger, concerned himself with her alone; and this very tender concern gradually restored his soul from the state into which the confidence he had made to her had thrown it. They found their carriage again at the foot of the mountain; they did not stop at the ruins of Herculaneum, which have, as it were, been buried anew so as not to demolish the town of Portici, which is built over that ancient city. They arrived in Naples toward midnight, and Corinne, on taking leave of Lord Nelvil, promised to give him the story of her life the following morning.


CHAPTER II

Indeed, the next morning Corinne resolved to impose upon herself the effort she had promised; and although the more intimate knowledge she had gained of Oswald’s character redoubled her anxiety, she left her room carrying what she had written, trembling, yet resolved to give it to him. She entered the sitting room of the inn where they were both staying. Oswald was there and had just received letters from England. One of those letters lay on the mantelpiece, and the handwriting struck Corinne so forcibly that, in indescribable agitation, she asked him from whom it came. “It is from Lady Edgermond,” Oswald replied.—“You correspond with her?” Corinne interrupted.—“Lord Edgermond was my father’s friend,” Oswald resumed; “and since chance has led me to speak to you of her, I shall not conceal from you that my father had thought that it might one day be suitable for me to marry Lucile Edgermond, her daughter.”—“Great God!” cried Corinne, and she sank onto a chair, almost fainting.

“Whence comes this cruel emotion?” said Lord Nelvil; “what can you fear from me, Corinne, when I love you with idolatrous devotion? If my father, as he was dying, had asked me to marry Lucile, I should doubtless not consider myself free, and I should have kept away from your irresistible charm; but he did no more than advise me to make this marriage, writing to me himself that he could not judge Lucile, since she was still only a child. I myself have seen her only once; she was scarcely twelve years old then. I entered into no engagement with her mother before leaving; nevertheless, the uncertainty and turmoil you may have noticed in my conduct arose solely from this wish of my father’s: before knowing you, I wished to be able to fulfill it, fleeting though it was, as a kind of expiation toward him, as a way of prolonging, after his death, the sway of his will over my resolutions; but you have triumphed over that feeling, you have triumphed over my entire self, and I need only obtain forgiveness for whatever in my conduct must have seemed to you weakness or irresolution. Corinne, one never entirely recovers from the grief I have suffered: it withers hope, it gives one a painful and distressing sense of timidity; destiny has done me so much harm that even when it seems to offer me the greatest good, I still mistrust it. But, dear friend, these anxieties have vanished; I am yours forever, yours! I tell myself that if my father had known you, it is you whom he would have chosen as the companion of my life; it is you…”—“Stop,” cried Corinne, bursting into tears, “I implore you, do not speak to me in this way.

—“Why should you oppose,” said Lord Nelvil, “the pleasure I find in uniting you in my thoughts with the memory of my father, in thus blending in my heart all that is dear and sacred to me?”—“You cannot do so,” Corinne interrupted; “Oswald, I know too well that you cannot.”—“Good heavens!” Lord Nelvil resumed, “what have you to tell me? Give me that document which is to contain the story of your life, give it to me.”—“You shall have it,” Corinne resumed; “but I implore you, grant me eight more days, only eight days. What I learned this morning obliges me to add a few more details.”—“What!” said Oswald, “what connection do you have…?”—“Do not require me to answer you now,” Corinne interrupted; “soon you will know everything, and it may be the end, the terrible end of my happiness; but before that moment, I want us to see the happy countryside of Naples together, while our feelings are still gentle, while our souls are still open to this enchanting nature: I want, in some way, in these beautiful places, to consecrate the most solemn period of my life; you must preserve one last memory of me, as I was, as I would always have been, if my heart had guarded itself against loving you.

—“Ah! Corinne,” said Oswald, “what do you mean to announce to me with these ominous words? It cannot be that you have anything to tell me that would cool either my tenderness or my admiration. Why, then, prolong for another eight days this anxiety, this mystery, which seems to raise a barrier between us?”—“Dear Oswald, I wish it so,” Corinne replied; “forgive me this last exercise of power; soon you alone will decide for us both; I shall await my fate from your lips without murmuring, if it is cruel; for on this earth I have neither feelings nor ties that condemn me to survive your love.” As she finished these words, she went out, gently pushing back with her hand Oswald, who wished to follow her.

“When you gave me back my freedom, I was angry with you; I returned to the opinions that ordinary men are bound to form upon seeing you. I told myself that so superior a person would easily do without me. Corinne, I have torn your heart apart, I know it; but I believed I was sacrificing no one but myself. I thought that I was more inconsolable than you, and that you would forget me, while I would always mourn your loss. At last circumstances ensnared me; and I do not wish to deny that Lucile is worthy both of the feelings she inspires in me and of far better still. But as soon as I learned of your journey to England and of the misfortune I had caused you, there was nothing left in my life but continual anguish. For four years I sought death amid the war, certain that, upon learning that I was no more, you would find me justified. No doubt you have to set against me a life of regrets and sorrows, a profound fidelity to an ungrateful man who did not deserve it; but consider that men’s destinies are entangled in a thousand different ties that disturb the constancy of the heart. Yet if it is true that I have been able neither to find nor to give happiness; if it is true that I have lived alone since I left you, that I never speak from the depths of my heart, that the mother of my child, she whom for so many reasons I ought to love, remains a stranger to my secrets as to my thoughts; if it is true that a habitual state of sadness has plunged me back into that illness from which your care, Corinne, once rescued me; if I have come to Italy, not to be cured—you do not believe that I love life—but to bid you farewell, will you refuse to see me once, only once? I wish it because I believe I would do you good. It is not my own suffering that determines me. What does it matter if I am utterly miserable! What does it matter if a dreadful weight lies forever upon my heart, if I leave here without having spoken to you, without having obtained your forgiveness! I must be unhappy, and I certainly shall be. But it seems to me that your heart would be relieved if you could think of me as your friend, if you had seen how dear you are to me, if you had felt it in those looks, in that tone of Oswald’s, of that guilty man whose fate has changed more than his heart.

“I respect my bonds, I love your sister; but the human heart, strange and inconsistent as it is, can contain both that tenderness and the tenderness I feel for you. I have nothing to tell you about myself that can be written; everything that must be explained condemns me. Nevertheless, if you saw me prostrate myself before you, you would perceive, through all my wrongs and all my duties, what you still are to me, and this conversation would leave you with a gentle feeling. Alas! the health of both of us is very frail, and I do not believe that heaven destines us for a long life. May whichever of us precedes the other feel mourned, feel loved by the friend left behind in this world! The innocent alone should have this joy; but let it be granted to the guilty as well!

“Corinne, sublime friend, you who read hearts, divine what I cannot say; understand me as you used to understand me. Let me see you; allow my pale lips to press your weakened hands: ah! I alone did not cause this harm; it is the same feeling that has consumed us both: it is destiny that has struck two beings who loved each other; but it has condemned one of them to guilt, and that one, Corinne, is perhaps not the less to be pitied!”


CORINNE’S REPLY.

“If all that were required for me to see you was to forgive you, I would not have refused for an instant. I do not know why I feel no resentment against you, although the pain you have caused me makes me shudder with terror. I must still love you, to feel no stirring of hatred; religion alone would not suffice to disarm me in this way. I have had moments when my reason was impaired; others—and they were the sweetest—when I thought I would die before the end of the day from the constriction of heart that oppressed me; and still others when I doubted everything, even virtue: you were its image for me here below, and I no longer had any guide for my thoughts or for my feelings when the same blow struck both admiration and love within me.

“What would have become of me without heavenly aid? There was nothing in this world that was not poisoned by the memory of you. One refuge alone remained to me in the depths of my soul. God received me there. My physical strength is declining; but it is not so with the ardor that sustains me. To make oneself worthy of immortality is, I delight in believing, the sole purpose of existence. Happiness, suffering, everything is a means to that end; and you were chosen to uproot my life from the earth: I was bound to it by too strong a tie.

“When I learned of your arrival in Italy, when I saw your handwriting again, when I knew that you were there, on the other side of the river, I felt a terrifying tumult in my soul. I had to remind myself constantly that my sister was your wife in order to combat what I felt. I do not conceal it from you: seeing you again seemed to me a happiness, an indefinable emotion, which my newly intoxicated heart preferred to centuries of calm; but Providence did not abandon me in this peril. Are you not another woman’s husband? What, then, could I have to say to you? Was I even permitted to die in your arms? And what would have remained for my conscience if I made no sacrifice, if I still desired one final day, one final hour! Now I shall perhaps appear before God with greater confidence, since I was able to renounce seeing you. This great resolution will bring peace to my soul. Happiness, such as I felt it when you loved me, is not in harmony with our nature: it agitates, it troubles, it is so ready to pass away! But habitual prayer, religious contemplation whose aim is to perfect oneself, to be guided in all things by the sense of duty, is a gentle state, and I cannot know what havoc the mere sound of your voice might wreak in this life of repose that I believe I have attained. You have caused me much pain by telling me that your health was impaired. Ah! I am not the one who tends it, but I am still the one who suffers with you. May God bless your days, my lord; be happy, but be so through piety. A secret communion with the Divinity seems to place within ourselves the being who confides and the voice that answers him; it makes two friends of a single soul. Would you still seek what is called happiness? Ah! will you find anything better than my tenderness? Do you know that in the deserts of the New World I would have blessed my fate if you had allowed me to follow you there? Do you know that I would have served you like a slave? Do you know that I would have prostrated myself before you as before a messenger from heaven, if you had loved me faithfully? Well then, what have you made of so much love? What have you made of this affection unique in the world? A misfortune as unique as itself. Aspire no longer, then, to happiness; do not offend me by believing that you may still attain it. Pray as I do, pray, and may our thoughts meet in heaven.”

One embarks on the Brenta to reach Venice, and on both sides of the canal one sees the palaces of the Venetians, large and somewhat dilapidated, like Italian magnificence. They are decorated in a bizarre manner that in no way recalls the taste of antiquity. Venetian architecture bears the mark of commerce with the East; it is a mixture of Moorish and Gothic that arouses curiosity without pleasing the imagination. The poplar, that tree as regular as architecture, borders the canal almost everywhere. The sky is a vivid blue that contrasts with the brilliant green of the countryside; this green is sustained by the excessive abundance of water: sky and earth are thus of two colors so sharply divided that this nature itself seems to have been arranged with a kind of artifice, and one does not find there the mysterious vagueness that makes one love southern Italy. The sight of Venice is more astonishing than pleasing; at first one thinks one sees a submerged city, and reflection is necessary in order to admire the genius of the mortals who conquered this dwelling-place from the waters. Naples is built in an amphitheater by the sea, but since Venice stands on entirely flat ground, the bell towers resemble the mast of a ship that remains motionless amid the waves. A feeling of sadness takes possession of the imagination upon entering Venice. One takes leave of vegetation; one does not see even a fly in this abode; all animals are banished from it, and man alone is there to struggle against the sea.

The silence is profound in this city, whose streets are canals, and the sound of oars is the sole interruption of that silence. It is not the countryside, since one does not see a tree there; it is not the city, since one does not hear the slightest movement there; it is not even a ship, since one does not advance: it is a dwelling-place that a storm turns into a prison, for there are times when one can leave neither the city nor one’s home. One finds common people in Venice who have never gone from one district to another, who have not seen Saint Mark’s Square, and for whom the sight of a horse or a tree would be a genuine marvel. Those black gondolas gliding over the canals resemble coffins or cradles, man’s last and first dwelling-places. In the evening one sees passing only the reflection of the lanterns that light the gondolas, for then their black color prevents one from distinguishing them. One would say they were shadows gliding over the water, guided by a little star. In this abode everything is mystery: the government, customs, and love. No doubt there are many delights for the heart and the reason when one succeeds in penetrating all these secrets; but foreigners must find the first impression singularly sad.

Corinne, who believed in premonitions, and whose shaken imagination made omens of everything, said to Lord Nelvil: “Whence comes the profound melancholy by which I feel myself seized upon entering this city? Is it not proof that some great misfortune will befall me here?” As she spoke these words, she heard three cannon shots fired from one of the islands in the lagoon. Corinne started at the sound and asked her gondoliers what had caused it. “It is a nun taking the veil,” they replied, “in one of those convents in the middle of the sea. The custom among us is that, at the moment when women pronounce their religious vows, they cast behind them a bouquet of flowers that they carried during the ceremony. It is the sign of renunciation of the world; and the cannon shots you have just heard announced that moment just as we entered Venice.” These words made Corinne shudder. Oswald felt her cold hands in his, and a deathly pallor covered her face. “Dear friend,” he said to her, “how can the simplest chance make so strong an impression upon you?”—“No,” said Corinne, “it is not simple; believe me, the flowers of life have been cast behind me forever.”—“When I love you more than ever,” Oswald interrupted, “when my whole soul is yours...” —“Those thunderbolts of war,” Corinne continued, “whose sound elsewhere announces either victory or death, are here consecrated to celebrating the obscure sacrifice of a young girl. It is an innocent use of those terrible weapons that convulse the world. It is a solemn warning that a resigned woman gives to women who are still struggling against fate.”

CHAPTER VIII

The power of the government of Venice, during the last years of its existence, consisted almost entirely in the sway of habit and imagination. It had been terrible; it had become very mild. It had been courageous; it had become timid. Hatred against it was easily reawakened because it had once been formidable; it was easily overthrown because it was so no longer. It was an aristocracy that greatly sought popular favor, but sought it in the manner of despotism, by entertaining the people but not by enlightening them. Nevertheless, being entertained is a fairly agreeable condition for a people, especially in countries where a taste for the things of the imagination is developed by the climate and the fine arts even in the lowest class of society. The people were not given the coarse pleasures that brutalize them, but music, paintings, improvisers, festivals; and the government tended its subjects there as a sultan does his seraglio. It asked them only, as it would women, not to concern themselves with politics and not to judge those in authority; but, at that price, it promised them much entertainment and even a fair amount of splendor; for the spoils of Constantinople that enrich the churches, the standards of Cyprus and Candia that fly over the public square, and the horses of Corinth delight the people’s eyes, and the winged lion of Saint Mark appears to them the emblem of their glory.

Since the system of government forbade its subjects to occupy themselves with political affairs, and the situation of the city made agriculture, walking, and hunting impossible, the Venetians had no interest left but amusement; and so this city was a city of pleasures. The Venetian dialect is gentle and light as a pleasant breath: one cannot conceive how those who resisted the League of Cambrai spoke so supple a language. This dialect is charming when devoted to grace or jesting; but when it is used for graver subjects, when one hears verses about death in those sounds so delicate and almost childlike, one would think that the event, sung in this way, was merely a poetic fiction.

Men in Venice generally have even more wit than in the rest of Italy, because the government, such as it was, more often afforded them opportunities to think; but their imagination is not naturally as ardent as in southern Italy; and most of the women, though very amiable, have acquired, through the habit of living in society, a language of “sentimentality” that, while in no way constraining freedom of morals, merely introduces affectation into gallantry. The great merit of Italian women, despite all their faults, is that they have no vanity: this merit is somewhat lost in Venice, where there is more society than in any other city in Italy, for vanity develops above all through society. One is applauded there so quickly and so often that every calculation is instantaneous, and, where success is concerned, “one does not extend time even a minute’s credit.” Nevertheless, one still found in Venice many traces of the originality and ease of Italian manners. The greatest ladies received all their visitors in the cafés of Saint Mark’s Square, and this bizarre mingling prevented drawing rooms from becoming too seriously an arena for the pretensions of self-love.

“He had spoken with singular vehemence, and I had remained confounded by what he had told me. The approach of danger, without unsettling him, nevertheless roused him still further, and I could not guess whether it was the truth escaping him, or a lie he was fabricating to avenge himself. Nevertheless, in this uncertainty, I was very careful to spare his life; he was less skilful than I in physical exercises, and ten times I could have plunged my sword into his heart, but I contented myself with wounding him in the arm and disarming him. He appeared touched by my conduct; and, as I led him home, I reminded him of the conversation that had preceded the moment when we fought. He then said to me: ‘I am sorry to have betrayed my cousin’s confidence; peril is like wine, it goes to one’s head; but after all, I console myself for it, because you would not have been happy with Madame d’Arbigny; she is too cunning for you. As for me, that is a matter of indifference; for although I find her charming and her wit pleases me exceedingly, she will never make me do anything to my detriment, and we shall serve each other very well in all things, because marriage will make our interests common. But you, who are romantic, would have been her dupe. You had only to kill me, and I owe you my life; I therefore cannot refuse you the letters I had promised you after my death. Read them, leave for England, and do not be too tormented by Madame d’Arbigny’s sorrows. She will weep, because she loves you; but she will console herself, because she is a woman reasonable enough not to wish to be unhappy, and above all not to wish to appear so. In three months she will be Madame de Maltigues.’ Everything he told me was true: the letters he showed me proved it. I remained convinced that Madame d’Arbigny was not in the condition she had pretended, blushing, to confess to me in order to compel me to marry her, and that in this respect she had shamefully deceived me. She undoubtedly loved me, since she said so in her letters to Monsieur de Maltigues himself; but she flattered him with such art, left him so much hope, and, in order to please him, displayed a character so different from the one she had always shown me, that it was impossible for me to doubt that she was keeping him well disposed toward her, with the intention of marrying him if our marriage did not take place. Such was the woman, Corinne, who has forever cost me the peace of my heart and of my conscience!

“I wrote to her as I departed, and I never saw her again; and, as Monsieur de Maltigues had predicted, I have since learned that she married him. But at that time I was far from foreseeing the misfortune that awaited me: I believed I would obtain my father’s forgiveness; I was sure that, when I told him how greatly I had been deceived, he would love me more, since he would know me to be more deserving of pity. After a journey of nearly a month, day and night, across Germany, I arrived in England full of confidence in the inexhaustible goodness of a father. Corinne, as I disembarked, a newspaper announced to me that my father was no more! Twenty months have passed since that moment, and it is still before me like a spectre pursuing me. The letters that formed these words, *Lord Nelvil has just died*, those letters were blazing; the fire of the volcano there before us is less terrifying than they were. Nor is that all; I learned that he had died profoundly distressed by my stay in France, fearing that I might renounce a military career, that I might marry a woman of whom he thought little, and that, by settling in a country at war with my own, I might utterly ruin my reputation in England! Who knows whether these painful thoughts did not shorten his days! Corinne, Corinne, am I not a murderer, am I not? Tell me.—No, she cried, no, you are only unfortunate; it was goodness, it was generosity that carried you away. I respect you as much as I love you: judge yourself within my heart; take it for your conscience. Grief is leading you astray: believe her who cherishes you. Ah! love, such as I feel it, is no illusion: it is because you are the best and most sensitive of men that I admire and adore you.—Corinne, Oswald said to her, I do not deserve this homage; yet it may be that I am not so guilty. My father forgave me before he died; in a final piece of writing from him, addressed to me, I found gentle words. A letter of mine had reached him and had justified me to some degree; but the harm was done, and the grief that came from me had torn his heart.

“When I returned to his castle, when his old servants surrounded me, I rejected their consolations, I accused myself before them; I went and prostrated myself upon his grave; there I swore, as though there still remained time for me to make amends, that I would never marry without my father’s consent. Alas! what was I promising to him who was no more! What meaning did those words of my delirium then have! I must at least regard them as an undertaking to do nothing that he would have disapproved of during his life. Corinne, dear friend, why do these words trouble you? My father may have required of me the sacrifice of a dissembling woman, who owed the liking she inspired in me to nothing but her artfulness; but the truest, most natural, and most generous person, she for whom I have felt my first love, the love that purifies the soul instead of leading it astray—why should celestial beings wish to separate me from her?

“When I entered my father’s room, I saw his cloak, his armchair, his sword, which were still there, as in former days; still there: but his place was empty, and my cries called to him in vain! This manuscript, this collection of his thoughts, is all that answers me: you already know some passages from it, Oswald said as he gave it to Corinne; I always carry it with me. Read what he wrote about the duty of children toward their parents; read, Corinne: your gentle voice may perhaps make these words familiar to me. Corinne obeyed Oswald’s voice and read what follows:

  “Ah! how little it takes to make a father and mother advanced in years distrust themselves! They readily believe that they are superfluous upon the earth. Of what use could they believe themselves to you, who no longer ask them for counsel? You live wholly in the present moment; you are confined within it by a ruling passion, and everything that does not relate to that moment appears ancient and obsolete to you. Finally, you are so entirely contained within your own person, in both heart and mind, that, believing yourselves alone to form a historical point, the eternal resemblances between times and men escape your attention; and the authority of experience seems to you a fiction, or a vain guarantee intended solely to sustain the credit of the aged and the final enjoyments of their self-esteem. How mistaken you are! The world, that vast theatre, does not change its actors; it is always man who appears upon its stage; but man does not renew himself, he diversifies himself; and as all his forms depend upon a few principal passions whose circle has long since been traversed, it is rare that, in the small combinations of private life, experience, that science of the past, is not the fruitful source of the most useful lessons.”

“I am delighted to see you,” he said to Lord Nelvil; “I am going to Naples in a fortnight; shall I find you there? I should like to, for I have little time left to stay in Italy, because my regiment must soon embark.—Your regiment?” repeated Lord Nelvil; and he blushed, as though he had forgotten that he had a year’s leave, his regiment not being due to be deployed before then; but he blushed at the thought that Corinne might perhaps make him forget even his duty. “Your own regiment,” continued Mr. Edgermond, “will not be called into active service anytime soon; so recover your health here without anxiety. Before leaving, I saw my young cousin, in whom you take an interest; she is more charming than ever; and in a year, when you return, I do not doubt that she will be the most beautiful woman in England.” Lord Nelvil said nothing, and Mr. Edgermond likewise remained silent on his side. They exchanged a few more words in a rather laconic, though kindly, manner; and Mr. Edgermond was about to leave when he retraced his steps and said: “By the way, my lord, you can do me a favor: I have been told that you know the famous Corinne; and although in general I do not like making new acquaintances, I am altogether curious about that one.—I shall ask Corinne’s permission to take you to her house, since you wish it,” Oswald replied. “Please arrange,” Mr. Edgermond resumed, “for me to see her on a day when she will improvise, sing, or dance in our presence.—Corinne,” said Lord Nelvil, “does not display her talents to strangers in that fashion; she is a woman who is your equal and mine in every respect.—Forgive my mistake,” Mr. Edgermond resumed; “since she is known by no name other than Corinne, and at the age of twenty-six lives entirely alone, without any member of her family, I thought that she lived by her talents and willingly seized the opportunity to make them known.—Her fortune,” Lord Nelvil replied sharply, “is entirely independent, and her soul more so still.” Mr. Edgermond immediately ceased speaking about Corinne, and regretted having mentioned her when he saw that this subject affected Oswald. The English are the men in the world who show the greatest discretion and consideration in everything pertaining to true affections.

Mr. Edgermond went away. Lord Nelvil, left alone, could not keep himself from exclaiming in his emotion: “I must marry Corinne; I must be her protector, so that henceforth no one may fail to recognize her for what she is. I shall give her the little that I can give—a rank, a name—while she will shower upon me all the felicities that she alone can bestow on earth.” In this frame of mind he hastened to Corinne’s house, and never had he entered it with a sweeter feeling of hope and love; but, through a natural impulse of timidity, he began the conversation by reassuring himself with insignificant words, among which was the request to bring Mr. Edgermond to her house. At this name, Corinne became visibly troubled, and in an emotional voice refused what Oswald desired. He was singularly astonished by this, and said to her: “I thought that in a house where you receive so many people, the title of my friend would not be grounds for exclusion.—Do not take offense, my lord,” Corinne replied; “believe me, I must have very powerful reasons for not consenting to what you desire.—And will you tell me these reasons?” Oswald resumed. “Impossible!” cried Corinne, “impossible!—So then…” said Oswald; and the violence of his emotion cutting him short, he made to leave. Corinne then, in tears, said to him in English: “In the name of God, if you do not wish to break my heart, do not go.”

These words, this accent, deeply stirred Oswald’s soul, and he sat down again at some distance from Corinne, his head resting against an alabaster vase that illuminated her room; then suddenly he said to her: “Cruel woman! You see that I love you, you see that twenty times a day I am ready to offer you both my hand and my life, and you will not tell me who you are! Tell me, Corinne, tell me,” he repeated, holding out his hand to her with the most touching expression of feeling. “Oswald,” cried Corinne, “Oswald, you do not know the harm you are doing me. If I were mad enough to tell you everything, if I were, you would no longer love me.—Great God!” he replied, “what, then, do you have to reveal?—Nothing that makes me unworthy of you; but chance events, but differences between our tastes, our opinions, which once existed, which would no longer exist. Do not require me to make myself known to you; one day perhaps, one day, if you love me enough, if… Ah! I do not know what I am saying,” continued Corinne; “you will know everything, but do not abandon me before hearing me out. Promise me, in the name of your father who dwells in heaven.—Do not utter that name!” cried Lord Nelvil; “do you know whether he unites us or separates us? Do you believe that he would have consented to our union? If you believe it, attest it to me; I shall no longer be troubled, torn apart. One day I shall tell you what my sorrowful life has been; but now see what state I am in, what state you are putting me in.”—And indeed, his brow was covered with a cold sweat, his face was pale, and his lips trembled as he barely articulated these last words. Corinne sat down beside him; and, holding his hands in hers, gently brought him back to himself. “My dear Oswald,” she said to him, “ask Mr. Edgermond whether he has ever been in Northumberland, or at least whether it is only within the last five years that he has been there; only in that case may you bring him here.” Oswald stared fixedly at Corinne at these words; she lowered her eyes and said nothing. Lord Nelvil replied to her: “I shall do as you command me.” And he left.

Back at home, he exhausted himself in conjectures about Corinne’s secrets; it seemed evident to him that she had spent a great deal of time in England, and that her name and family must be known there; but what motive made her hide them, and why had she left England, if she had been settled there? These various questions agitated Oswald’s heart extremely; he was convinced that nothing bad could be discovered in Corinne’s life, but he feared a combination of circumstances that might make her appear guilty in the eyes of others; and what he dreaded most for her was England’s disapproval. He felt strong against that of any other country; but the memory of his father was so intimately joined in his thoughts with his native land that these two feelings heightened one another. Oswald learned from Mr. Edgermond that he had been in Northumberland for the first time the preceding year, and promised to take him to Corinne’s house that very evening. He arrived first to warn her of the notions Mr. Edgermond had formed about her, and asked her to make him feel, through cold and reserved manners, how greatly he had been mistaken.

Of all that he had said, a single word had struck Oswald to the heart: it was the memory of his mother and of the deep attachment his father had had for her. He had lost her when he was only fourteen years old, but he recalled with profound respect both her virtues and the timid and reserved character of those virtues. “Madman that I am!” he exclaimed when he was alone. “I want to know what sort of wife my father intended for me: and do I not know, since I can summon up the image of my mother, whom he loved so much? What more, then, do I want? And why deceive myself by pretending not to know what he would think now if I could still consult him?” Yet it was dreadful for Oswald to return to Corinne’s home, after what had happened the day before, without saying anything to her that would confirm the feelings he had shown her. His agitation and his distress became so intense that they brought back an attack from which he believed himself cured: the healed blood vessel in his chest reopened. While his frightened servants called for help from every quarter, he secretly wished that the end of his life might put an end to his sorrows. “If only I could die,” he said to himself, “after seeing Corinne again, after she had called me her Romeo!” And tears escaped from his eyes: they were the first that any grief other than his father’s death had wrung from him.

He wrote to Corinne of the attack that was keeping him at home, and a few melancholy words concluded his letter. Corinne had begun that very day with very deceptive presentiments: she delighted in the impression she had made on Oswald; and, believing herself loved, she was happy, for apart from that she did not know very clearly what she desired. A thousand circumstances caused the idea of marrying Lord Nelvil to be mingled for her with much fear; and as she was a person more passionate than provident, ruled by the present but little concerned with the future, that day which was to cost her so much suffering had dawned for her as the purest and most serene day of her life.

On receiving Oswald’s note, a cruel agitation took possession of her soul: she believed him to be in great danger and set out at once on foot, crossing the Corso at the hour when the entire city promenades there, and entering Oswald’s house in the sight of almost all Roman society. She had not given herself time to reflect; and she had hastened there so quickly that, upon arriving in Oswald’s room, she could no longer breathe or utter a single word. Lord Nelvil understood all that she had just risked in order to see him; and, exaggerating to himself the consequences of this action, which in England would have entirely ruined a woman’s reputation, and all the more so that of an unmarried woman, he felt himself overcome by generosity, love, and gratitude; and, rising, weak though he was, he clasped Corinne to his heart and exclaimed: “Dear friend, no, I will not abandon you, when your feeling for me compromises you! when I must make amends...” Corinne understood his thought; and, interrupting him at once as she gently freed herself from his arms, she said to him, after inquiring about his condition, which had improved: “You are mistaken, my lord; in coming to see you, I am doing nothing that most women in Rome would not have done in my place. I learned that you were ill; you are a stranger here, you know no one here but me; it is for me to care for you. Established conventions are highly respectable when one need sacrifice only oneself to them; but must they not yield to the true and profound feelings aroused by a friend’s danger or suffering? What, then, would a woman’s fate be if those same social conventions, while permitting her to love, forbade only the irresistible impulse that sends one flying to the aid of the person one loves? But, I repeat, my lord, do not fear that by coming here I have compromised myself. By virtue of my age and my talents, I have in Rome the freedom of a married woman. I do not conceal from my friends that I have come to your home; I do not know whether they blame me for loving you, but surely they will not blame me for being devoted to you, when I love you.”

On hearing these words, so natural and so sincere, Oswald experienced a confused mixture of different impressions; he was touched by the delicacy of Corinne’s reply, but he was almost vexed that what he had first thought was not true; he would have wished her to have committed for his sake a great fault in the eyes of society, so that this very fault, making it his duty to marry her, might put an end to his uncertainties. He thought resentfully of that freedom of Italian manners, which prolonged his anxiety by leaving him much happiness without imposing any bond upon him. He would have liked honor to command him to do what he desired. These painful thoughts once again caused him dangerous attacks. Corinne, in the most dreadful anxiety, knew how to lavish upon him care full of gentleness and charm.

Toward evening, Oswald seemed to have greater difficulty breathing; and Corinne, kneeling beside his bed, supported his head in her arms, although she herself was far more deeply moved than he. He often looked at her with an impression of happiness through his suffering. “Corinne,” he said to her in a low voice, “read to me from this collection, in which my father’s thoughts are written, his reflections on death. Do not think,” he said, seeing Corinne’s terror, “that I believe myself threatened by it; but I am never ill without rereading his consolations, which I seem still to hear from his own lips; and besides, dear friend, in this way I want to let you know what sort of man my father was; you will better understand both my grief and his hold over me, and all that I want to confide to you one day.” Corinne took the collection, from which Oswald never parted, and in a trembling voice she read several pages from it:

  “You who are righteous, beloved of the Lord, you will speak of death without fear, for it will be for you only a change of dwelling; and the one you leave is perhaps the least of all. O innumerable worlds, which to our eyes fill the infinity of space! unknown communities of God’s creatures, communities of his children, scattered across the firmament and arrayed beneath its vaults! May our praises join with yours: we know nothing of your condition; we know nothing of your first, your second, your last share in the bounties of the Supreme Being; but in speaking of death and life, of time past and time to come, we reach, we touch upon the interests of all intelligent and sentient beings, regardless of the places and distances that separate them. Families of peoples, families of nations, assemblages of worlds, you say with us: Glory to the master of the heavens, to the king of nature, to the God of the universe! Glory and homage to him who can, at his will, transform barrenness into abundance, shadow into reality, and death itself into eternal life!

  “Ah! Without doubt, the end of the righteous man is the death to be desired; but few among us, few among our forebears, have witnessed it. Where is that man who would present himself without fear before the gaze of the Eternal? Where is that man who has loved God without distraction, who has served him from his youth, and who, upon reaching an advanced age, finds in his memories no cause for anxiety? Where is that man who is moral in all his actions, without ever thinking of praise or of the rewards of public opinion? Where is that man so rare among men, that being so worthy of serving as a model for us all? Where is he? Where is he? Ah! If he exists among us, let our reverence surround him; and ask—you will do well—ask to be present at his death as at the most beautiful of spectacles: only arm yourself with courage, so that you may follow him attentively upon the bed of terror from which he will never rise. He foresees it, he is certain of it, and serenity reigns in his gaze, and his brow seems surrounded by a heavenly aureole: he says with the Apostle: ‘I know in whom I have believed’; and this confidence, as his strength dies away, still animates his features. He already beholds his new homeland; but, without forgetting the one he is about to leave, he belongs to his Creator and his God, without casting far from him the feelings that have charmed his life.”

While Corinne was thus explaining her paintings to Lord Nelvil, she had stopped several times, hoping that he would speak to her; but his wounded soul betrayed itself in no words: only, whenever she expressed a tender idea, he sighed and turned his head away, so that she might not see how easily moved he was in his present state of mind. Corinne, oppressed by this silence, sat down, covering her face with her hands. Lord Nelvil paced briskly about the room for some time; then he approached Corinne and was on the point of voicing his grievance and yielding to what he felt; but a movement of pride, utterly invincible in his character, repressed his tenderness, and he returned to the paintings as though waiting for Corinne to finish showing them to him. She hoped for much from the effect of the last of all; and, making an effort in her turn to appear calm, she rose and said: “Milord, I still have three landscapes left to show you; two allude to certain interesting ideas: I do not much like rural scenes, which are insipid in painting, like idylls, when they make no allusion to Fable or history. What is best, it seems to me, in this genre, is the manner of Salvator Rosa, who represents, as you see in this painting, a rock, torrents, and trees, without a single living being, without even the flight of a bird to recall the idea of life. The absence of man amid nature arouses profound reflections. What would this earth be, thus forsaken? A work without a purpose, and yet a work still so beautiful, whose mysterious impression would be addressed only to the Divinity!

“Finally, here are the two paintings in which, in my opinion, history and poetry are happily united with landscape. One represents the moment when Cincinnatus is invited by the consuls to leave his plough in order to command the Roman armies. It is all the luxuriance of the South that you will see in this landscape: its abundant vegetation, its burning sky, that cheerful air of all nature which is found even in the countenance of the plants. And this other painting, which contrasts with it, is the son of Cairbar asleep upon his father’s tomb. For three days and three nights he has been awaiting the bard who is to pay honors to the memory of the dead. That bard can be seen in the distance, descending the mountain; the father’s shade hovers over the clouds; the countryside is covered with frost; the trees, though stripped bare, are shaken by the winds, and their dead branches and withered leaves still follow the direction of the storm.”

Until then Oswald had continued to feel resentment over what had happened in the garden; but at the sight of this painting, his father’s tomb and the mountains of Scotland rose again in his thoughts, and his eyes filled with tears. Corinne took her harp and, before this painting, began to sing the Scottish ballads whose simple notes seem to accompany the sound of the wind moaning through the valleys. She sang the farewells of a warrior leaving his homeland and his beloved, and Corinne pronounced that word never (_no more_), one of the most harmonious and most affecting in the English language, with the most touching expression. Oswald did not resist the emotion that oppressed him, and both yielded freely to their tears. “Ah!” cried Lord Nelvil, “does that homeland, which is mine, say nothing to thy heart? Wouldst thou follow me into those retreats peopled by my memories? Wouldst thou be the worthy companion of my life, as thou art its charm and enchantment?”—“I believe so,” replied Corinne, “I believe so, since I love you.”—“In the name of love and pity, conceal nothing more from me,” said Oswald.—“You wish it,” Corinne interrupted; “I consent. My promise is given; I attach only one condition to it: that you will not ask me to fulfill it before the approaching time of our religious solemnities. At the moment when I am about to decide my fate, is the support of heaven not more necessary to me than ever?”—“Be assured,” cried Lord Nelvil, “if that fate depends upon me, Corinne, it is no longer in doubt.”—“You believe so,” she resumed; “I do not have the same confidence; but at last, I implore you, show my weakness the indulgence I desire.” Oswald sighed, neither granting nor refusing the requested delay. “Let us leave now,” said Corinne, “and return to the city. How could I conceal anything from you in this solitude! And if what I have to tell you were to estrange you from me, must it be so soon... Let us leave. Oswald, you will return here, whatever may happen; my ashes will rest here.” Oswald, moved and troubled, obeyed Corinne. He returned with her, and during the journey they scarcely spoke to each other. From time to time they looked at one another with an affection that said everything; but nevertheless a feeling of melancholy reigned in the depths of their souls when they reached the heart of Rome.




BOOK NINE

THE POPULAR FESTIVAL AND MUSIC


CHAPTER ONE

It was the day of the noisiest festival of the year, at the end of Carnival, when the Roman people are seized by something like a fever of joy, a frenzy of amusement of which no example is to be found elsewhere. The whole city puts on disguises; scarcely any spectators without masks remain at the windows to watch those who have them; and this gaiety begins on the appointed day at the appointed time, without the public or private events of the year almost ever preventing anyone from enjoying themselves at that season.

It is there that one may judge the full extent of the common people’s imagination. Italian is full of charms, even in their mouths. Alfieri used to say that in Florence he went to the public market to learn good Italian. Rome has the same advantage; and these two cities are perhaps the only ones in the world where the people speak so well that intellectual amusement may be encountered at every street corner.

The kind of gaiety that shines in the authors of harlequinades and comic opera is very commonly found even among uneducated men. During those Carnival days, when exaggeration and caricature are permitted, the most comical scenes take place between the masked revelers.

Often a grotesque gravity contrasts with the Italians’ vivacity, and one would say that their bizarre garments inspire in them a dignity not natural to them. At other times, in the disguises they devise, they display so singular a knowledge of mythology that one would think the ancient fables still popular in Rome. More often, they mock the various ranks of society with a wit full of force and originality. The nation appears a thousand times more distinguished in its games than in its history. The Italian language lends itself to every shade of gaiety with an ease that requires only a slight inflection of the voice, a slightly different ending, to heighten or diminish, ennoble or travesty the meaning of words. It has grace above all in the mouths of children. The innocence of that age and the language’s natural mischievousness form a very piquant contrast. Finally, one might say that it is a language that goes by itself, expresses things without anyone’s intervention, and almost always appears to have more wit than the person who speaks it.

The aspect of the countryside around Rome has something singularly remarkable about it: it is doubtless a desert, for there are neither trees nor dwellings; but the earth is covered with wild plants, ceaselessly renewed by the vigor of vegetation. These parasitic plants creep into the tombs, adorn the ruins, and seem to be there only to honor the dead. One would say that proud nature has rejected all the works of man since the Cincinnatuses ceased to guide the plow that furrowed her bosom; she produces plants at random, without allowing the living to make use of her wealth. These uncultivated plains must displease farmers, administrators, all those who speculate upon the land and wish to exploit it for the needs of man; but dreamy souls, occupied with death as much as with life, delight in contemplating this countryside of Rome, upon which the present time has left no trace; this earth that cherishes its dead and lovingly covers them with useless flowers, with useless plants that trail along the ground and never rise high enough to separate themselves from the ashes they appear to caress.

Oswald agreed that in this place one must experience more tranquillity than anywhere else. The soul does not suffer there as much from the images that grief presents to it; it seems that one still shares with those who are no more the charms of this air, this sun, and this greenery. Corinne observed the impression lord Nelvil was receiving from it, and conceived some hope from it. She did not flatter herself that she could console Oswald; she would not even have wished to efface from his heart the rightful regrets he owed to the loss of his father; but in the very feeling of regret there is something sweet and harmonious that one must endeavor to make known to those who have so far experienced only its bitterness: that is the only good one can do them.

“Let us stop here,” said Corinne, “facing this tomb, the only one that still remains almost intact: it is not the tomb of a famous Roman; it is that of Cecilia Metella, a young woman for whom her father had this monument erected.—Happy,” said Oswald, “happy are the children who die in their father’s arms, and who receive death in the bosom that gave them life! Death itself then loses its sting for them.”

“Yes,” said Corinne with emotion, “happy are those who are not orphans! Look, weapons have been carved upon this tomb, although it is that of a woman; but the daughters of heroes may have the trophies of their father upon their graves: the union of innocence and valor is a beautiful one. There is an elegy by Propertius that portrays, better than any other work of antiquity, this dignity of women among the Romans, more imposing and purer than even the splendor they enjoyed during the age of chivalry. Cornelia, who died in her youth, addresses the most touching farewells and consolations to her husband, and in it one feels, in almost every word, all that is worthy of respect and sacred in family bonds. The noble pride of a spotless life is portrayed in that majestic poetry of the Latins, in that poetry noble and austere like the masters of the world. ‘Yes,’ says Cornelia, ‘no stain has sullied my life: from the nuptial rite to the funeral pyre, I lived pure between the two torches.’ What an admirable expression!” exclaimed Corinne; “what a sublime image! And how enviable is the fate of the woman who can thus preserve the most perfect unity in her destiny, and carry but one memory to the grave! That is enough for a lifetime.”

As she finished these words, Corinne’s eyes filled with tears; a cruel feeling, a painful suspicion, took possession of Oswald’s heart. “Corinne,” he exclaimed, “Corinne! Has your delicate soul nothing with which to reproach itself? If I could dispose of myself, if I could offer myself to you, would I have no rivals in the past? Could I be proud of my choice? Would cruel jealousy not disturb my happiness?—I am free, and I love you as I have never loved before,” Corinne replied; “what more do you want? Must I be condemned to confess to you that, before I knew you, my imagination may have deceived me concerning the interest someone inspired in me! And is there not in the heart of man a divine pity for the errors that feeling, or at least the illusion of feeling, might have caused one to commit!” As she finished these words, a modest blush covered her face. Oswald shuddered, but remained silent. There was in Corinne’s gaze an expression of repentance and timidity that did not permit him to judge her harshly, and it seemed to him that a ray from heaven descended upon her to absolve her. He took her hand, pressed it against his heart, and knelt before her, uttering nothing, promising nothing, but contemplating her with a look of love that left room for every hope.

“Believe me,” Corinne said to lord Nelvil, “let us make no plans for the years to come: the happiest moments of life are still those that a benevolent chance grants us. Is it here, then, is it in the midst of tombs, that we should place so much faith in the future?—No,” exclaimed lord Nelvil, “no, I do not believe in the future that would separate us! These four days of absence have taught me all too well that I now exist only through you.” Corinne made no reply to these tender words, but devoutly gathered them into her heart; she was always afraid that, by prolonging the conversation about the feeling that alone occupied her, she might incite Oswald to declare his plans before longer habit had made separation impossible for him. Often, indeed, she deliberately directed his attention toward external objects; like that sultana of the Arabian tales who sought, through a thousand different stories, to captivate the interest of the man she loved, so as to postpone the decision of her fate until the moment when the charms of her mind won the victory.


CHAPTER II

Not far from the Appian Way, Oswald and Corinne had themselves shown the columbaria, where slaves are reunited with their masters, where one sees within a single tomb all those who lived under the protection of a single man or woman. Livia’s women, for example, those who, once devoted to the care of her beauty, struggled on her behalf against time and contested with the years for some of her charms, are placed beside her in small urns. One seems to see a collection of obscure dead surrounding an illustrious dead person, no less silent than the retinue. A short distance from there, one perceives a field where Vestal Virgins unfaithful to their vows were buried alive: a singular example of fanaticism in a naturally tolerant religion.

“I shall not take you to the catacombs,” Corinne said to lord Nelvil, “although, by a singular chance, they lie beneath this Appian Way, so that tombs rest upon tombs. But this refuge of persecuted Christians has something so dark and so terrible about it that I cannot bring myself to return there: it is not that touching melancholy one breathes in open places; it is the dungeon beside the sepulcher, the torment of life alongside the horrors of death. Doubtless one feels filled with admiration for the men who, through the sole power of enthusiasm, were able to endure this subterranean life and thus separated themselves entirely from the sun and from nature; but the soul is so ill at ease in that place that no good can result from it. Man is a part of creation; he must find his moral harmony in the whole of the universe, in the customary order of destiny; and certain violent and dreadful exceptions may astonish the mind, but they so greatly frighten the imagination that the soul’s habitual disposition cannot benefit from them. Let us go instead,” Corinne continued, “to see the Pyramid of Cestius: the Protestants who die here are all buried around that pyramid, and it is a gentle, tolerant, and liberal refuge.—Yes,” Oswald replied, “it is there that several of my compatriots have found their final resting place. Let us go there; perhaps that, at least, is how I shall never leave you.” Corinne shuddered at these words, and her hand trembled as she leaned upon lord Nelvil’s arm. “I am better,” he resumed, “much better since I have known you.” And Corinne’s face was once more illuminated by that sweet and tender joy, its habitual expression.

“Do speak more quietly,” she said to him with a frightened look. Julien was trying to recall the phrases from an odd volume of the New Heloise that he had found at Vergy. His memory served him well; for ten minutes he had been reciting the New Heloise to a delighted Mademoiselle Amanda, and he was pleased with his own daring, when suddenly the beautiful woman from Franche-Comté assumed an icy expression. One of her lovers had appeared in the doorway of the café.

He approached the counter, whistling and rolling his shoulders as he walked; he looked at Julien. At once, Julien’s imagination, always prone to extremes, was filled with nothing but thoughts of a duel. He turned very pale, pushed his cup away, assumed a self-assured expression, and looked at his rival very intently. As this rival lowered his head while casually pouring himself a glass of brandy at the counter, Amanda ordered Julien with a glance to lower his eyes. He obeyed and, for two minutes, remained motionless in his place, pale, resolute, and thinking only of what was about to happen; he was truly admirable at that moment. The rival had been astonished by Julien’s eyes; after swallowing his glass of brandy in a single draught, he said a word to Amanda, thrust both hands into the side pockets of his heavy frock coat, and approached a billiard table, breathing noisily and looking at Julien. Julien rose, beside himself with anger; but he did not know how to go about being insolent. He put down his little bundle and, with the most swaggering air he could manage, walked toward the billiard table.

In vain prudence told him: But with a duel as soon as you arrive in Besançon, your ecclesiastical career is ruined.

What does it matter? It shall not be said that I let an insolent fellow escape me.

Amanda saw his courage; it made a charming contrast with the artlessness of his manners; in an instant, she preferred him to the tall young man in the frock coat. She rose and, while pretending to be following with her eyes someone passing in the street, quickly came and placed herself between him and the billiard table:

“Take care not to look askance at that gentleman; he is my brother-in-law.”

“What do I care? He looked at me.”

“Do you want to make me unhappy? Of course he looked at you; perhaps he is even going to come and speak to you. I told him that you are a relative of my mother’s and that you have come from Genlis. He is from Franche-Comté and has never gone beyond Dole on the road to Burgundy; so say whatever you like, and do not be afraid.”

Julien was still hesitating; she quickly added, her barmaid’s imagination supplying her with lies in abundance:

“Of course he looked at you, but that was when he was asking me who you were; he is a man who is boorish with everyone; he did not mean to insult you.”

Julien’s eyes followed the supposed brother-in-law; he saw him buy a number in the pool being played at the farther of the two billiard tables. Julien heard his loud voice cry in a threatening tone, “I’ll take the next game.” He moved swiftly behind Mademoiselle Amanda and took a step toward the billiard table. Amanda seized him by the arm:

“Come and pay me first,” she said to him.

That is fair, thought Julien; she is afraid I may leave without paying.

Amanda was as agitated as he was and very red; she gave him his change as slowly as she could, all the while repeating to him in a low voice:

“Leave the café this instant, or I shall not love you anymore; and yet I do love you dearly.”

Julien did leave, but slowly. Is it not my duty, he kept asking himself, to go and stare in my turn, breathing noisily, at that coarse fellow? This uncertainty kept him for an hour on the boulevard in front of the café; he watched to see whether his man would come out. He did not appear, and Julien went away.

He had been in Besançon for only a few hours, and already he had acquired something to reproach himself for. The old surgeon-major had once given him, despite his gout, a few fencing lessons; that was all the skill Julien could call upon in the service of his anger. But this difficulty would have been nothing if he had known how to become angry in any way other than by delivering a slap in the face; and if it came to blows, his rival, an enormous man, would have beaten him and then left him there.

For a poor devil like me, Julien told himself, without protectors and without money, there will not be much difference between a seminary and a prison; I must leave my civilian clothes at some inn, where I shall put my black coat back on. If I ever manage to get out of the seminary for a few hours, I shall be perfectly able, in my civilian clothes, to see Mademoiselle Amanda again. The reasoning was sound; but as Julien passed each inn, he did not dare enter any of them.

At last, as he passed the Hôtel des Ambassadeurs again, his anxious eyes met those of a stout woman, still fairly young, ruddy-faced, with a happy and cheerful air. He approached her and told her his story.

“Certainly, my pretty little abbé,” the landlady of the Ambassadeurs said to him, “I shall keep your civilian clothes for you and shall even have them dusted often. At this time of year, it is not good to leave a cloth coat untouched.” She took a key and led him herself to a room, instructing him to write down a list of what he was leaving.

“Good Lord! How handsome you look like that, Monsieur l’Abbé Sorel,” the stout woman said to him when he came down to the kitchen. “I am going to have a good dinner served to you, and,” she added in a low voice, “it will cost you only twenty sous instead of the fifty everyone else pays; for you must take good care of your little purse.”

“I have ten louis,” Julien replied with a certain pride.

“Oh! Good Lord!” the kindly landlady answered in alarm. “Do not speak so loudly; there are many bad characters in Besançon. You will have it stolen from you in no time. Above all, never go into the cafés; they are full of bad characters.”

“Really!” said Julien, to whom these words gave food for thought.

“Never go anywhere but my establishment; I shall have coffee made for you. Remember that you will always find a friend here and a good dinner for twenty sous—that is speaking plainly, I hope. Go and sit down at the table; I am going to serve you myself.”

“I could not eat,” Julien said to her. “I am too agitated; I am going to enter the seminary when I leave your establishment.”

The good woman did not let him leave until she had filled his pockets with provisions. At last Julien set off toward the terrible place; standing in her doorway, the landlady pointed out the way to him.

Observing M. de Croisenois with the stern eye of misfortune, Julien noticed the extreme influence that this amiable and good young man attributed to hidden causes. It went so far that he would grow sad and ill-tempered if he saw a somewhat important event ascribed to a simple and entirely natural cause. There is the beginning of madness in that, Julien said to himself. This character bears a striking resemblance to that of the Emperor Alexander, as Prince Korasoff described him to me. During the first year of his stay in Paris, poor Julien, fresh from the seminary and dazzled by the graces, so new to him, of all these amiable young men, had been able only to admire them. Their true character was only just beginning to take shape before his eyes.

I am playing an unworthy role here, he suddenly thought. The matter was to leave his little straw chair in a manner that was not too awkward. He tried to invent something; he was asking something new of an imagination wholly occupied elsewhere. He had to resort to memory; his own was, it must be confessed, rather poor in resources of this kind. The poor boy still had very little experience, and so he was perfectly awkward, in a way noticed by everyone, when he rose to leave the drawing room. His unhappiness was all too evident in his whole manner of being. For three quarters of an hour he had been playing the role of an importunate subordinate from whom no one takes the trouble to conceal what one thinks of him.

The critical observations he had just made about his rivals nevertheless kept him from taking his unhappiness too tragically; to sustain his pride, he had the memory of what had happened the day before yesterday. Whatever their thousand advantages over me, he thought as he entered the garden alone, Mathilde has been for none of them what, twice in my life, she deigned to be for me.

His wisdom went no further. He understood nothing whatever of the character of the singular person whom chance had just made the absolute mistress of all his happiness.

The next day, he confined himself to exhausting both himself and his horse. In the evening he made no further attempt to approach the blue sofa, to which Mathilde remained faithful. He noticed that Count Norbert did not even deign to look at him when they encountered each other in the house. He must be doing himself a strange violence, he thought, he who is naturally so polite.

For Julien, sleep would have been happiness. In spite of his physical fatigue, memories that were all too alluring were beginning to invade his entire imagination. He did not have the insight to see that, by means of his long rides in the woods around Paris, acting only upon himself and not at all upon Mathilde’s heart or mind, he was leaving the disposition of his fate to chance.

It seemed to him that one thing would bring infinite relief to his pain: it would be to speak to Mathilde. But what, however, would he dare say to her?

That was what he was pondering deeply one morning at seven o’clock when, all at once, he saw her enter the library.

“I know, monsieur, that you wish to speak to me.”

“Great God! Who told you?”

“I know it; what does it matter to you? If you have no honor, you can ruin me, or at least attempt to; but this danger, which I do not believe to be real, will certainly not prevent me from being sincere. I no longer love you, monsieur; my foolish imagination deceived me...”

At this terrible blow, distraught with love and unhappiness, Julien tried to justify himself. Nothing could have been more absurd. Does one justify oneself for being displeasing? But reason no longer had any sway over his actions. A blind instinct drove him to postpone the decision of his fate. It seemed to him that as long as he was speaking, everything was not over. Mathilde did not listen to his words; the sound of them irritated her, and she could not conceive that he had the audacity to interrupt her.

The remorse of virtue and that of pride made her equally unhappy that morning. She was in some sense crushed by the dreadful idea of having given rights over her to a little abbé, the son of a peasant. It is almost, she told herself in moments when she exaggerated her unhappiness, as though I had to reproach myself for a weakness for one of the footmen.

In bold and proud characters, there is only one step from anger against oneself to rage against others; in such a case, transports of fury are a keen pleasure.

In an instant, Mademoiselle de La Mole reached the point of overwhelming Julien with the most extreme marks of contempt. She had infinite wit, and that wit triumphed in the art of torturing people’s self-esteem and inflicting cruel wounds upon it.

For the first time in his life, Julien found himself subjected to the action of a superior mind animated against him by the most violent hatred. Far from thinking in the least of defending himself at that moment, his changeable imagination came to despise itself. Hearing himself overwhelmed by such cruel marks of contempt, calculated with so much wit to destroy every good opinion he might have of himself, it seemed to him that Mathilde was right and that she did not say enough.

As for her, she found a delicious pleasure of pride in thus punishing herself and him for the adoration she had felt a few days earlier.

She had no need to invent and think for the first time of the cruel things she addressed to him with such complacency. She was merely repeating what, for the past week, the advocate of the party opposed to love had been saying in her heart.

Every word increased Julien’s dreadful unhappiness a hundredfold. He tried to flee; Mademoiselle de La Mole held him back by the arm with authority.

“Deign to observe,” he said to her, “that you are speaking very loudly; you will be heard from the next room.”

“What does it matter!” Mademoiselle de La Mole replied proudly. “Who will dare say that I am being heard? I intend to cure your petty self-esteem forever of the notions it may have imagined about me.”

When Julien was able to leave the library, he was so astonished that he felt his unhappiness less. Well! She no longer loves me, he kept repeating to himself, speaking aloud as though to teach himself his position. It seems that she loved me for eight or ten days, and I shall love her all my life.

Can it really be possible? She was nothing, nothing to my heart, only a few days ago!

The pleasures of pride flooded Mathilde’s heart; so she had been able to break with him forever! To triumph so completely over so powerful an inclination would make her perfectly happy. Thus this little monsieur will understand, once and for all, that he has and never will have any power over me. She was so happy that at that moment she truly no longer felt any love.

This woman, the most distinguished in the region, whom for six years he had surrounded with so many attentions, and unfortunately in full view and with the full knowledge of everyone; this proud woman, whose disdain had so often made him blush, had just taken as her lover a little workman disguised as a tutor. And so that nothing might be lacking to the vexation of the director of the poorhouse, Madame de Rênal adored this lover.

“And,” the chambermaid added with a sigh, “Monsieur Julien took no trouble at all to make this conquest; for Madame he did not depart from his customary coldness.”

Élisa had obtained certainty only in the country, but she believed that this intrigue dated from much further back.

“That is no doubt why,” she added spitefully, “he refused at the time to marry me. And I, fool that I was, went to consult Madame de Rênal! went to beg her to speak to the tutor!”

That very evening, Monsieur de Rênal received from town, along with his newspaper, a long anonymous letter informing him in the greatest detail of what was going on in his own house. Julien saw him turn pale as he read this letter, written on bluish paper, and cast malicious glances at him. Throughout the evening, the mayor did not recover from his agitation; in vain did Julien court his favor by asking him for explanations concerning the genealogy of the finest families of Burgundy.




CHAPTER XX

THE ANONYMOUS LETTERS

    Do not give dalliance
    Too much the rein; the strongest oaths are straw
    To the fire i’ the blood.

    TEMPEST.


As they were leaving the drawing room around midnight, Julien had time to say to his beloved:

“Let us not see each other tonight; your husband has suspicions. I would swear that the large letter he was reading with sighs is an anonymous letter.”

Fortunately, Julien locked himself into his room. Madame de Rênal conceived the mad idea that this warning was merely a pretext for not seeing her. She lost her head completely and came to his door at the usual hour. Julien, who heard a noise in the corridor, instantly blew out his lamp. Someone was trying to open his door: was it Madame de Rênal, was it a jealous husband?

Very early the next morning, the cook, who protected Julien, brought him a book on the cover of which he read these words written in Italian: Look at page 130.

Julien shuddered at the imprudence, looked for page one hundred and thirty, and found pinned to it the following letter, written in haste, bathed in tears, and without the slightest regard for spelling. Ordinarily Madame de Rênal spelled very well; he was touched by this detail and partly forgot the appalling imprudence.

Thou wouldst not receive me last night? There are moments when I believe that I have never read to the depths of thy soul. Thy looks frighten me. I am afraid of thee. Great God! can it be that thou hast never loved me? In that case, let my husband discover our love, and let him shut me up in an eternal prison, in the country, far from my children. Perhaps God wills it so. I shall soon die. But thou wilt be a monster.

Dost thou not love me, art thou weary of my follies, of my remorse, impious man? Dost thou wish to ruin me? I give thee an easy means of doing so. Go, show this letter throughout Verrières, or rather show it to Monsieur Valenod alone. Tell him that I love thee; but no, do not utter such blasphemy; tell him that I adore thee, that life began for me only on the day when I saw thee; that in the maddest moments of my youth, I had never even dreamed of the happiness I owe thee; that I have sacrificed my life to thee, that I sacrifice my soul to thee. Thou knowest that I sacrifice far more to thee.

But does that man know anything of sacrifices? Tell him, tell him, to enrage him, that I defy all wicked men, and that there is now only one misfortune in the world for me: to see the only man who keeps me alive change. What happiness it would be for me to lose my life, to offer it in sacrifice, and no longer to fear for my children!

Do not doubt it, dear friend: if there is an anonymous letter, it comes from that odious creature who, for six years, has pursued me with his booming voice, the account of his feats on horseback, his conceit, and the endless enumeration of all his advantages.

Is there an anonymous letter? Wretch, that is what I wished to discuss with thee; but no, thou didst well. Holding thee in my arms, perhaps for the last time ever, I could never have discussed matters coldly, as I do when alone. From this moment on, our happiness will no longer be so easy. Will that be an annoyance to you? Yes, on the days when you have not received some amusing book from Monsieur Fouqué. The sacrifice is made; tomorrow, whether or not there is an anonymous letter, I too shall tell my husband that I have received an anonymous letter and that he must at once build thee a golden bridge, find some honorable pretext, and send thee back to thy parents without delay.
